# Overview



ESM is EvolutionaryScale's open-source framework for protein modeling, built around two complementary model families: **ESM3**, a multimodal generative model that jointly reasons across sequence, structure, and function, and **ESM C**, a representation model that creates rich biological embeddings with dramatically improved efficiency over predecessors. The `esm` Python package (v3.2.4) provides a unified SDK for both local inference and cloud-based API access, enabling everything from rapid prototyping on a single GPU to large-scale batch processing on Forge or AWS SageMaker. Whether you are designing novel proteins from partial prompts or extracting embeddings for downstream prediction tasks, this repository gives you the tools and abstractions to do so through a consistent, typed interface.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L50), [esm/__init__.py](/esm/__init__.py#L1-L2), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L10)

## Two Model Families, One Framework

The ESM ecosystem is organized around two distinct but interoperable model families, each designed for a different primary use case. **ESM3** is a generative masked language model: you provide partial information across any combination of tracks (sequence, structure, secondary structure, SASA, function), and the model iteratively samples masked positions until all tracks are complete. **ESM C** is a representation model: it encodes protein sequences into high-quality embeddings that can be used for downstream tasks like property prediction, variant effect analysis, or similarity search. Both families share the same `ESMProtein` data model and SDK abstractions, so switching between them or composing their outputs requires minimal code changes.

Sources: [esm/models/esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L118-L125), [esm/models/esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L29-L50)

### ESM3: Multimodal Generative Model

ESM3 operates as a **generative masked language model** over discrete token sequences. It jointly reasons across six input tracks — sequence, structure tokens, secondary structure (SS8), solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), function annotations (InterPro), and residue annotations — and can be prompted with any subset of these tracks partially filled. The model's transformer backbone uses geometric attention in its initial layers to condition on 3D structure, enabling SE(3)-invariant reasoning over atomic coordinates. At its largest scale, ESM3 was trained with 1.07×10²⁴ FLOPs on 2.78 billion proteins, and the open-source 1.4B parameter variant (`esm3-sm-open-v1`) is available for local inference.

![ESM3 Diagram](_assets/esm3_diagram.png)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L69-L86), [esm/models/esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L44-L97)

### ESM C: Representation Model

ESM C (Cambrian) is a **sequence-to-embedding** model designed as a drop-in replacement for ESM2, but with major efficiency gains. The 300M parameter ESM C delivers similar performance to ESM2 650M, while the 600M variant rivals ESM2 3B. ESM C uses a standard transformer stack (without geometric attention layers), making it lighter and faster. It exposes `encode()` → `logits()` → `embeddings` as its primary workflow, and supports Flash Attention for further acceleration on GPU. ESM C is available in open-weight variants (300M, 600M) and a larger 6B model via Forge API or SageMaker.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L147-L155), [esm/models/esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L29-L65)

## Model Comparison

| Feature | ESM3 | ESM C |
|---------|------|-------|
| **Primary Purpose** | Controllable protein generation | Protein representation learning |
| **Input Modalities** | Sequence + Structure + SS + SASA + Function + Residue | Sequence only |
| **Output Tracks** | All 6 tracks + embeddings | Sequence logits + embeddings + hidden states |
| **Geometric Attention** | Yes (initial layers) | No |
| **Generation** | Iterative masked sampling | Not supported |
| **Open Weights** | 1.4B (`esm3-sm-open-v1`) | 300M, 600M |
| **Forge API Sizes** | 1.4B, 7B, 98B | 6B |
| **SageMaker** | — | 300M, 600M, 6B |
| **Flash Attention** | — | Yes (auto-detected) |
| **Core API** | `ESM3InferenceClient` | `ESMCInferenceClient` |

| ESM3 Model | Parameters | d_model | Heads | Layers | Release |
|------------|-----------|---------|-------|--------|---------|
| esm3-large-2024-03 | 98B | — | — | — | 2024-03 |
| esm3-medium-2024-08 | 7B | — | — | — | 2024-08 |
| esm3-small-2024-08 (open) | 1.4B | 1536 | 24 | 48 | 2024-08 |

| ESM C Model | Parameters | d_model | Heads | Layers | Release |
|-------------|-----------|---------|-------|--------|---------|
| esmc-6b-2024-12 | 6B | — | — | 80 | 2024-12 |
| esmc-600m-2024-12 | 600M | 1152 | 18 | 36 | 2024-12 |
| esmc-300m-2024-12 | 300M | 960 | 15 | 30 | 2024-12 |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L52-L67), [esm/pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L77-L117), [esm/models/esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L118-L138), [esm/models/esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L29-L50)

## High-Level Architecture

The following diagram shows the major components of ESM and how data flows from raw protein input through tokenization, the transformer core, and output decoding back to a rich `ESMProtein` object. The shaded region represents the model's internal forward pass; everything outside it is the SDK layer that handles encoding, generation orchestration, and decoding.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph SDK["SDK Layer (esm/sdk/)"]
        direction TB
        ESMProtein["ESMProtein<br/>Raw data: sequence, coords,<br/>SS, SASA, function annots"]
        Forge["Forge API Client<br/>(esm/sdk/forge.py)"]
        Local["Local Inference<br/>(ESM3 / ESMC models)"]
        SM["SageMaker Client<br/>(esm/sdk/sagemaker.py)"]
    end

    subgraph Tokenization["Tokenization (esm/tokenization/)"]
        SeqTok["Sequence Tokenizer"]
        StructTok["Structure Tokenizer<br/>+ VQ-VAE Encoder"]
        SSTok["SS8 Tokenizer"]
        SASATok["SASA Tokenizer"]
        FuncTok["Function Tokenizer<br/>(InterPro)"]
        ResTok["Residue Annotation<br/>Tokenizer"]
    end

    subgraph Core["Transformer Core (esm/layers/)"]
        GeomAttn["Geometric Attention<br/>(SE(3) Invariant)"]
        StdAttn["Standard Multi-Head<br/>Attention + SwiGLU FFN"]
        OutHeads["Output Heads<br/>(6 regression heads)"]
    end

    subgraph Decode["Decode (esm/utils/decoding.py)"]
        StructDec["VQ-VAE Structure<br/>Decoder"]
        FuncDec["Function Token<br/>Decoder"]
    end

    ESMProtein -->|"encode()"| Tokenization
    Tokenization -->|"ESMProteinTensor"| Core
    Core -->|"ESMOutput / ESMCOutput"| OutHeads
    OutHeads -->|"decode()"| Decode
    Decode -->|"ESMProtein"| ESMProtein

    Forge -.->|"HTTP API"| Tokenization
    Local -.->|"Direct call"| Tokenization
    SM -.->|"AWS endpoint"| Tokenization
```

> [!TIP]
> The `encode()` → `forward()` → `decode()` pipeline is the fundamental pattern. When you call `model.generate()`, it orchestrates this pipeline multiple times via iterative masked sampling, progressively unmasking tokens until the target track is complete.

Sources: [esm/sdk/api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L200-L260), [esm/models/esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L200-L350), [esm/tokenization/__init__.py](/esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L1-L67), [esm/layers/transformer_stack.py](/esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L1-L50)

## Project Structure

The repository is organized into four main subsystems: the **model implementations**, the **SDK and deployment clients**, the **tokenization pipeline**, and the **utility layers**. Tutorials and cookbook examples live in the top-level `cookbook/` directory.

```
esm/
├── models/              # Model architectures
│   ├── esm3.py          # ESM3 multimodal generative model
│   ├── esmc.py          # ESM C representation model
│   ├── function_decoder.py   # InterPro function token decoder
│   └── vqvae.py         # VQ-VAE structure encoder/decoder
│
├── sdk/                 # Client SDK for inference
│   ├── api.py           # ESMProtein, ESMProteinTensor, client ABCs
│   ├── forge.py         # Forge API remote client
│   ├── sagemaker.py     # AWS SageMaker deployment client
│   └── __init__.py      # esm.sdk.client() factory function
│
├── tokenization/        # Input/output tokenizers
│   ├── sequence_tokenizer.py
│   ├── structure_tokenizer.py
│   ├── ss_tokenizer.py
│   ├── sasa_tokenizer.py
│   ├── function_tokenizer.py
│   └── residue_tokenizer.py
│
├── layers/              # Neural network building blocks
│   ├── attention.py     # Standard multi-head attention
│   ├── geom_attention.py # SE(3) geometric attention
│   ├── blocks.py        # UnifiedTransformerBlock
│   ├── transformer_stack.py  # Transformer stack
│   ├── rotary.py        # Rotary position embeddings
│   └── ffn.py           # SwiGLU feed-forward network
│
├── utils/               # Encoding, decoding, sampling, constants
├── pretrained.py        # Model registry and from_pretrained loaders
└── widgets/             # Jupyter notebook visualization tools

cookbook/
├── tutorials/           # Step-by-step notebook tutorials
├── snippets/            # Minimal code examples for ESM3, ESM C, folding
└── local/               # Local inference examples with raw forward passes
```

Sources: [esm/pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L123-L135), [esm/tokenization/__init__.py](/esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L1-L67), [esm/sdk/__init__.py](/esm/sdk/__init__.py#L1-L37)

## Deployment Options

The `esm` SDK provides three deployment paths, all sharing the same `ESM3InferenceClient` or `ESMCInferenceClient` interface. This means you can swap a local model for a Forge client with a single line change — no other code modifications needed.

| Deployment | How to Instantiate | Best For |
|------------|-------------------|----------|
| **Local** | `ESM3.from_pretrained("esm3-sm-open-v1").to("cuda")` | Rapid prototyping, full model access, offline use |
| **Forge API** | `esm.sdk.client("esm3-medium-2024-08", token=...)` | Largest models (98B, 6B), no GPU required, batch execution |
| **SageMaker** | `ESM3SageMakerClient(endpoint_name=..., model=...)` | Commercial use, dedicated GPU, AWS integration |

> [!TIP]
> Forge and SageMaker clients both support async methods via `async_` prefix (e.g., `async_generate`, `async_encode`) for concurrent workloads. Use the `batch_executor()` context manager for high-throughput Forge jobs.

Sources: [esm/sdk/__init__.py](/esm/sdk/__init__.py#L1-L37), [esm/sdk/forge.py](/esm/sdk/forge.py#L1-L50), [README.md](/README.md#L104-L130)

# Quick Start



Get from zero to your first protein generation in under five minutes. This page walks you through installing the `esm` library, choosing between the two model families, and running your first inference — whether on local hardware or through the cloud API.

## Prerequisites and Installation

The `esm` package requires **Python 3.12** and **PyTorch ≥ 2.2**. Install everything with a single command:

```bash
pip install esm
```

For accelerated attention on NVIDIA GPUs, optionally install Flash Attention:

```bash
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
```

That's it — all core dependencies (transformers, biotite, BioPython, scikit-learn, etc.) are pulled in automatically.

> [!TIP]
> If you're on macOS ARM or Linux x86_64, you can also use the bundled **pixi** environment. Running `pixi install` from the repo root creates an isolated conda-like environment with pinned versions of every dependency, including build tools.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L6-L9), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L21-L45), [README.md](/README.md#L33-L36)

## Choose Your Model Family

ESM ships two distinct model families, each optimized for a different primary task:

| | **ESM3** (Generative) | **ESM C** (Representation) |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Controllable protein *generation* — fold, inverse-fold, design | Protein *representation* — embeddings, logits, hidden states |
| **Input Modalities** | Sequence + Structure + Function (multimodal) | Sequence only |
| **Key Method** | `generate()` with `GenerationConfig` | `logits()` with `LogitsConfig` |
| **Open Models** | `esm3-sm-open-v1` (1.4B params) | `esmc-300m` (300M), `esmc-600m` (600M) |
| **Largest via Forge** | `esm3-large-2024-03` (98B) | `esmc-6b-2024-12` (6B) |
| **Client Class** | `ESM3InferenceClient` | `ESMCInferenceClient` |

**New to ESM?** Start with **ESM3** if you want to design or complete proteins; start with **ESM C** if you need embeddings for downstream ML tasks.

![ESM3 Diagram](https://github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm/blob/main/_assets/esm3_diagram.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L50-L69), [README.md](/README.md#L128-L146), [esm/sdk/api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L435-L520)

## Two Ways to Run: Local vs. Forge API

Every model in the ESM ecosystem can be accessed through one of two interchangeable clients. The API surface is identical — swap one line and the rest of your code stays the same.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Your Code"] --> B{"Local or Cloud?"}
    B -->|Local| C["ESM3.from_pretrained()<br/>or ESMC.from_pretrained()"]
    B -->|Cloud| D["esm.sdk.client()"]
    C --> E["ESM3InferenceClient<br/>/ ESMCInferenceClient"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["encode → generate/logits → decode"]
```

### Local Inference (Open Weights)

Model weights are downloaded from the HuggingFace Hub on first use and cached locally. You'll need a HuggingFace account with a **Read** access token.

```python
from huggingface_hub import login
from esm.models.esm3 import ESM3
from esm.sdk.api import ESM3InferenceClient

login()  # One-time: authenticates with HuggingFace Hub

# Downloads weights, instantiates model on GPU
model: ESM3InferenceClient = ESM3.from_pretrained("esm3-sm-open-v1").to("cuda")
```

The `from_pretrained()` class method handles weight download, device placement, and automatic bfloat16 conversion on CUDA devices.

Sources: [esm/models/esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L247-L261), [esm/pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L93-L110), [README.md](/README.md#L71-L80)

### Forge API (Cloud Inference)

For larger models that don't fit on local hardware, use the **EvolutionaryScale Forge** cloud service. Get an API token at [forge.evolutionaryscale.ai](https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai).

```python
import esm
from esm.sdk.api import ESM3InferenceClient

model: ESM3InferenceClient = esm.sdk.client(
    model="esm3-medium-2024-08",
    token="<your-forge-token>",       # or set ESM_API_KEY env var
)
```

The `esm.sdk.client()` factory returns an `ESM3ForgeInferenceClient` that implements the same `ESM3InferenceClient` interface — so all `.generate()`, `.encode()`, `.decode()`, and `.logits()` calls work identically to local inference. An async variant (`async_generate`, `async_encode`, etc.) is also available for concurrent workloads.

> [!TIP]
> Set the `ESM_API_KEY` environment variable to your Forge token. Then `esm.sdk.client()` picks it up automatically — no need to pass `token=` explicitly. The cookbook snippets use this pattern: `if os.environ.get("ESM_API_KEY", ""): main(client())`.

Sources: [esm/sdk/__init__.py](/esm/sdk/__init__.py#L5-L24), [esm/sdk/forge.py](/esm/sdk/forge.py#L1-L30), [README.md](/README.md#L96-L111), [cookbook/snippets/esm3.py](/cookbook/snippets/esm3.py#L200-L207)

## Your First Generation (ESM3)

ESM3 is a **masked language model** that jointly reasons over sequence, structure, and function. You prompt it with partial (masked) inputs, and it iteratively fills in the blanks. The underscore character `_` represents a masked position.

### Step-by-step: Sequence Completion

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. Create ESMProtein\nwith masked sequence"] --> B["2. Call model.generate()\nwith track='sequence'"]
    B --> C["3. Call model.generate()\nwith track='structure'"]
    C --> D["4. Export to PDB\nwith protein.to_pdb()"]
```

```python
from esm.models.esm3 import ESM3
from esm.sdk.api import ESM3InferenceClient, ESMProtein, GenerationConfig

model: ESM3InferenceClient = ESM3.from_pretrained("esm3-sm-open-v1").to("cuda")

# Step 1: Define a partial Carbonic Anhydrase sequence.
# Underscores are masked positions the model will fill in.
prompt = "___________________________________________________DQATSLRILNNGHAFNVEFDDSQDKAVLKGGPLDGTYRLIQFHFHWGSLDGQGSEHTVDKKKYAAELHLVHWNTKYGDFGKAVQQPDGLAVLGIFLKVGSAKPGLQKVVDVLDSIKTKGKSADFTNFDPRGLLPESLDYWTYPGSLTTPP___________________________________________________________"
protein = ESMProtein(sequence=prompt)

# Step 2: Generate the sequence (iteratively unmasks the sequence track).
protein = model.generate(
    protein,
    GenerationConfig(track="sequence", num_steps=8, temperature=0.7)
)

# Step 3: Predict the 3D structure for the completed sequence.
protein = model.generate(
    protein,
    GenerationConfig(track="structure", num_steps=8)
)

# Step 4: Save the result as a PDB file.
protein.to_pdb("./my_first_generation.pdb")
```

### Understanding `GenerationConfig`

The `GenerationConfig` controls how iterative unmasking proceeds. Here are the parameters you'll touch most often:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `track` | `str` | `""` | Which modality to generate: `"sequence"`, `"structure"`, `"secondary_structure"`, `"sasa"`, or `"function"` |
| `num_steps` | `int` | `20` | Number of iterative unmasking rounds (diminishing returns past ~20) |
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | Sampling temperature; lower = more conservative, higher = more diverse |
| `schedule` | `str` | `"cosine"` | Unmasking schedule: `"cosine"` (fast early, slow late) or `"linear"` |
| `strategy` | `str` | `"random"` | Which tokens to unmask first: `"random"` or `"entropy"` (lowest-entropy first) |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold |

Sources: [esm/sdk/api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L295-L330), [README.md](/README.md#L82-L94), [cookbook/snippets/esm3.py](/cookbook/snippets/esm3.py#L42-L56)

## Your First Embedding (ESM C)

ESM C produces rich numerical representations of protein sequences — useful for property prediction, similarity search, or as input to downstream models.

```python
from esm.models.esmc import ESMC
from esm.sdk.api import ESMProtein, ESMProteinTensor, LogitsConfig

model = ESMC.from_pretrained("esmc-300m").to("cuda")

# Encode a protein sequence into token tensors.
protein = ESMProtein(sequence="MKWVTFISLLFLFSSAYSRGVFRRDAHKSE")
protein_tensor: ESMProteinTensor = model.encode(protein)

# Run forward pass to get logits and embeddings.
output = model.logits(
    protein_tensor,
    LogitsConfig(sequence=True, return_embeddings=True)
)

print(f"Logits shape:   {output.logits.sequence.shape}")
print(f"Embedding shape: {output.embeddings.shape}")
```

The `LogitsConfig` controls what the model returns:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sequence` | `False` | Return per-position sequence logits |
| `return_embeddings` | `False` | Return final-layer embeddings |
| `return_hidden_states` | `False` | Return hidden states from every layer |
| `ith_hidden_layer` | `-1` | Index of a specific hidden layer to extract (`-1` = all layers) |

Sources: [esm/models/esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L83-L105), [esm/models/esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L161-L226), [cookbook/snippets/esmc.py](/cookbook/snippets/esmc.py#L21-L46), [esm/sdk/api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L383-L399)

## The Core Data Flow

Both ESM3 and ESM C share a common **encode → compute → decode** pipeline. Understanding this three-stage flow is the key to using the SDK effectively:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Human-Readable
        EP["ESMProtein\n(strings, coordinates)"]
        DP["ESMProtein\n(strings, coordinates)"]
    end
    subgraph Token-Space
        ET["ESMProteinTensor\n(token IDs)"]
    end
    EP -->|"encode()"| ET
    ET -->|"generate() / logits()"| ET
    ET -->|"decode()"| DP
```

| Stage | Input | Output | Method | When to Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Encode** | `ESMProtein` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `client.encode()` | Converting raw protein data to tokens |
| **Compute** | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProteinTensor` or `LogitsOutput` | `client.generate()` / `client.logits()` | Running model inference |
| **Decode** | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProtein` | `client.decode()` | Converting tokens back to human-readable form |

The high-level `generate()` method chains all three stages automatically when you pass an `ESMProtein` directly — it encodes, iteratively samples, and decodes in one call. Power users can operate at the `ESMProteinTensor` level for fine-grained control over multi-step chain-of-thought generation.

Sources: [esm/sdk/api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L30-L132), [esm/sdk/api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L435-L470), [esm/models/esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L500-L540)

## Common Tasks at a Glance

Here are the five most frequent operations you'll perform, with the minimal code for each:

| Task | Key Code |
|---|---|
| **Sequence completion** | `model.generate(protein, GenerationConfig(track="sequence", num_steps=8))` |
| **Structure prediction** | `model.generate(protein, GenerationConfig(track="structure", num_steps=len(protein)//16))` |
| **Inverse folding** | Set `protein.sequence = None`, then `model.generate(protein, GenerationConfig(track="sequence"))` |
| **Function prediction** | `model.generate(protein, GenerationConfig(track="function", num_steps=len(protein)//16))` |
| **Get embeddings** | `model.logits(model.encode(protein), LogitsConfig(return_embeddings=True)).embeddings` |

Sources: [cookbook/snippets/esm3.py](/cookbook/snippets/esm3.py#L42-L104), [README.md](/README.md#L82-L94)

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| `Model not found in local model registry` | Misspelled model name | Use exact names: `"esm3-sm-open-v1"`, `"esmc-300m"`, `"esmc-600m"` |
| `huggingface_hub.errors.LocalEntryNotFoundError` | Not authenticated with HuggingFace | Run `huggingface_hub.login()` with a Read token |
| CUDA out-of-memory on ESM3 | 1.4B model requires ~6 GB VRAM | Use `.to("cpu")` for inference (slower), or switch to Forge API |
| `flash-attn` import errors | Flash Attention not compiled for your GPU | Install with `pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation`, or pass `use_flash_attn=False` |
| `ESMProteinError` from Forge | Invalid input (e.g., no masked positions) | Ensure the target track has `_` (sequence) or `None` (coordinates) for positions to generate |

Sources: [esm/pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L122-L126), [esm/models/esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L36-L42), [cookbook/snippets/esm3.py](/cookbook/snippets/esm3.py#L175-L198)

# ESMProtein Data Model



The **ESMProtein** class is the central data object you will encounter at every stage of working with ESM3. It is a container that holds multiple *tracks* — parallel representations of a single protein across sequence, structure, and function — and it serves as both the input you provide to the model and the output you receive back. Understanding what each track contains, how they relate to one another, and how to construct and convert an `ESMProtein` is the foundation for everything from simple embedding lookups to full generative design.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L26-L55), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L7-L31)

## The Five Input Tracks

ESM3 reasons jointly over three fundamental biological properties of proteins: sequence, structure, and function. These are decomposed into **five promptable tracks** inside `ESMProtein`. Each track is optional (`None` by default), and you can set any subset of them to be partially or fully unmasked when calling the model — this is the mechanism by which you *prompt* ESM3 for generation or inference.

| Track | Attribute | Python Type | Biological Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sequence** | `sequence` | `str \| None` | 1-letter amino acid sequence (e.g. `"MKTLL..."`) |
| **Coordinates** | `coordinates` | `torch.Tensor \| None` | 3D atom positions in atom37 format, shape `(L, 37, 3)` |
| **Secondary Structure** | `secondary_structure` | `str \| None` | 8-class DSSP label per residue (e.g. `"HHHEEC..."`) |
| **SASA** | `sasa` | `list[float \| None] \| None` | Solvent-accessible surface area per residue |
| **Function Annotations** | `function_annotations` | `list[FunctionAnnotation] \| None` | InterPro-derived keyword annotations over residue ranges |

> [!TIP]
> All five tracks are optional and default to `None`. When a track is `None`, it is treated as fully masked during model input. Setting a track to a string with `_` characters (the mask short-hand) partially masks that track, giving you fine-grained control over which residues the model should predict.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L26-L32), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L23-L31)

### Sequence Track

The `sequence` attribute is the simplest track: a Python string of single-letter amino acid codes following the standard 20-residue alphabet plus special tokens. The underscore `_` character acts as the **mask token** in the raw string representation — any position marked `_` signals the model to predict that residue. The full vocabulary includes standard amino acids (`L, A, G, V, S, E, R, T, I, D, P, K, Q, N, F, Y, M, H, W, C`), non-standard codes (`X, B, U, Z, O`), gap (`.`), chain break (`|`), and mask (`<mask>` which maps from `_`).

```python
# A fully masked protein of length 10 (model will predict everything)
protein = ESMProtein(sequence="__________")

# A partially masked protein (model predicts positions 4-6)
protein = ESMProtein(sequence="MKT___VILP")

# A fully specified sequence (no prediction needed)
protein = ESMProtein(sequence="MKTLIVILPF")
```

Sources: [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L46-L59), [encoding.py](/esm/utils/encoding.py#L22-L45)

### Coordinates Track

The `coordinates` attribute stores 3D atomic positions as a `torch.Tensor` of shape `(L, 37, 3)`, where `L` is the number of residues. The **atom37** representation encodes up to 37 heavy atoms per amino acid (a fixed superset that covers all standard residue types). Atoms not present in a given residue are filled with `NaN` values. The three values along the last dimension are the `(x, y, z)` Cartesian coordinates in Ångströms.

```python
# After loading from PDB, coordinates are populated automatically
protein = ESMProtein.from_pdb("1cm4.pdb", chain_id="A")
print(protein.coordinates.shape)  # torch.Size([L, 37, 3])
```

> [!TIP]
> When initializing an `ESMProtein` with only coordinates (no sequence), the model treats all residues as alanine during PDB conversion. Always pair coordinates with a sequence when you need the correct amino acid identity for downstream analysis or visualization.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L28-L32), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L120-L127)

### Secondary Structure Track

The `secondary_structure` attribute uses the **8-class DSSP classification** (SS8). Each residue is assigned one of eight characters representing its local structural motif:

| SS8 Code | Class | 3-Class Mapping | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `H` | α-helix | H | Standard alpha helix |
| `G` | 3₁₀-helix | H | Short helix (3 residues per turn) |
| `I` | π-helix | H | Wide helix (5 residues per turn) |
| `E` | Extended strand | E | Beta sheet (participating) |
| `B` | Isolated beta-bridge | E | Single beta bridge residue |
| `T` | Turn | C | Hydrogen-bonded turn |
| `S` | Bend | C | Non-helical bend |
| `C` | Coil | E → C | Loop / irregular |

The 8-class labels can be collapsed to a 3-class representation (`H`, `E`, `C`) using the built-in mapping. When you don't have DSSP installed locally, a 3-class approximation can be obtained from `biotite.structure.annotate_sse`.

```python
# SS8 string: one character per residue
protein.secondary_structure = "HHHHHHEEEESSSCCCCTTT"
```

Sources: [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L61-L72), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L215-L245)

### SASA Track

The **Solvent-Accessible Surface Area** (SASA) track quantifies how exposed each residue is to solvent, expressed as a continuous float value per residue. Internally, ESM3 discretizes SASA into bins defined by the boundaries `[0.8, 4.0, 9.6, 16.4, 24.5, 32.9, 42.0, 51.5, 61.2, 70.9, 81.6, 93.3, 107.2, 125.4, 151.4]`, producing 16 discrete tokens. As a user, you provide a list of floats (or `None` for masked positions), and the tokenizer handles discretization automatically.

```python
# SASA values per residue — computed from ProteinChain or model output
protein.sasa = protein_chain.sasa()  # list of floats
# Partially masked: [12.5, None, 33.1, ...] — None signals "predict here"
```

Residues buried in the protein core tend to have low SASA values (below ~10), while surface-exposed residues can exceed 100.

Sources: [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L74-L90), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L627-L643)

### Function Annotations Track

The `function_annotations` track is the most structurally complex, consisting of a list of `FunctionAnnotation` objects rather than a simple per-residue array. Each `FunctionAnnotation` spans a range of residues and carries a label:

```python
@dataclass
class FunctionAnnotation:
    label: str    # InterPro ID or keyword string
    start: int    # 1-indexed, inclusive
    end: int      # 1-indexed, inclusive
```

ESM3 supports two types of function annotations: **InterPro entry annotations** (e.g. `"IPR011992"`) and **keyword annotations** derived from InterPro entry descriptions and Gene Ontology mappings. The model is designed to work with keyword annotations, which expand each InterPro entry into multiple descriptive keywords covering the same residue range. You can convert between the two using the `InterProQuantizedTokenizer`:

```python
from esm.tokenization import InterProQuantizedTokenizer
from esm.utils.types import FunctionAnnotation

# Define InterPro annotations (1-indexed, inclusive)
interpro_annotations = [
    FunctionAnnotation(label="IPR011992", start=1, end=143),
    FunctionAnnotation(label="IPR018247", start=17, end=29),
]

# Convert to keyword annotations for ESM3 input
tokenizer = InterProQuantizedTokenizer()
keyword_annotations = []
for ann in interpro_annotations:
    keywords = tokenizer.interpro2keywords.get(ann.label, [])
    keyword_annotations.extend(
        FunctionAnnotation(label=kw, start=ann.start, end=ann.end)
        for kw in keywords
    )
protein.function_annotations = keyword_annotations
```

Sources: [types.py](/esm/utils/types.py#L14-L33), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L456-L593)

## Confidence Metrics

Beyond the five promptable input tracks, `ESMProtein` carries three **read-only metric** fields that are populated by the model during structure prediction. These are not inputs — they are outputs that quantify the model's confidence in its generated coordinates.

| Metric | Attribute | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **pLDDT** | `plddt` | `(L,)` | Per-residue confidence score (0–100) |
| **pTM** | `ptm` | scalar | Predicted TM-score for the whole chain |
| **pAE** | `pae` | `(L, L)` | Predicted aligned error between all residue pairs |

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L34-L37)

## Construction and Conversion Methods

`ESMProtein` provides several class methods and instance methods for constructing proteins from external sources and converting them to other formats. The diagram below illustrates the full conversion surface:

```mermaid
graph LR
    PDB["PDB File / RCSB"] -->|from_pdb| EP["ESMProtein"]
    PC["ProteinChain"] -->|from_protein_chain| EP
    PX["ProteinComplex"] -->|from_protein_complex| EP
    EPT["ESMProteinTensor"] -->|decode_protein_tensor| EP
    EP -->|to_pdb / to_pdb_string| PDB2["PDB File / String"]
    EP -->|to_protein_chain| PC2["ProteinChain"]
    EP -->|to_protein_complex| PX2["ProteinComplex"]
    EP -->|encode| EPT
```

### From External Sources

The most common way to create an `ESMProtein` is from a PDB file or an RCSB entry. The `from_pdb` class method loads a PDB file, parses it into a `ProteinChain`, and converts it to an `ESMProtein` with `sequence` and `coordinates` populated:

```python
from esm.sdk.api import ESMProtein
from esm.utils.structure.protein_chain import ProteinChain

# Option 1: Direct from PDB file
protein = ESMProtein.from_pdb("my_structure.pdb", chain_id="A")

# Option 2: From a ProteinChain (more control)
protein_chain = ProteinChain.from_rcsb("1cm4", "A")
protein = ESMProtein.from_protein_chain(protein_chain)

# Option 3: From ProteinChain with annotations (populates SASA too)
protein = ESMProtein.from_protein_chain(protein_chain, with_annotations=True)
```

When `with_annotations=True`, the factory method also populates the `sasa` track from the `ProteinChain`'s computed SASA values. Without it, only `sequence`, `coordinates`, and `plddt` are filled.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L57-L90), [1_esmprotein.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/1_esmprotein.ipynb#L74-L94)

### To External Formats

Converting back to standard structural formats is equally straightforward:

```python
# Write to a PDB file
protein.to_pdb("output.pdb")

# Get PDB string directly (for visualization or streaming)
pdb_string = protein.to_pdb_string()

# Convert to ProteinChain for structural analysis
chain = protein.to_protein_chain()

# Convert to ProteinComplex (requires both sequence and coordinates)
complex_ = protein.to_protein_complex()
```

Note that `to_protein_chain` requires `coordinates` to be set, and `to_protein_complex` requires *both* `sequence` and `coordinates`. The `to_pdb` and `to_pdb_string` methods internally convert to a `ProteinComplex` and infer oxygen atom positions before serialization.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L112-L194)

## The Tokenized Counterpart: ESMProteinTensor

When ESM3 actually processes a protein, the human-readable `ESMProtein` is **encoded** into `ESMProteinTensor` — a parallel structure where every track is represented as discrete integer tokens (PyTorch tensors) rather than raw strings or floats. This encoding step is handled by the tokenization pipeline, and you typically don't construct `ESMProteinTensor` manually. However, understanding the mapping between the two types is essential:

| ESMProtein Track | ESMProteinTensor Track | Token Type |
|---|---|---|
| `sequence` (str) | `sequence` (Tensor) | Amino acid token IDs with BOS/EOS |
| `coordinates` (Tensor) | `structure` (Tensor) | VQ-VAE codebook indices |
| `secondary_structure` (str) | `secondary_structure` (Tensor) | SS8 class token IDs |
| `sasa` (list[float]) | `sasa` (Tensor) | Discretized bin token IDs |
| `function_annotations` (list) | `function` (Tensor) | Quantized InterPro keyword IDs |
| *(no equivalent)* | `residue_annotations` (Tensor) | Per-residue annotation token IDs |

All tokenized tensors include BOS (begin-of-sequence) and EOS (end-of-sequence) special tokens, making their length `L + 2`. The `ESMProteinTensor.empty(length, tokenizers)` factory creates a fully masked tensor of the specified length, ready for generation.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L201-L283), [encoding.py](/esm/utils/encoding.py#L156-L229)

## Length and Masking Semantics

The `__len__` method on `ESMProtein` determines the protein length from the first non-`None` track it finds, checking in order: `sequence` → `secondary_structure` → `sasa` → `coordinates`. If all tracks are `None`, it raises a `ValueError`. This design means you don't need to specify a length explicitly — it is always inferred from the data you provide.

Masking uses the `_` character in string tracks (`sequence`, `secondary_structure`) and `None` entries in list tracks (`sasa`). The mask short-hand `_` is translated to `<mask>` during tokenization. For `coordinates`, masking is handled at the `ESMProteinTensor` level through structure token masking.

```python
# Protein length is inferred automatically
protein = ESMProtein(sequence="MKTL_III__")
print(len(protein))  # 10

# Copy a protein for safe modification
protein_copy = protein.copy()
```

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L45-L55), [encoding.py](/esm/utils/encoding.py#L35-L44)

## Quick Reference: ESMProtein at a Glance

| Category | Attribute / Method | Type / Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Track** | `sequence` | `str \| None` | Amino acid string, `_` = mask |
| **Track** | `coordinates` | `Tensor \| None` | Shape `(L, 37, 3)`, atom37 format |
| **Track** | `secondary_structure` | `str \| None` | SS8 string, `_` = mask |
| **Track** | `sasa` | `list[float \| None] \| None` | Per-residue float, `None` = mask |
| **Track** | `function_annotations` | `list[FunctionAnnotation] \| None` | Labeled spans over residues |
| **Metric** | `plddt` | `Tensor \| None` | Per-residue confidence |
| **Metric** | `ptm` | `Tensor \| None` | Predicted TM-score |
| **Metric** | `pae` | `Tensor \| None` | Predicted aligned error matrix |
| **Factory** | `from_pdb(path, chain_id)` | `→ ESMProtein` | Load from PDB file |
| **Factory** | `from_protein_chain(chain)` | `→ ESMProtein` | Convert from ProteinChain |
| **Factory** | `from_protein_complex(cpx)` | `→ ESMProtein` | Convert from ProteinComplex |
| **Export** | `to_pdb(path)` | `→ None` | Write PDB file |
| **Export** | `to_pdb_string()` | `→ str` | PDB format string |
| **Export** | `to_protein_chain()` | `→ ProteinChain` | Convert to ProteinChain |
| **Export** | `to_protein_complex()` | `→ ProteinComplex` | Convert to ProteinComplex |
| **Utility** | `copy()` | `→ ESMProtein` | Deep copy |
| **Utility** | `__len__()` | `→ int` | Inferred from first non-None track |

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L26-L199)

# Latest Updates



The ESM repository has been anything but quiet. Between mid-2025 and early 2026, the team at EvolutionaryScale shipped a steady stream of patches, architectural cleanups, and new features—while the community surfaced bugs that cut to the core of how the model processes protein data. Here's a structured look at what matters.

## The Big Picture: A Post-3.2 Maturation Phase

Since the [ESM Cambrian announcement](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm-cambrian) in December 2024—which introduced the ESM C family at 300M, 600M, and 6B parameter scales—the open-source repository has been in a consolidation phase. The version history tells the story clearly:

```mermaid
timeline
    title ESM Repository Timeline (Jul 2025 – Jan 2026)
    Jul 2025 : CI pipeline added (then reverted, then re-added)
    Aug 2025 : Major internal code sync ; Binary encoding format fixes
    Sep 2025 : Flash attention removed ; MPS support landed ; v3.2.2.post2 released ; PAE exposed in ESMProtein
    Oct 2025 : Covalent bond sync ; Oxygen inference ; Version constraints loosened ; SASA BOS/EOS fix
    Jan 2026 : README update ; Alpha tag v3.2.4.a2 in development
```

The pattern is familiar to anyone who's maintained a fast-growing ML library: **sync internal code, fix what breaks, tighten the build, then repeat**. But beneath that routine cycle, several individual changes deserve scrutiny.

## Flash Attention: Removed, Not Replaced

In what is arguably the most architecturally significant commit, Zeming Lin [Remove flash attention (#269)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/7454c3d77bc731990c534936ef091db3851455a3) stripped out the `flash_attn` dependency entirely. This was followed immediately by [pyright ignore flash_attn import (#274)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/97eb26b2fe04386205bd8049033cc14f022d1fa3), which added type-checking ignores for the now-guarded import.

Why does this matter? Flash Attention has been a performance staple for transformer-based models, offering significant speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. Removing it signals one of two things: either the team found compatibility issues too painful (Flash Attention's CUDA kernel requirements are notoriously fragile across PyTorch versions), or they've substituted an alternative path that doesn't require it. The fact that `flash_attn` is still *guarded* rather than deleted entirely suggests they're keeping the door open—but the default path no longer depends on it. For users on non-NVIDIA hardware, this is unambiguously good news.

## Mac Silicon Support: Finally

One of the most-requested features landed in September: [Enable running ESM on Mac silicon using MPS (#99)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/c8969198c62129fd76eba5e450b091d2d3b012ac), authored by Imran Qureshi with co-authorship from Zeming Lin. This enables the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend, letting researchers run inference on Apple M-series chips.

The timing is interesting. PyTorch's MPS backend [has had a rocky maintenance trajectory](https://docs.pytorch.org/serve/hardware_support/apple_silicon_support.html), with an official notice that it's "no longer actively maintained." ESM's decision to add MPS support *now* suggests the team sees enough researcher demand on Apple hardware to justify it—perhaps at the inference-only level rather than for training. Either way, it lowers the barrier to entry for a significant chunk of the academic community.

## Structural and Encoding Fixes: The Quietly Important Ones

A cluster of commits in September–October addressed encoding and structural correctness:

| Commit | Author | What Changed |
|--------|--------|--------------|
| [sasa BOS/EOS fix (#286)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/6e89bf7d127b06e95d8243c020936cd67d862229) | Ishaan Mathur | Fixed SASA tokens not starting/ending with proper BOS/EOS markers |
| [syncing covalent bonds (#280)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/23b084b94f3b5f6fd700ae41f46a2787a9a5c12b) | Ishaan Mathur | Synchronized covalent bond handling between internal and open-source |
| [Ishaan/infer oxygen (#283)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/232a1041d807cce2d58ab8501750e0bfda6c26c4) | Ishaan Mathur | Added oxygen atom inference in protein complexes |
| [sync (#278)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e8117a2f68b264657eb9717308d55e5f8690588c) | Ishaan Mathur | General internal-to-external code sync |
| [Exposing pae in ESMProtein (#164)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/79c1208e96e84f9cce4479d243daf9865263c50e) | Ventura Rivera | Exposed Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) scores in the ESMProtein data model |

**The SASA BOS/EOS fix** is worth highlighting because it directly connects to [a user-reported issue](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/258) where function prediction code crashed with `ValueError: SASA does not start with 0 corresponding to BOS token`. The root cause was that SASA tokens were being padded with `inf` instead of `0` at BOS/EOS positions—a subtle encoding bug that only manifested when decoding function annotations.

**The PAE exposure** is a developer-experience win. Predicted Aligned Error is critical for assessing confidence in predicted structures, and having it directly on `ESMProtein` rather than buried in the raw output tensor makes the API significantly more ergonomic.

**The oxygen inference** commit speaks to a real practical gap: PDB files generated by ESM3 were [missing O atoms](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/279) in backbone carbonyl groups. Rather than requiring users to post-process their structures, the team added inference logic directly into the pipeline.

## Dependency and Build Hygiene

Several commits addressed the less glamorous but critical task of keeping the package buildable:

- [loosen version (#284)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e103c9c1c4047c38e8c7f1215c91f8481268e366): Relaxed the `transformers` version cap from `<=4.48.2` to allow newer versions, directly responding to [a user request](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/265) that pointed out ESM works fine with `transformers>=4.49.0`.
- [adding CI (#257)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/b237fe781ccd290bf458d9d4a7484a21ac00c7bc): Added a CI pipeline checking linting, type-checking, and running tests—after [an earlier attempt was reverted](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e0669a4a05a05395dde08d4ff2eb0219bcc2f79e).
- [various merge errors for the new binary encoding format (#261)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/2a19c4edde933c171dcb78baa304942338fbb23f): Fixed merge-related bugs in a new binary encoding format that was synced from internal code.

The version-constraint relaxation is particularly notable because **overly strict dependency pins are a chronic pain point in scientific Python**. They create dependency conflicts when users need to combine ESM with other ML libraries in the same environment. The fact that EvolutionaryScale responded to this within a couple of months of the issue being filed is a good sign.

## What's Coming: Alpha Tags and SAE Work

The GitHub activity feed reveals two active development branches that haven't landed on `main` yet:

1. **Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) support** — Branches `ishaan/sae` and `thomas-a-neil`'s contributions to it show work on integrating SAE feature extraction. This aligns with the growing research interest in mechanistic interpretability for protein language models, as demonstrated at [ICLR 2025's LMRL Workshop](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2025/35912). The branch includes examples for extracting SAE features and a 6B-scale SAE name, suggesting the team is scaling interpretability tools to their largest model.

2. **Folding examples** — The `ishaan/folding` branch adds protein folding examples with support for sequences longer than 800 residues and pLDDT output to mmCIF format.

3. **Version 3.2.4** — A tag `mga esm v3.2.4.a2` was created, indicating the next release is in alpha testing.

## The Bugs That Matter: What's Still Open

While the commit log shows progress, several open issues reveal structural problems that haven't been addressed yet:

| Issue | Severity | Core Problem |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| [Attention mask bug (#299)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/299) | **High** | Pad tokens attend to each other instead of nothing—incorrect hidden states for padding |
| [NaN coordinates vs None (#294)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/294) | **High** | Passing `coordinates=torch.full(..., nan)` produces dramatically worse pTM scores (0.096) than `coordinates=None` (0.426) |
| [cls_token setter error (#240)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/240) | **Medium** | `ESMC.from_pretrained` fails with `AttributeError: property 'cls_token' has no setter` on versions ≥3.1.5 |
| [Forge API 403 errors (#296)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/296) | **Medium** | Users with valid Forge credits still get "User does not have access to model" |
| [Unused dependencies (#303)](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/303) | **Low** | `torchvision` and deprecated `torchtext` still listed in `pyproject.toml` |

The **attention mask bug** is the most concerning from a correctness standpoint. The issue provides a precise reproduction: the current implementation uses equality comparison on `seq_id` (`seq_id.unsqueeze(-1) == seq_id.unsqueeze(-2)`), which makes pad tokens form their own attention cluster. The correct behavior—using a logical AND (`seq_id[:, None, :, None] & seq_id[:, None, None, :]`)—would ensure pad tokens attend to *nothing*. The impact isn't just on correctness of pad hidden states; as the reporter notes, it also **wastes computation** on large batches with variable-length sequences.

The **NaN vs None coordinate discrepancy** is equally troubling because it's counterintuitive. A user would reasonably expect that explicitly passing NaN-filled coordinates should be equivalent to `coordinates=None`, yet the pTM score drops by over 4x. This suggests the model's coordinate handling has different code paths for explicit vs. implicit null coordinates, with the explicit NaN path silently degrading quality.

## Version Release Timeline

```mermaid
gantt
    title ESM Version Releases (2025)
    dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat %b %d
    section Releases
    v3.2.2.post1 (reverted)       :2025-09-17, 1d
    v3.2.2.post2                  :2025-09-19, 1d
    v3.2.3 (implicit)             :2025-10-30, 1d
    v3.2.4.a2 (alpha)             :2026-01-26, 1d
```

The post-release versioning (`.post1`, `.post2`) and the fact that `3.2.2.post1` was [immediately reverted](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/cbaccc1693c033b5e7e9517c929d22b24370ddca) before being [re-released as `.post2`](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/3e109e2d1bc1d25445c14b41706cf3eb6f313d7d) suggests the team is still finding its footing with release engineering. The addition of CI in July 2025 is a step in the right direction, but the revert-and-reapply pattern indicates the sync between internal and external codebases is still bumpy.

## Bottom Line

The ESM repository is in a **transition from fast iteration to stabilization**. The flash attention removal, MPS support, and version-constraint relaxation all point to a team trying to broaden hardware and software compatibility. The structural fixes (SASA, oxygen inference, covalent bonds) show they're paying attention to the details that make the difference between a demo and a production tool.

But the open bugs tell a parallel story: the attention mask issue, the NaN coordinate discrepancy, and the persistent Forge access problems are not edge cases—they affect anyone doing batch inference, structure prediction from partial coordinates, or cloud-based API calls. The incoming SAE and folding work is promising, but the team would do well to close out the correctness issues before piling on features. A protein language model that silently produces wrong hidden states for padded sequences isn't a model you can trust in production.

# Issues and Feedbacks



The ESM repository sits at an unusual intersection: a research-grade protein language model with production-level ambitions, backed by EvolutionaryScale and the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub. But as with any project straddling the research-to-production divide, the cracks show when real users start pushing on the edges. This page catalogs the most significant recurring issues, community frustrations, and the areas where the project's open-source ambitions collide with its closed-infrastructure reality.

## The Issue Landscape at a Glance

Before diving in, here's a high-level map of where the community's pain points cluster:

| Category | Open Issues | Closed Issues | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core Model Bugs | 3 | 2 | High |
| Dependency & Compatibility | 2 | 3 | Medium |
| Forge API Access | 1 | 0 | High |
| Generation Quality & Limitations | 2 | 1 | High |
| SDK & API Design | 2 | 1 | Medium |
| Documentation Gaps | 2 | 1 | Low |

```mermaid
timeline

    section 2024 Q4

    section 2025 Q1-Q2
        Tokenizer cls_token setter bug : Issue #240

    section 2025 Q3

    section 2025 Q4
```

---

## Core Model Bugs: The Ones That Matter Most

### Attention Mask: Pad Tokens Attend to Each Other

This is arguably the most technically significant open bug. [Issue #299](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/299) demonstrates that the current attention mask implementation in ESM3 and ESMC allows pad tokens to attend to each other during batched inference.

The current mask calculation in [`esm/layers/attention.py`](https://github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm/blob/main/esm/layers/attention.py#L67):

```python
mask_BLL = seq_id.unsqueeze(-1) == seq_id.unsqueeze(-2)
mask_BHLL = mask_BLL.unsqueeze(1)
```

The problem: `seq_id` is derived from `batch != PAD_TOKEN`, which produces a boolean where pad tokens are `False`. The equality check `False == False` evaluates to `True`, meaning **pad positions attend to other pad positions**. The fix is straightforward -- use a logical AND instead of equality:

```python
correct_mask = seq_id[:, None, :, None] & seq_id[:, None, None, :]
```

The issue author provided a complete reproduction script showing the discrepancy. While non-pad token outputs are unaffected (their attention correctly excludes pad positions), this bug **wastes computation** on pad-to-pad attention and produces **incorrect hidden states for pad positions**. For anyone downstream who uses the full hidden state tensor -- not just the non-pad slice -- this is a silent correctness trap.

As of this writing, this issue remains open with no maintainer response.

### NaN Coordinates vs. coordinates=None: A 4x Performance Gap

[Issue #294](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/294) reveals a startling performance discrepancy: passing `coordinates=torch.full((256, 3, 3), float("nan"))` versus `coordinates=None` produces drastically different generation quality.

| Input | Mean pTM (30 runs) |
|---|---|
| `coordinates=None` | **0.4264** |
| `coordinates=NaN tensor` | **0.0958** |

That's a ~4.5x degradation. The root cause appears to be in how the encoding pipeline handles null coordinates: when `coordinates=None`, the model internally fills with NaN values, but when explicitly passed as a NaN tensor, `torch.inf` padding is added for BOS/EOS tokens. This means the model sees fundamentally different coordinate inputs depending on whether you pass "nothing" or "explicit nothing."

For a model that claims to reason jointly across sequence, structure, and function, this is a particularly dangerous footgun. Users who reasonably expect `NaN` coordinates to be equivalent to `None` will get silently degraded results.

### SASA BOS/EOS Token Mismatch

[Issue #258](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/258) (closed) exposed a related encoding/decoding inconsistency: when performing function prediction, the SASA decoding step would raise `ValueError: SASA does not start with 0 corresponding to BOS token` because `inf` values were being inserted at BOS/EOS positions instead of the expected `0`. This was fixed in [PR #286](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/6e89bf7d127b06e95d8243c020936cd67d862229) ("sasa BOS/EOS fix"), but the pattern is consistent: **the encode-decode pipeline has fragile boundary conditions around special tokens**, and fixes tend to be band-aids rather than systematic corrections.

---

## The Tokenizer Versioning Trap

[Issue #240](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/240) documents a particularly frustrating version regression: starting from ESM v3.1.5, calling `ESMC.from_pretrained("esmc_300m")` throws:

```
AttributeError: property 'cls_token' of 'EsmSequenceTokenizer' object has no setter
```

The issue affects ESMC models (esmc-300m and esmc-600m) and persists through the current version. The community-discovered workaround: **downgrade to ESM v3.1.4**. This is the kind of regression that suggests the internal codebase (which gets synced to open-source via bulk pushes like [PR #266](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/95239e2d195f797bc224e2d07e38cec082c14bbe)) diverges from what's published on PyPI, and the sync process doesn't include adequate version-gated testing.

---

## Forge API: The Closed Door Problem

If there's a single theme that generates the most community frustration, it's access to EvolutionaryScale's Forge API. [Issue #296](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/296) is the latest in a chain that includes issues #187 and #222, all asking the same question: **why can't I access models on Forge even with valid credits?**

The reporter followed the README instructions exactly, created an API key via [forge.evolutionaryscale.ai/apikeys](https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai/apikeys), and received:

```
(403, 'Failure in generate: {"status":"error","message":"User does not have access to model"}')
```

When asked to check which models were available at [forge.evolutionaryscale.ai/models](https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai/models), the answer was revealing: **only `esm3-open` was accessible**. No flagship, published, or experimental models.

This points to a fundamental tension in the project's architecture: the open-source repository is a gateway to a mostly-closed API. The README directs users to Forge, but Forge's access model is opaque -- there's no documented process for gaining access to models beyond the open-weight variant. The issue remains unresolved.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User reads README] --> B[Creates Forge API key]
    B --> C[Calls esm.sdk.client with token]
    C --> D{Model access?}
    D -->|esm3-open only| E[403: User does not have access]
    D -->|Full access| F[Works as documented]
    E --> G[Check forge.evolutionaryscale.ai/models]
    G --> H[Only esm3-open listed]
    H --> I[No documented process to gain access]
    I --> J[Stuck. Issues #187, #222, #296 unanswered]
    style E fill:#ff6b6b
    style J fill:#ff6b6b
```

---

## Generation Quality: When Function Conditioning Doesn't

[Issue #302](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/302) (closed, but telling) presents a rigorous empirical finding: **ESM3-open fails to generate sequences that adhere to provided functional domain annotations** for the majority of tested protein domains. Out of 20 distinct InterPro domains, only 2 produced sequences matching the target domain when verified via [InterPro Sequence Search](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/search/sequence/).

The author tested exhaustively:
- Multiple ESM3 versions (v3.0.8 through v3.2.3)
- Various prompting strategies (sequence lengths, annotation delimiters, temperatures, sampling strategies)
- Using ESM3's own function predictions from natural sequences as prompts

The pattern: **highly populated families like PF00072 work; less common families like PF00076 fail entirely**. This suggests the function conditioning mechanism is effectively memorizing high-frequency domains rather than generalizing from the annotation track -- a significant limitation for a model marketed as capable of "controllable protein generation."

Compared to the [ESM3 paper's claims](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ads0018) about prompt consistency and function keyword recovery, real-world function-conditioned generation appears to be far less reliable than the benchmarks suggest.

---

## Dependency Hell and the Sync Problem

### Unused Dependencies

[Issue #303](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/303) points out that both `torchvision` and `torchtext` are listed as dependencies in `pyproject.toml` but are never imported in the source or examples. Worse, **torchtext was deprecated in 2024**. These are not harmless extras -- they add installation overhead, potential version conflicts, and security surface area.

### The Transformers Version Cap

[Issue #265](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/265) (closed) requested lifting the `transformers<=4.48.2` cap, which prevented users from combining ESM with newer libraries. This was resolved in [PR #284](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e103c9c1c4047c38e8c7f1215c91f8481268e366) ("loosen version"), but the underlying pattern is worth noting: **the version constraints tend to be overly conservative**, likely because the internal codebase isn't tested against newer dependency versions before sync.

### Flash Attention: Removed but Not Forgotten

[PR #269](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/7454c3d77bc731990c534936ef091db3851455a3) removed flash attention entirely, followed by [PR #274](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/97eb26b2fe04386205bd8049033cc14f022d1fa3) adding a `pyright` ignore for the now-guarded import. This was likely a pragmatic decision -- flash attention's hardware-specific requirements were a constant source of installation issues -- but it does mean ESM forgoes a significant inference speedup on compatible hardware.

### MPS Support: A Welcome Addition

On the positive side, [PR #99](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/c8969198c62129fd76eba5e450b091d2d3b012ac) enabled running ESM on Apple Silicon via MPS, co-authored by Zeming Lin. This is a meaningful quality-of-life improvement for the many researchers working on Mac hardware.

---

## SDK Design Friction Points

### ESMProteinError: The Silent Failure

[Issue #224](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/224) highlights that when Forge API calls fail, the return type is `ESMProteinError` rather than an exception. This means code like:

```python
all_mean_embeddings = [
    torch.mean(output.hidden_states, dim=-2).squeeze() for output in outputs
]
```

...crashes with `AttributeError: 'ESMProteinError' object has no attribute 'hidden_states'` instead of providing a clear error message. The [official quickstart notebook](https://virtualcellmodels.cziscience.com/quickstart/esmc-quickstart) even includes a defensive `try/except` wrapper for this exact reason, suggesting it's a known but unaddressed pattern. **Using error objects instead of exceptions is a design choice that pushes error-handling burden onto every caller** without providing the type-safety to match.

### API Returns All Hidden States When Mean Requested

[Issue #292](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/292) reports that setting `LogitsConfig(return_mean_hidden_states=True)` for ESM-C-6B also returns full hidden states for all layers, making API calls unnecessarily slow. For the 6B model, full hidden states are enormous -- sending them over the wire when only mean-pooled states were requested is a clear backend bug that directly impacts user experience.

### The 2048-Token Wall

[Issue #289](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/289) asks the inevitable question: can ESM handle proteins longer than 2048 amino acids? The answer is no -- both the API and local models enforce this context window. For a model trained on proteins up to 2048 residues, this is an architectural limit, but it's a meaningful one: many biologically important proteins (titin, dystrophin, mucins) exceed this length. There's currently no documented chunking or sliding-window workaround.

---

## Documentation and Usability Gaps

### Sequence Logit Mapping: Undocumented and Confusing

[Issue #252](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/252) (closed) asked a straightforward question: how do the 64 dimensions of the sequence logit tensor map to amino acid tokens? The `SEQUENCE_VOCAB` constant lists 33 tokens, and the paper's Appendix A.1.3 specifies 29 meaningful tokens, but the logit tensor is 64-dimensional.

After community discussion, the answer emerged: **indices 0-28 map to the meaningful tokens in vocabulary order, and indices 29-63 should be ignored** (they're padded with large negative values like -18.625, acting as effective -inf). But this mapping is nowhere in the official documentation. Anyone porting code from ESM2 to ESM3/ESMC has to reverse-engineer it.

### The Two Extra Embedding Tokens

[Issue #241](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/241) (closed) asked why ESMC embeddings have two more tokens than the input sequence length. The answer: BOS and EOS tokens are prepended/appended. Again, this is standard transformer practice but was not documented, forcing users to discover it experimentally and manually strip the first and last embeddings.

### Missing Vocabulary File

[Issue #139](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/139) reports that `data/uniref90_and_mgnify90_residue_annotations_gt_1k_proteins.csv` -- required for residue annotation tokenization -- is not included in the repository. This issue has been open since November 2024 with no resolution, effectively making the residue annotation feature unusable for anyone who doesn't have access to the internal codebase.

---

## The Bigger Picture: A Sync-Driven Open Source Model

Many of these issues share a common root cause: **ESM's open-source repository is a downstream sync of an internal codebase**, not a community-first project. The evidence is in the commit history:

| Pattern | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Bulk code dumps | [PR #266](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/95239e2d195f797bc224e2d07e38cec082c14bbe): "Sync over internal code to open source" |
| Revert-and-resync | [PR #272](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/cbaccc1693c033b5e7e9517c929d22b24370ddca) reverted [PR #270](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/f4f97929b2d0b278a32b4d953f0b838bd34b9682) due to merge errors |
| CI instability | [PR #257](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/b237fe781ccd290bf458d9d4a7484a21ac00c7bc) added CI, was [immediately reverted](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e0669a4a05a05395dde08d4ff2eb0219bcc2f79e), then re-added later |
| Binary encoding format errors | [PR #261](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/2a19c4edde933c171dcb78baa304942338fbb23f): "various merge errors for the new binary encoding format" |
| Missing files | Vocabulary files, model configs, and data that exist internally but aren't synced |

This sync-driven model explains why issues linger: the maintainers are primarily focused on the internal codebase, and the GitHub repository is a release channel rather than a development surface. It also explains why version regressions like the tokenizer bug (#240) slip through -- the internal codebase may have moved past the breaking change, but the published PyPI package hasn't been tested in isolation.

---

## What's Working

Fairness demands acknowledging what the team has done right:

- **MPS support** ([PR #99](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/c8969198c62129fd76eba5e450b091d2d3b012ac)) opened ESM to the Mac research community
- **SASA BOS/EOS fix** ([PR #286](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/6e89bf7d127b06e95d8243c020936cd67d862229)) addressed a real encoding bug
- **Version pin loosening** ([PR #284](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e103c9c1c4047c38e8c7f1215c91f8481268e366)) resolved dependency conflicts
- **Flash attention removal** ([PR #269](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/7454c3d77bc731990c534936ef091db3851455a3)) eliminated a major installation pain point
- **PAE exposure** ([PR #164](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/79c1208e96e84f9cce4479d243daf9865263c50e)) added predicted aligned error access
- **Oxygen atom fix** for PDB output ([Issue #279](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/279), closed) restored backbone O atoms

---

## Summary of Open Questions for Users

If you're considering building on ESM, here are the unresolved issues that should inform your decision:

1. **Attention mask bug** (#299): Batched inference with padding produces incorrect pad hidden states. Use single-sample inference or patch the mask calculation yourself.
2. **NaN vs None coordinates** (#294): Always use `coordinates=None` for unconditional structure generation. Explicit NaN tensors produce severely degraded results.
3. **Tokenizer regression** (#240): Pin to ESM <=3.1.4 if using ESMC models, or patch the tokenizer.
4. **Forge access** (#296): Only `esm3-open` is reliably accessible. Don't depend on larger models via Forge for production work.
5. **Function-conditioned generation** (#302): Don't expect ESM3-open to reliably generate sequences matching specific InterPro domains, especially for less common families.
6. **Missing vocabulary file** (#139): Residue annotation features are non-functional without the absent CSV file.
7. **2048-token limit** (#289): No workaround for long proteins. Plan to truncate or split.

The ESM project represents genuinely impressive science. But the gap between the paper's claims and the SDK's reliability is wider than it should be -- and the sync-driven release model means that gap may persist until the team invests in treating the open-source repository as a first-class artifact rather than a downstream mirror.

# About Contributors



The ESM repository is not just a codebase -- it's the public artifact of one of the most consequential research lineages in AI-for-biology. The people behind these commits trace a path from Meta's FAIR lab through a $142M startup to Biohub, a nonprofit research institute backed by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Understanding who they are and where they came from tells you a lot about why ESM looks and works the way it does.

## From Meta FAIR to EvolutionaryScale to Biohub

The ESM project was born at Meta's Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) lab. Alexander Rives started and led the Evolutionary Scale Modeling project there, building what is [widely recognized as the first large-scale transformer language model for proteins](https://press.aboutamazon.com/aws/2024/6/evolutionaryscale-launches-with-esm3-a-milestone-ai-model-for-biology) (ESM-1, in 2019). The original `facebookresearch/esm` repository housed ESM-1b, ESM-2, ESMFold, and the MSA Transformer -- models that collectively became foundational infrastructure for computational biology worldwide.

In April 2023, after their team at FAIR was disbanded, three key figures -- **Alexander Rives**, **Tom Sercu**, and **Salvatore Candido** -- left Meta to continue the work independently. They founded [EvolutionaryScale](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai) in July 2023 as a public-benefit corporation, raising a [$142M seed round](https://techcrunch.com/2024/06/25/evolutionaryscale-backed-by-amazon-and-nvidia-raises-142m-for-protein-generating-ai) led by Nat Friedman, Daniel Gross, and Lux Capital, with participation from Amazon and NVentures (Nvidia's venture arm). The open-source repository migrated from `facebookresearch/esm` to `evolutionaryscale/esm` (now `Biohub/esm`).

Then came the next pivot. In 2025, the EvolutionaryScale team joined [Biohub](https://biohub.org/blog/frontier-ai-biology-initiative), the nonprofit research institute launched by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Rives became Head of Science at CZI, leading an initiative to combine frontier AI with frontier biology. The Biohub announcement described it as "the first large scale scientific effort to combine frontier AI and frontier biology," with compute capacity scaling to 10,000 GPUs by 2028.

```mermaid
timeline
    title ESM Team Journey
    2019 : ESM-1 at Meta FAIR : First large transformer for proteins
    2021 : ESM-1b released : Widely adopted by researchers worldwide
    2022 : ESM-2 & ESMFold : 15B params, Science paper, Metagenomic Atlas
    2023 Jul : EvolutionaryScale founded : Rives, Sercu, Candido leave Meta
    2024 Jun : ESM3 launched : $142M seed, esmGFP, Forge API
    2025 : Team joins Biohub : Frontier AI + biology initiative at CZI
```

## The Core Contributors

### Alexander Rives -- The Architect

[Alex Rives](https://biohub.org/team/alex-rives) is the intellectual founder of the ESM project. He started and led ESM at Meta FAIR, co-founded EvolutionaryScale as Chief Scientist, and now serves as Head of Science at Biohub. He is also a **Core Institute Member at the Broad Institute** and an **Assistant Professor in EECS at MIT** -- unusual simultaneous affiliations that speak to the cross-institutional gravity of this work.

His academic path is itself noteworthy: a BA in **philosophy and biology** from Yale, followed by a PhD in **computer science** from NYU. That dual background -- philosophical reasoning about biological systems, formalized through computation -- is arguably the intellectual DNA of the entire ESM lineage. As he [told the press at the ESM3 launch](https://www.synbiobeta.com/read/evolutionaryscale-raises-142m-and-unveils-ai-model-esm3-to-transform-biology): "ESM3 takes a step toward a future of biology where AI is a tool to engineer from first principles, the way we engineer structures, machines, and microchips, and write computer programs."

Rives is not a frequent committer on the open-source repo -- his role has always been research leadership -- but his fingerprints are on every architectural decision, from the masked language modeling objective of ESM-1 through the multimodal generative design of ESM3.

### Zeming Lin -- The Lead Engineer

If Rives is the architect, **Zeming Lin** is the builder. Lin is the **lead author** of the landmark [ESM-2/ESMFold Science paper](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36927031) ("Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic-level protein structure with a language model," *Science*, 2023), which demonstrated that 15B-parameter protein language models learn atomic-resolution structure directly from sequence. The paper's footnote marks Lin and Rives as sharing "research and engineering leadership."

On the repository, Lin's commits reveal a focus on performance and infrastructure. He authored the [Remove flash attention](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/7454c3d77bc731990c534936ef091db3851455a3) commit, the [version bump preparing for release](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/35c2088b75ee606c03b6d6848f694e8d656f4537), and CI reverts that suggest he's the person who ultimately decides what ships and what doesn't. He was at Meta FAIR before EvolutionaryScale, and is now at Biohub.

### Salvatore Candido -- The Systems Thinker

[Sal Candido](https://biohub.org/team/salvatore-candido) is Engineering Fellow and VP at Biohub, and was previously co-founder and CTO of EvolutionaryScale. His career arc is the most unconventional of the trio: a **PhD in control systems and AI from the University of Illinois**, followed by distinguished engineering roles at Google and Meta. At Google[x], he was the **technical lead who created the AI navigation algorithms for Project Loon** -- the autonomous stratospheric balloon project. Before that, he worked on the Google Search algorithm.

At Meta FAIR, he co-led the AI for math and science pillar. His Biohub profile notes that he "spearheaded or made foundational technical contributions to all of the company's flagship research efforts" at EvolutionaryScale. Candido's background in control theory and autonomous systems likely shapes ESM's iterative masked sampling approach -- a feedback-driven generation process that, structurally, is closer to control systems than to the one-shot autoregressive generation familiar from LLMs.

### Tom Sercu -- The Co-Founder

**Tom Sercu** is the third co-founder of EvolutionaryScale, having also come from Meta FAIR. He is a co-author on the ESM-2 Science paper and a key member of the ESM3 research team. While less visible in the commit log than some other contributors, Sercu's role as a founding researcher places him at the center of every major design decision in the ESM lineage.

### Roshan Rao -- The Protein ML Researcher

**Roshan Rao** is another key researcher from the FAIR era who transitioned to EvolutionaryScale and then Biohub. His [personal page](https://rmrao.github.io) reads like a chronicle of the ESM project: ESM3, ESMFold and the Metagenomic Atlas, programmable protein design with language models, variant effect prediction, MSA Transformers, contact prediction, and the TAPE benchmark. He was a co-author on both the ESM-2 Science paper and the earlier factored attention / contact prediction work that established the theoretical foundations for why Transformers learn protein structure.

Rao's work on TAPE (Tasks Assessing Protein Embeddings) is particularly notable -- it created the evaluation framework that the entire protein language model community adopted, essentially defining how "good" a protein representation is. This is the kind of infrastructure work that doesn't make headlines but shapes an entire field.

### Halil Akin -- The Researcher-Engineer

**Halil Akin** is another co-author from the FAIR era, listed on the ESM-2 Science paper. He appears in the Zenodo release credits for ESM v3.2.3 as "halilakin," confirming his continued involvement through the EvolutionaryScale and Biohub transitions.

## The Open-Source Maintainers

While the founders set the research direction, the day-to-day work of maintaining the open-source repository falls to a smaller, more operationally focused group. These are the people whose names appear most frequently in the commit log and who respond to the issues that users file.

### Ishaan Mathur -- The Busiest Committer

**Ishaan Mathur** (`ishaan@evolutionaryscale.ai`) is, by commit volume, the most active contributor in the recent history of the repository. His commits reveal a maintainer doing the unglamorous but essential work of keeping the project alive:

| Commit | What it tells us |
|--------|-----------------|
| [sasa BOS/EOS fix](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/6e89bf7d127b06e95d8243c020936cd67d862229) | Fixing the exact bug reported in [Issue #258](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/258) |
| [loosen version](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e103c9c1c4047c38e8c7f1215c91f8481268e366) | Responding to [Issue #265](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/265) on dependency pinning |
| [infer oxygen](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/232a1041d807cce2d58ab8501750e0bfda6c26c4) | Fixing missing O atoms from PDB output, per [Issue #279](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/issues/279) |
| [syncing covalent bonds](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/23b084b94f3b5f6fd700ae41f46a2787a9a5c12b) | Internal-to-external code sync |
| [adding CI](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/b237fe781ccd290bf458d9d4a7484a21ac00c7bc) | Setting up linting, typechecking, and test CI |
| [Sync over internal code to open source](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/95239e2d195f797bc224e2d07e38cec082c14bbe) | The critical "open-source mirror" commit |

Mathur is the bridge between EvolutionaryScale's internal development and the public repository. The "sync" commits are particularly revealing: they indicate that the open-source repo is a downstream mirror of an internal codebase, not the primary development surface. This explains why many issues linger -- the fix often exists internally but hasn't been synced.

### Neil Thomas -- The Release Manager

**Neil Thomas** (`neil@evolutionaryscale.ai`) appears primarily in version-bump and release commits: [3.2.2.post2](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/3e109e2d1bc1d25445c14b41706cf3eb6f313d7d), the [revert of sync 3.2.2.post1](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/cbaccc1693c033b5e7e9517c929d22b24370ddca), and the [README update](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/453b2e2e713ee35a1dcbc684b11d03303a59294e). The revert-then-re-release pattern suggests he's the person responsible for package integrity -- when a release breaks, he's the one rolling it back.

### Steve Chan -- The CI and Encoding Fixer

**Steve Chan** handled critical infrastructure work: [fixing the CI](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/7e0ebdb788b7c0d5de046d8d8c6aea2c97e8c7f9) for test requisites and [fixing merge errors in the binary encoding format](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/2a19c4edde933c171dcb78baa304942338fbb23f). The encoding format fix is notable because it affected how structure tokens are serialized -- a core part of the ESM3 pipeline.

### Imran Qureshi -- The Platform Enabler

**Imran Qureshi** authored the [Enable running ESM on Mac silicon using MPS](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/c8969198c62129fd76eba5e450b091d2d3b012ac) commit, co-authored with Zeming Lin. This is the kind of change that doesn't advance the research frontier but massively expands the user base -- suddenly, every researcher with an M-series MacBook can run ESM locally.

### Ventura Rivera -- The Community Contributor

**Ventura Rivera** (affiliated with [Albert Invent](https://zenodo.org/records/17353381) per the Zenodo metadata) contributed [Exposing pae in ESMProtein](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/79c1208e96e84f9cce4479d243daf9865263c50e). This is interesting because PAE (Predicted Aligned Error) is a critical quality metric for structure prediction, and exposing it in the `ESMProtein` data model was an explicit request from the community. Rivera appears to be an external contributor rather than an EvolutionaryScale employee.
