## What the Commit Patterns Reveal

The commit history tells a structural story about how this project is run:

**The open-source repo is a downstream mirror.** The repeated "sync" commits from Ishaan Mathur -- [Sync over internal code to open source](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/95239e2d195f797bc224e2d07e38cec082c14bbe), [sync](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/e8117a2f68b264657eb9717308d55e5f8690588c), [syncing covalent bonds](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/23b084b94f3b5f6fd700ae41f46a2787a9a5c12b) -- confirm that primary development happens internally and is periodically pushed to GitHub. This is why issue resolution can feel slow: the feedback loop is longer than it appears.

**The team is small and stretched thin.** With ~18 contributors on the Zenodo record and only a handful making regular commits, the ratio of users to maintainers is enormous. ESM has thousands of users in pharma and academia, but the open-source maintenance burden falls largely on Mathur and Thomas.

**Release discipline is high but error-prone.** The [revert of 3.2.2.post1](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/cbaccc1693c033b5e7e9517c929d22b24370ddca) followed by [3.2.2.post2](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/3e109e2d1bc1d25445c14b41706cf3eb6f313d7d) shows a team that ships fast but also rolls back quickly when things break. The `.postN` versioning pattern suggests they're using post-release patches rather than cutting full minor versions -- a pragmatic choice for a research codebase, but one that can confuse downstream dependency managers.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "FAIR Era (2019-2023)"

        ZL[Zeming Lin] -->|Lead engineer| ESM2[ESM-2 / ESMFold]
```

## Why It Matters

The ESM team is unusual in that they have persisted through three organizational homes while maintaining a coherent technical vision. Most research projects die when the team disperses after a paper; ESM evolved from ESM-1 through ESM-3 and ESMC across two corporate reorganizations and a transition to nonprofit status. The core team -- Rives, Lin, Candido, Sercu, Rao, Akin -- has stayed together for over six years, which is nearly unheard of in ML research.

This continuity has a technical consequence: **the ESM codebase carries fewer architectural U-turns than most projects of its age.** The fundamental design decisions (masked language modeling, iterative unmasking for generation, VQ-VAE structure tokens) have been refined rather than replaced. When Zeming Lin [removed flash attention](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/commit/7454c3d77bc731990c534936ef091db3851455a3), it wasn't because the team changed their mind about the attention mechanism -- it was a pragmatic infrastructure simplification.

The risk, looking forward, is organizational dilution. The Biohub mission is broader than protein language models -- it encompasses virtual cells, immune system modeling, and cryoET. Whether the ESM-specific team can maintain the same intensity of focus on the open-source repository while also pursuing these broader goals remains an open question. The commit frequency in recent months -- dominated by sync and patch commits rather than feature work -- suggests that the center of gravity may already be shifting.

# Architecture Overview



The ESM codebase is a **multitrack protein language model framework** built around two distinct model families—ESM3 and ESMC—unified under a shared transformer infrastructure, a composable tokenization pipeline, and a client-abstracted SDK layer. At its core, the architecture follows a **encode → transformer forward → decode** data flow where protein information (sequence, structure, secondary structure, solvent accessibility, function annotations, and residue annotations) travels through parallel token tracks, is embedded into a shared latent space, processed by a stack of transformer blocks with optional geometric reasoning, and then projected back out through independent output heads. This page maps the high-level structural topology of the repository so you can navigate the deeper dives that follow.

![ESM3 Diagram](https://github.com/Biohub/esm/blob/main/_assets/esm3_diagram.png?raw=true)

## System-Level Data Flow

The entire system can be understood as a three-stage pipeline. **Stage 1 (Encode)** converts raw protein representations (`ESMProtein`) into tokenized tensor representations (`ESMProteinTensor`) via per-track tokenizers and the VQ-VAE structure encoder. **Stage 2 (Forward)** passes the summed multi-track embeddings through a `TransformerStack` of `UnifiedTransformerBlock` instances—each optionally enriched with SE(3)-equivariant geometric attention—then applies a final `LayerNorm`. **Stage 3 (Decode)** projects the transformer output through independent `RegressionHead` modules to produce per-track logits, and for generation, iteratively samples and unmasks tokens until the specified track is fully resolved.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["ESMProtein (Raw)"]
        SEQ["sequence"]
        COORD["coordinates"]
        SS["secondary_structure"]
        SASA["sasa"]
        FUNC["function_annotations"]
        RES["residue_annotations"]
    end

    subgraph Tokenize["Encode Stage"]
        SEQ_T["EsmSequenceTokenizer"]
        VQVAE["StructureTokenEncoder (VQ-VAE)"]
        SS_T["SecondaryStructureTokenizer"]
        SASA_T["SASADiscretizingTokenizer"]
        FUNC_T["InterProQuantizedTokenizer"]
        RES_T["ResidueAnnotationsTokenizer"]
    end

    subgraph Tensor["ESMProteinTensor (Tokenized)"]
        SEQ_TK["sequence tokens"]
        STR_TK["structure tokens"]
        SS_TK["ss8 tokens"]
        SASA_TK["sasa tokens"]
        FUNC_TK["function tokens"]
        RES_TK["residue tokens"]
    end

    subgraph Core["Transformer Core"]
        ENC["EncodeInputs<br/>(sum embeddings)"]
        STACK["TransformerStack<br/>(UnifiedTransformerBlock × N)"]
        HEADS["OutputHeads<br/>(RegressionHead per track)"]
    end

    subgraph Output["ESMOutput"]
        SEQ_LO["sequence_logits"]
        STR_LO["structure_logits"]
        SS_LO["secondary_structure_logits"]
        SASA_LO["sasa_logits"]
        FUNC_LO["function_logits"]
        RES_LO["residue_logits"]
        EMB["embeddings"]
    end

    SEQ --> SEQ_T --> SEQ_TK
    COORD --> VQVAE --> STR_TK
    SS --> SS_T --> SS_TK
    SASA --> SASA_T --> SASA_TK
    FUNC --> FUNC_T --> FUNC_TK
    RES --> RES_T --> RES_TK

    SEQ_TK --> ENC
    STR_TK --> ENC
    SS_TK --> ENC
    SASA_TK --> ENC
    FUNC_TK --> ENC
    RES_TK --> ENC

    ENC --> STACK --> HEADS --> Output
```

Sources: [esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L61-L178), [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L26-L58), [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L201-L278)

## Two Model Families

The repository implements two architecturally distinct model families, each designed for a different class of protein modeling tasks. **ESM3** is a full multimodal generative model that processes all six protein tracks and supports iterative masked generation across any combination of tracks. **ESM C** is a streamlined representation model that operates on sequence alone and is optimized for extracting high-quality embeddings and hidden states. Both share the same `TransformerStack` backbone but differ in their encoder complexity, attention mechanisms, and output capabilities.

| Dimension | ESM3 (Multimodal Generative) | ESM C (Representation) |
|---|---|---|
| **Input Tracks** | Sequence, Structure, SS8, SASA, Function, Residue | Sequence only |
| **Encoder** | `EncodeInputs` (8 embedding modules, summed) | `nn.Embedding(64, d_model)` |
| **Geometric Attention** | Yes (configurable `n_layers_geom`) | No (`n_layers_geom=0`) |
| **Output Heads** | 6 independent `RegressionHead` modules | 1 `RegressionHead` for sequence |
| **VQ-VAE Codec** | Structure encoder + decoder, Function decoder | None |
| **Generation** | Iterative masked sampling across tracks | Not supported |
| **Client Interface** | `ESM3InferenceClient` (7 methods) | `ESMCInferenceClient` (3 methods) |
| **Pretrained Sizes** | Small Open (d=1536, 48 layers) | 300M (d=960, 30 layers), 600M (d=1152, 36 layers) |
| **Flash Attention** | Not enabled by default | Enabled by default |
| **Hidden States** | Not returned by default | Stacked and returned as `[n_layers, B, L, D]` |

The ESM3 `EncodeInputs` module projects each track into a shared `d_model`-dimensional space and then **sums all embeddings element-wise**—this is the critical architectural decision that enables any-track conditioning, since missing tracks simply contribute zero-valued padding embeddings. The ESMC model, by contrast, dispenses with this multi-track machinery entirely, embedding only sequence tokens and routing them directly into a pure-attention transformer stack. Both models are loaded through the `LOCAL_MODEL_REGISTRY` in `pretrained.py`, which maps model name strings to builder functions that instantiate the model, load weights, and optionally cast to `bfloat16` on GPU.

Sources: [esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L181-L234), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L44-L98), [pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L95-L135)

## Transformer Core Architecture

The `TransformerStack` is the shared computational backbone for both model families. It consists of a sequence of `UnifiedTransformerBlock` instances followed by a final `LayerNorm`. Each block is a **dual-attention residual module** that can optionally include geometric attention alongside standard multi-head attention, making the same block architecture serve both the SE(3)-aware ESM3 and the pure-sequence ESM C.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    X_IN["x (input)"] --> ATTN["MultiHeadAttention<br/>or FlashMultiHeadAttention"]
    ATTN --> R1["r1"]
    X_IN --> ADD1["x + r1 / scaling_factor"]
    ADD1 --> X_MID["x (post-attention)"]
    X_MID --> GEOM["GeometricReasoning<br/>(if enabled)"]
    GEOM --> R2["r2"]
    X_MID --> ADD2["x + r2 / scaling_factor"]
    ADD2 --> X_PRE_FFN["x (post-geom)"]
    X_PRE_FFN --> FFN["SwiGLU FFN<br/>or GELU FFN"]
    FFN --> R3["r3"]
    X_PRE_FFN --> ADD3["x + r3 / scaling_factor"]
    ADD3 --> X_OUT["x (output)"]
```

Three architectural details deserve emphasis. First, the **residue scaling factor** (`math.sqrt(n_layers / 36)`) normalizes the residual stream by depth, preventing signal explosion in deep stacks—this is applied to both attention residuals and the FFN residual in ESM3, while ESM C disables it (`scale_residue=False` when `v_heads=None`). Second, the **SwiGLU FFN** is the default feed-forward variant, computing `Linear(SiLU(x1) * x2)` where the input is chunked in half, with the hidden dimension rounded to the nearest multiple of 256 for hardware efficiency. Third, the **geometric attention** layer computes attention weights as a learned combination of a rotation term (dot product of rotation-transformed queries and keys) and a negative distance term (L2 norm of translation-transformed query-key differences), ensuring SE(3) invariance of the attention pattern while preserving equivariance of the value stream.

> [!TIP]
> When `n_layers_geom > 0` in ESM3, only the first `n_layers_geom` blocks include geometric attention. The remaining blocks use standard multi-head attention only. This layered design means the model processes 3D structural information in early layers and refines representations through standard attention in deeper layers.

Sources: [transformer_stack.py](/esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L10-L94), [blocks.py](/esm/layers/blocks.py#L51-L157), [geom_attention.py](/esm/layers/geom_attention.py#L9-L149)

## SDK Abstraction Layer

The SDK layer provides a **uniform inference interface** across different deployment backends through abstract client protocols. `ESM3InferenceClient` and `ESMCInferenceClient` define the contract that concrete implementations—local models, Forge API, and SageMaker—must satisfy. This means the same `encode → generate → decode` workflow works identically whether you are calling a remote API or running on a local GPU.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ESM3InferenceClient {
        <<abstract>>
        +generate(input, config) ProteinType
        +encode(input) ESMProteinTensor
        +decode(input) ESMProtein
        +logits(input, config) LogitsOutput
        +"forward_and_sample(input, config)" ForwardAndSampleOutput
        +raw_model
    }
    class ESMCInferenceClient {
        <<abstract>>
        +encode(input) ESMProteinTensor
        +decode(input) ESMProtein
        +logits(input, config) LogitsOutput
        +raw_model
    }
    class ESM3 {
        +"forward()"
        +"generate()"
        +"encode()"
        +"decode()"
        +"logits()"
        +"forward_and_sample()"
    }
    class ESMC {
        +"forward()"
        +"encode()"
        +"decode()"
        +"logits()"
    }
    class ESM3ForgeInferenceClient {
        +"generate()"
        +"encode()"
        +"decode()"
        +"logits()"
    }
    
    ESM3InferenceClient <|.. ESM3 : implements
    ESMCInferenceClient <|.. ESMC : implements
    ESM3InferenceClient <|.. ESM3ForgeInferenceClient : implements
```

The **client factory function** `esm.sdk.client()` returns a `ESM3ForgeInferenceClient` configured with the Forge API URL and your API key. For local inference, `ESM3.from_pretrained()` and `ESMC.from_pretrained()` return model instances that directly implement the same client protocols, eliminating any code changes when switching between local and remote execution. The `ForgeBatchExecutor` context manager wraps batch API calls with retry logic and progress tracking.

> [!TIP]
> The `ESM3` model class inherits from both `nn.Module` and `ESM3InferenceClient`, making it simultaneously a PyTorch module and an inference client. This dual nature means you can call `model.generate(protein, config)` directly on a loaded model without wrapping it in any adapter—local models are first-class inference clients.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L431-L531), [esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L181-L258), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L44-L76), [__init__.py](/esm/sdk/__init__.py#L1-L36)

## Project Directory Map

The codebase is organized into six top-level subsystems under `esm/`, each with a clear responsibility boundary:

```
esm/
├── models/              # Model architectures
│   ├── esm3.py          # ESM3: EncodeInputs + TransformerStack + OutputHeads
│   ├── esmc.py          # ESMC: Embed + TransformerStack + SequenceHead
│   ├── vqvae.py         # StructureTokenEncoder/Decoder (VQ-VAE codec)
│   └── function_decoder.py  # FunctionTokenDecoder
├── layers/              # Reusable neural network components
│   ├── blocks.py        # UnifiedTransformerBlock (dual-attention + FFN)
│   ├── transformer_stack.py  # Stack of blocks + LayerNorm
│   ├── attention.py     # MultiHeadAttention, FlashMultiHeadAttention
│   ├── geom_attention.py    # SE(3) geometric reasoning
│   ├── rotary.py        # Rotary position embeddings
│   ├── codebook.py      # EMA codebook for VQ-VAE
│   └── structure_proj.py    # 6D rotation structure head
├── tokenization/        # Per-track tokenizer implementations
│   ├── sequence_tokenizer.py     # Amino acid tokenizer (HuggingFace-based)
│   ├── structure_tokenizer.py    # Structure token mapping
│   ├── ss_tokenizer.py           # 8-class secondary structure
│   ├── sasa_tokenizer.py         # Discretized solvent accessibility
│   ├── function_tokenizer.py     # InterPro quantized function tokens
│   └── residue_tokenizer.py      # Residue annotation tokenizer
├── sdk/                 # Inference client abstractions
│   ├── api.py           # ESMProtein, ESMProteinTensor, client protocols
│   ├── forge.py         # Forge API client (fold, generate, encode, etc.)
│   ├── sagemaker.py     # SageMaker deployment client
│   └── retry.py         # Exponential backoff retry logic
├── utils/               # Shared utilities
│   ├── encoding.py      # Tokenize/detokenize helper functions
│   ├── decoding.py      # ESMProteinTensor → ESMProtein conversion
│   ├── generation.py    # Iterative sampling orchestration
│   ├── sampling.py      # Logit sampling (temperature, top-p, entropy)
│   ├── noise_schedules.py   # Cosine/linear unmask schedules
│   └── structure/       # Affine3D, ProteinChain, ProteinComplex
└── data/                # Static data files (InterPro mappings, keyword vocab)
```

Sources: [esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L1-L47), [vqvae.py](/esm/models/vqvae.py#L1-L10), [__init__.py](/esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L1-L22), [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L1-L18), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L1-L34)

## Reading Path

The architecture you've seen here is the foundation for understanding the specialized subsystems documented in the pages that follow. The recommended progression moves from model families inward to transformer internals, then outward to generation and deployment:

1. **Model Families** — Start with [ESM3 Multimodal Generative Model](8-esm3-multimodal-generative-model) and [ESM C Representation Model](9-esm-c-representation-model) to understand how each model configures the shared components
2. **Tokenization Pipeline** — Then explore [Sequence and Structure Tokenizers](10-sequence-and-structure-tokenizers) and [VQ-VAE Structure Encoding](11-vq-vae-structure-encoding) to understand how raw protein data enters the model
3. **Transformer Core** — Deep-dive into [Geometric Attention and SE(3) Invariance](13-geometric-attention-and-se-3-invariance) and [Transformer Stack Design](14-transformer-stack-design) for the computational heart of the system
4. **Generation and Sampling** — Understand the iterative decode loop via [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling) and [Noise Schedules and Unmasking Strategies](17-noise-schedules-and-unmasking-strategies)
5. **SDK and Deployment** — Finally, see how everything is exposed to users through [Forge API Client](19-forge-api-client) and [Local Inference Client](20-local-inference-client)

# ESM3 Multimodal Generative Model



ESM3 is a generative language model for proteins that simultaneously reasons over **sequence**, **structure**, and **function** — the three fundamental modalities of protein biology. Unlike representation-only models (such as [ESM C](9-esm-c-representation-model)), ESM3 is a full **masked-language-model** architecture capable of conditional generation: given partial observations across any combination of tracks, it iteratively samples the missing information. The open-source release ships the `esm3_sm_open_v1` checkpoint (1.4B parameters, 48 transformer layers, d_model=1536), along with dedicated sub-models for structure encoding/decoding and function decoding.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L181-L217), [pretrained.py](esm/pretrained.py#L95-L111), [models.py](esm/utils/constants/models.py#L1-L8)

## Architecture Overview

The ESM3 architecture follows a **track-fusion encoder** pattern: every protein modality is independently tokenized and embedded, the embeddings are summed into a single hidden state, and a shared transformer stack processes the combined representation. Output heads then predict logits for each track independently. This design ensures that any subset of tracks can be provided as input — the model gracefully fills missing modalities with learned defaults (mask or pad tokens) and pLDDT conditioning signals.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Input Tracks
        SEQ["Sequence Tokens<br/>(64 vocab)"]
        STR["Structure Tokens<br/>(4096+5 vocab)"]
        SS["SS8 Tokens<br/>(8+3 vocab)"]
        SASA["SASA Tokens<br/>(16+3 vocab)"]
        FUNC["Function Tokens<br/>(8 × 260 vocab)"]
        RES["Residue Annotations<br/>(1478 vocab)"]
        PLDDT["pLDDT Signals<br/>(RBF → 16-dim)"]
    end

    subgraph Encoder
        EI["EncodeInputs<br/>Sum of all embeddings"]
    end

    subgraph Transformer
        TS["TransformerStack<br/>48 × UnifiedTransformerBlock"]
        GA["Geometric Attention<br/>(layer 0, SE(3)-invariant)"]
        SA["Standard Multi-Head Attention<br/>(layers 1–47)"]
        FFN["SwiGLU FFN<br/>(expansion ratio 8/3)"]
    end

    subgraph Output Heads
        OSEQ["Sequence Logits"]
        OSTR["Structure Logits"]
        OSS["SS8 Logits"]
        OSASA["SASA Logits"]
        OFUNC["Function Logits"]
        ORES["Residue Logits"]
        EMB["Embeddings"]
    end

    SEQ --> EI
    STR --> EI
    SS --> EI
    SASA --> EI
    FUNC --> EI
    RES --> EI
    PLDDT --> EI
    EI --> TS
    TS --> GA
    TS --> SA
    TS --> FFN
    TS --> OSEQ
    TS --> OSTR
    TS --> OSS
    TS --> OSASA
    TS --> OFUNC
    TS --> ORES
    TS --> EMB
```

The key insight of this architecture is that **modalities are fused additively at the embedding level** rather than through cross-attention or late-fusion strategies. This means each residue position carries a single `d_model`-dimensional vector that encodes information from *all* provided tracks simultaneously. The transformer's self-attention then propagates information across positions, allowing the model to resolve interdependencies between sequence, structure, and function during both forward passes and iterative generation.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L61-L147), [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L260-L374), [transformer_stack.py](esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L10-L94)

## Multimodal Track Embedding

The `EncodeInputs` module is the entry point where all protein tracks are projected into the shared `d_model`-dimensional space. Each track uses an embedding strategy tailored to its data type:

| Track | Embedding Strategy | Vocabulary Size | Output Dim |
|-------|-------------------|-----------------|------------|
| Sequence | `nn.Embedding` | 64 (amino acids + special tokens) | d_model |
| Structure | `nn.Embedding` | 4096 + 5 (codebook + special) | d_model |
| Secondary Structure (SS8) | `nn.Embedding` | 8 + 3 (classes + special) | d_model |
| SASA | `nn.Embedding` | 16 + 3 (discretized bins + special) | d_model |
| Function | 8 × `nn.Embedding` (concatenated) | 260 per depth, depth=8 | d_model |
| Residue Annotations | `nn.EmbeddingBag` (sum mode) | 1478 | d_model |
| Average pLDDT | RBF(16 bins) → `nn.Linear` | 16 → d_model | d_model |
| Per-residue pLDDT | RBF(16 bins) → `nn.Linear` | 16 → d_model | d_model |

The **function track** uses a factored embedding: 8 separate `nn.Embedding(260, d_model // 8)` modules are applied to each of the 8 depth positions, and the resulting vectors are concatenated along the feature dimension to produce a full `d_model`-dimensional embedding. This reflects the fact that function tokens are quantized via locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), where each of the 8 depth dimensions independently encodes a different bit-slice of the hash.

The **residue annotation track** uses `nn.EmbeddingBag` with `mode="sum"` because each residue position can carry multiple annotation labels (up to 16). The bag collapses the variable-length annotation list into a single vector by summing the corresponding embeddings, which is then reshaped back to `(B, L, d_model)`.

**pLDDT conditioning** applies radial basis function (RBF) expansion to scalar confidence values, projecting them through a linear layer. The average pLDDT broadcasts a global confidence signal across all positions, while per-residue pLDDT provides position-specific conditioning. These signals tell the model how much to trust any provided coordinate information.

> [!TIP]
> When no coordinates are provided, `per_res_plddt` defaults to 0 and `average_plddt` defaults to 1 — this signals "no structural constraint" to the model. When coordinates *are* provided, `per_res_plddt` is automatically set to 1.0 for positions with valid (non-NaN) coordinates, anchoring the model's structural predictions to the observed data.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L61-L147), [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L299-L348)

## Transformer Stack and Unified Block Design

The `TransformerStack` is the computational core of ESM3, consisting of `n_layers` `UnifiedTransformerBlock` instances followed by a final `LayerNorm`. For the open-source small model, this is 48 layers with 24 attention heads and 256 voting heads.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "UnifiedTransformerBlock"
        ATTN["Multi-Head Attention<br/>(with sequence_id masking)"]
        GEOM["Geometric Attention<br/>(SE(3)-invariant, layer 0 only)"]
        FFN2["SwiGLU FFN<br/>(expansion ratio 8/3)"]
    end

    X["Input x"] --> ATTN
    ATTN -->|"residual / scale"| X1["x + r1/scale"]
    X1 --> GEOM
    GEOM -->|"residual / scale"| X2["x + r2/scale"]
    X2 --> FFN2
    FFN2 -->|"residual / scale"| X3["x + r3/scale"]
```

Each `UnifiedTransformerBlock` contains up to three sub-layers applied sequentially with **scaled residual connections**:

1. **Standard Multi-Head Attention** — Applies rotary position embeddings and QK-LayerNorm. The `sequence_id` tensor creates a block-diagonal attention mask, ensuring residues from different chains or sequences don't attend to each other.

2. **Geometric Attention** (layer 0 only) — Implements SE(3)-invariant geometric reasoning via the `GeometricReasoningOriginalImpl` module, which conditions on 3D affine frames derived from backbone coordinates. The `mask_and_zero_frameless` flag ensures positions without valid coordinates are properly masked.

3. **SwiGLU Feed-Forward Network** — Uses the SwiGLU activation (`SiLU(x1) * x2`) with an expansion ratio of 8/3. The hidden dimension is rounded to the nearest multiple of 256 for hardware efficiency.

> [!TIP]
> The `residue_scaling_factor` in each block is `sqrt(n_layers / 36)`, which scales residual contributions to prevent magnitude explosion in deep stacks. For the 48-layer open model, this factor is `sqrt(48/36) ≈ 1.155`, meaning residual contributions are slightly *amplified* relative to a 36-layer baseline.

The transformer returns three outputs: the **post-norm** hidden states (used by output heads), the **pre-norm** hidden states (used as embeddings), and a list of **per-layer hidden states** (available for deeper analysis).

Sources: [transformer_stack.py](esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L10-L94), [blocks.py](esm/layers/blocks.py#L51-L157)

## Output Heads and Logit Prediction

The `OutputHeads` module projects the transformer's output back to per-track logit spaces. Each head is a `RegressionHead` — a two-layer MLP with GELU activation and LayerNorm:

```
Linear(d_model → d_model) → GELU → LayerNorm → Linear(d_model → vocab_size)
```

| Output Head | Logit Dimensions | Notes |
|-------------|-----------------|-------|
| Sequence | `(B, L, 64)` | Amino acid vocabulary |
| Structure | `(B, L, 4096)` | VQ-VAE codebook entries |
| Secondary Structure | `(B, L, 11)` | 8 SS8 classes + 3 special |
| SASA | `(B, L, 19)` | 16 discretized bins + 3 special |
| Function | `(B, L, 8, 260)` | Reshaped from flat `(B, L, 2080)` |
| Residue Annotations | `(B, L, 1478)` | Annotation vocabulary |

The function logits undergo a reshape from `(B, L, 260*8)` to `(B, L, 8, 260)`, reflecting the 8-depth quantized structure of function tokens. The `ESMOutput` dataclass also carries the raw `embeddings` tensor from the transformer's pre-norm output.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L150-L178), [regression_head.py](esm/layers/regression_head.py#L1-L112)

## Forward Pass: Token-Level Data Flow

The `forward` method orchestrates the complete token-level pipeline. It accepts raw token tensors for each track, applies intelligent defaults for any missing inputs, processes coordinate data into SE(3) frames, and returns full `ESMOutput`:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    INPUT["Token Inputs<br/>(any subset of tracks)"] --> DEFAULTS["Apply Defaults<br/>(mask/pad for missing tracks)"]
    DEFAULTS --> COORDS{"structure_coords<br/>provided?"}
    COORDS -->|Yes| AFFINE["build_affine3d_from_coordinates<br/>(N,CA,C → SE(3) frames)"]
    COORDS -->|No| NAN_AFFINE["NaN affine<br/>(no geometric constraint)"]
    AFFINE --> ALIGN["Align structure tokens<br/>with sequence special tokens<br/>(BOS/EOS/PAD/CHAINBREAK)"]
    NAN_AFFINE --> ALIGN
    ALIGN --> ENCODE["EncodeInputs<br/>(sum all track embeddings)"]
    ENCODE --> TRANSFORMER["TransformerStack<br/>(48 layers)"]
    TRANSFORMER --> HEADS["OutputHeads<br/>(per-track logits + embeddings)"]
    HEADS --> OUTPUT["ESMOutput"]
```

A critical detail in the forward pass is the **structure token alignment** logic. After default filling, structure tokens are selectively replaced to match the sequence track's special token positions — BOS, EOS, PAD, and CHAINBREAK tokens in the sequence track force corresponding special tokens in the structure track. Additionally, any structure tokens with value `-1` (a pre-tokenization placeholder) are replaced with the structure mask token. This ensures the two tracks remain synchronized at special positions even when only partial data is provided.

When no tracks are provided at all, the method raises a `ValueError` — at least one input must be non-None so the model can infer the sequence length `L` and device.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L260-L374)

## ESM3 Inference Client Interface

The `ESM3` class implements the `ESM3InferenceClient` protocol, providing a high-level API with four core operations that mirror the SDK's client interface:

| Method | Input | Output | Description |
|--------|-------|--------|-------------|
| `encode` | `ESMProtein` | `ESMProteinTensor` | Tokenizes all raw tracks into integer tensors |
| `decode` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProtein` | Detokenizes tensor tracks back to raw data |
| `logits` | `ESMProteinTensor` + `LogitsConfig` | `LogitsOutput` | Single forward pass returning selected logits/embeddings |
| `generate` | `ESMProtein` + `GenerationConfig` | `ESMProtein` | Iterative masked sampling over multiple steps |

### Encode

The `encode` method converts an `ESMProtein` (raw string/float/tensor data) into an `ESMProteinTensor` (integer token tensors). It dispatches to specialized encoding functions for each track:

- **Sequence**: `tokenize_sequence` with the `EsmSequenceTokenizer`, adding BOS/EOS special tokens.
- **Structure**: `tokenize_structure` which first runs the `StructureTokenEncoder` (VQ-VAE) on 3D coordinates to produce discrete structure tokens, then wraps them with special tokens.
- **Secondary Structure / SASA**: Discretizing tokenizers that map continuous or categorical values to integer bins.
- **Function / Residue Annotations**: `tokenize_function_annotations` which maps InterPro labels and residue-level annotations to the quantized function token vocabulary.

The method infers the protein length from whichever track is first available (sequence → secondary_structure → sasa → structure). If no length can be inferred, it raises an error.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L414-L493), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L26-L199)

### Decode

The `decode` method delegates to `decode_protein_tensor`, which reverses the tokenization for each track using the appropriate tokenizer and sub-model decoder:

- **Structure tokens → coordinates**: The `StructureTokenDecoder` (a 30-layer transformer with d_model=1280) reconstructs 3D backbone coordinates from discrete structure tokens, also producing pLDDT, PAE, and distance predictions.
- **Function tokens → annotations**: The `FunctionTokenDecoder` maps quantized function tokens back to InterPro annotations and keyword predictions.
- **Other tracks**: Standard tokenizer detokenization (SS8 class labels, SASA float values, amino acid letters).

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L495-L501)

### Logits

The `logits` method performs a single forward pass and returns only the requested outputs as specified by `LogitsConfig`. Key behaviors:

- **Automatic pLDDT conditioning**: If coordinates are provided, `per_res_plddt` is set to 1.0 for positions with valid coordinates; otherwise it is `None`.
- **Automatic mixed precision**: On CUDA, the forward pass runs under `torch.autocast` with `bfloat16` dtype, then output logits are upcast to `float32`.
- **Selective output**: The `LogitsConfig` allows requesting only specific logit tracks and optional embeddings/hidden states, avoiding unnecessary computation and memory.

```python
# Example: Get only sequence logits and embeddings
config = LogitsConfig(sequence=True, return_embeddings=True)
output = model.logits(protein_tensor, config)
# output.logits.sequence → (B, L, 64) tensor
# output.embeddings → (B, L, d_model) tensor
```

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L503-L559), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L378-L398)

### Generate

The `generate` method is the primary entry point for protein design. It wraps `batch_generate` and dispatches to one of two iterative sampling paths:

- **`iterative_sampling_raw`**: Called when inputs are `ESMProtein` objects. Encodes to tokens, runs iterative sampling, then decodes back.
- **`iterative_sampling_tokens`**: Called when inputs are `ESMProteinTensor` objects. Operates entirely in token space, avoiding encode/decode overhead.

Both paths implement the same core algorithm: iterative masked sampling over multiple steps, controlled by `GenerationConfig`.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L377-L412)

## Iterative Masked Sampling

ESM3 generates protein data through an **iterative masked denoising** process. Starting from a fully or partially masked input, the model repeatedly (1) performs a forward pass to predict logits for all positions, (2) samples tokens at a subset of masked positions, and (3) fills those positions with the sampled tokens. This continues until all masks are resolved.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Partially Masked Input<br/>(some tracks have <mask> tokens)"] --> COUNT["Count total masked positions<br/>per track"]
    COUNT --> STEP["Step i / num_steps"]
    STEP --> FWD["Forward Pass<br/>(logits for all tracks)"]
    FWD --> SCHEDULE["Decoding Schedule<br/>(cosine or linear)"]
    SCHEDULE --> NUM["Compute # tokens to unmask<br/>this step"]
    NUM --> STRATEGY{"Unmasking Strategy"}
    STRATEGY -->|entropy|"Select lowest-entropy<br/>masked positions"
    STRATEGY -->|random|"Randomly select<br/>masked positions"
    STRATEGY --> SAMPLE["Sample tokens from logits<br/>(temperature, top-p)"]
    SAMPLE --> FILL["Fill sampled tokens<br/>into masked positions"]
    FILL --> DONE{"All masks<br/>resolved?"}
    DONE -->|No| STEP
    DONE -->|Yes| OUTPUT["Fully Decoded Output"]
```

The sampling loop is governed by the `GenerationConfig` parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `track` | `""` | Which track to generate (e.g., `"sequence"`, `"structure"`, `"sasa"`) |
| `schedule` | `"cosine"` | How many tokens to unmask per step — cosine reveals more early, linear is uniform |
| `strategy` | `"random"` | Which masked positions to unmask — `"entropy"` picks most confident, `"random"` picks randomly |
| `num_steps` | `20` | Total number of iterative forward-sample rounds |
| `temperature` | `1.0` | Sampling temperature for logit softmax |
| `temperature_annealing` | `True` | If enabled, temperature decreases quadratically from initial to 0.001 over steps |
| `top_p` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold |
| `condition_on_coordinates_only` | `True` | If true, clears structure tokens so the model generates from coordinate frames only |

The **temperature annealing** formula is `max(initial_temp - step_ratio, 0.001)²`, where `step_ratio = step / (num_steps - 1)`. This means sampling becomes increasingly deterministic in later steps, which helps the model refine its predictions without introducing noise at the final stage.

The **decoding schedule** determines what fraction of tokens remain masked after each step. For the cosine schedule, the fraction of still-masked tokens follows a cosine curve from 1 to 0, meaning more tokens are revealed in early steps and fewer in later steps — a coarse-to-fine generation strategy.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L99-L398), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326)

## Pretrained Models and Configuration

The open-source ESM3 release includes the following pretrained models, all registered in `LOCAL_MODEL_REGISTRY`:

| Model Name | Constant | Architecture | Parameters |
|------------|----------|-------------|------------|
| `esm3_sm_open_v1` | `ESM3_OPEN_SMALL` | ESM3 (d_model=1536, 24 heads, 48 layers) | ~1.4B |
| `esm3_structure_encoder_v0` | `ESM3_STRUCTURE_ENCODER_V0` | StructureTokenEncoder (d_model=1024, 2 layers) | — |
| `esm3_structure_decoder_v0` | `ESM3_STRUCTURE_DECODER_V0` | StructureTokenDecoder (d_model=1280, 30 layers) | — |
| `esm3_function_decoder_v0` | `ESM3_FUNCTION_DECODER_V0` | FunctionTokenDecoder (d_model=1024, 3 layers) | — |

The model name normalization system accepts several aliases for the same checkpoint — `"esm3-open-2024-03"`, `"esm3-sm-open-v1"`, and `"esm3-open"` all resolve to `ESM3_OPEN_SMALL`. Models are loaded via `ESM3.from_pretrained()`, which automatically selects CUDA if available and casts to `bfloat16` on GPU:

```python
model = ESM3.from_pretrained("esm3_sm_open_v1")
# Equivalent: ESM3.from_pretrained("esm3-open")
```

The structure encoder, structure decoder, and function decoder are **lazily instantiated** — they are stored as factory functions (`structure_encoder_fn`, `structure_decoder_fn`, `function_decoder_fn`) and only loaded to GPU when first accessed via `get_structure_encoder()`, `get_structure_decoder()`, or `get_function_decoder()`. This avoids loading ~1B additional decoder parameters until they are actually needed.

Sources: [pretrained.py](esm/pretrained.py#L24-L134), [models.py](esm/utils/constants/models.py#L1-L29), [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L220-L258)

## Track Tokenizer Collection

ESM3 relies on a coordinated set of six tokenizers, packaged as a `TokenizerCollection` that satisfies the `TokenizerCollectionProtocol`:

| Tokenizer | Class | Key Behavior |
|-----------|-------|-------------|
| `sequence` | `EsmSequenceTokenizer` | BPE tokenizer, 64 vocab, adds BOS/EOS |
| `structure` | `StructureTokenizer` | Wraps VQ-VAE encoder output, 4096 codebook |
| `secondary_structure` | `SecondaryStructureTokenizer` | 8-class SS8 discretization |
| `sasa` | `SASADiscretizingTokenizer` | 16-bin solvent accessibility |
| `function` | `InterProQuantizedTokenizer` | LSH-based 8-depth quantization, 260 vocab per depth |
| `residue_annotations` | `ResidueAnnotationsTokenizer` | 1478-label residue annotation vocabulary |

Each tokenizer provides `mask_token_id`, `pad_token_id`, `bos_token_id`, and `eos_token_id` — these special tokens are essential for the iterative sampling process, as they define which positions are "unknown" and need to be generated.

Sources: [tokenization/__init__.py](esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L15-L46)

## Sub-Models: Structure Encoder and Decoder

### StructureTokenEncoder

The structure encoder compresses 3D backbone coordinates (N, CA, C atoms) into discrete tokens via a VQ-VAE pipeline. It operates on **local structural neighborhoods**:

1. **KNN Graph Construction**: For each residue, find the 16 nearest neighbors in 3D space (by CA distance).
2. **Local Neighborhood Encoding**: Reshape to `(B*L, 16)` batches of local neighborhoods. Apply relative positional embeddings, then pass through a `GeometricEncoderStack` (2 geometric-only transformer layers with d_model=1024).
3. **Query Node Extraction**: Take the embedding of the query residue (always the first KNN neighbor since self-distance is 0).
4. **VQ-VAE Quantization**: Project through `pre_vq_proj` (1024→128), then quantize via `EMACodebook` (4096 codes, 128 dimensions).

This local receptive field design means each structure token captures the **local backbone geometry** around a residue, not global fold information. Global structural coherence emerges from the main ESM3 transformer's attention mechanism operating on the sequence of structure tokens.

### StructureTokenDecoder

The structure decoder reconstructs 3D coordinates from discrete structure tokens using a 30-layer `TransformerStack` (d_model=1280, 20 heads, no geometric attention). It produces:

- **Backbone coordinates** via `Dim6RotStructureHead` (6D rotation representation)
- **Pairwise predictions** (distogram, direction, predicted aligned error) via `PairwisePredictionHead`
- **Per-residue pLDDT** via a `RegressionHead`

Sources: [vqvae.py](esm/models/vqvae.py#L179-L322), [vqvae.py](esm/models/vqvae.py#L325-L398), [function_decoder.py](esm/models/function_decoder.py#L54-L176)

## Sub-Models: Function Token Decoder

The `FunctionTokenDecoder` translates quantized function tokens back into human-interpretable annotations. It uses a compact 3-layer transformer (d_model=1024, 8 heads, GELU FFN) that:

1. **Unpacks LSH bits**: Each of the 8 depth positions has 8 bits, yielding 64 binary features per residue. Each bit gets its own embedding offset so they receive distinct representations.
2. **Pools across positions**: Mean-pools the transformer output across the sequence dimension.
3. **Predicts three heads**: `keyword_logits` (58,641 keywords), `keyword_tfidf` (regressed TF-IDF values), and `interpro_logits` (29,026 InterPro classes).

The decode method supports thresholding (`annotation_threshold`, `keywords_threshold`) and merging of nearby annotations (`annotation_gap_merge_max`) to produce clean `FunctionAnnotation` objects with label, start, and end positions.

Sources: [function_decoder.py](esm/models/function_decoder.py#L21-L176)

## Where to Go Next

- For a deep understanding of how raw protein data becomes tokens, read [Sequence and Structure Tokenizers](10-sequence-and-structure-tokenizers) and [VQ-VAE Structure Encoding](11-vq-vae-structure-encoding).
- For the geometric attention mechanism that gives ESM3 its 3D reasoning capability, see [Geometric Attention and SE(3) Invariance](13-geometric-attention-and-se-3-invariance).
- For the iterative sampling algorithm in full detail, see [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling) and [Noise Schedules and Unmasking Strategies](17-noise-schedules-and-unmasking-strategies).
- For deployment options (Forge API, local inference, SageMaker), see [Forge API Client](19-forge-api-client) and [Local Inference Client](20-local-inference-client).
- For the lighter-weight representation-only alternative, see [ESM C Representation Model](9-esm-c-representation-model).

# ESM C Representation Model



ESM C is EvolutionaryScale's **sequence-only representation model** — a streamlined transformer designed for extracting high-quality protein embeddings without the overhead of multi-track generative infrastructure. Where [ESM3](8-esm3-multimodal-generative-model) processes sequence, structure, secondary structure, SASA, and function tokens through geometric attention layers, ESM C strips the architecture down to its essence: a deep transformer stack operating on amino acid tokens alone, producing per-residue embeddings and hidden states that power downstream tasks from enzyme activity prediction to remote homology detection. This design philosophy yields a model that is simpler to deploy, faster to infer, and whose representations often outperform multimodal alternatives on tasks that do not require structure conditioning.

## Architectural Philosophy: Sequence-Only by Design

The central insight behind ESM C is that **not every protein understanding task requires structural or functional token tracks**. Many downstream applications — predicting solubility, classifying enzyme class, or computing similarity between sequences — benefit primarily from rich contextual embeddings rather than full generative capabilities. ESM C exploits this by removing all auxiliary tokenization pipelines (structure VQ-VAE, SASA discretization, secondary structure classification, InterPro function tokens) and all geometric attention blocks, leaving a pure sequence-to-embedding transformer.

This architectural decision has three concrete implications. First, the `encode` step accepts only an `ESMProtein.sequence` string and tokenizes it with the standard `EsmSequenceTokenizer` — no structure encoder, no coordinate processing. Second, the transformer stack is constructed with `n_layers_geom=0`, meaning every block uses standard multi-head attention with rotary embeddings rather than the SE(3)-equivariant geometric attention used in ESM3. Third, the output head produces only `sequence_logits` over the 64-token vocabulary; there are no structure, SASA, or function prediction heads.

Sources: [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L56-L95), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L108-L138), [pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L69-L88)

## Model Architecture

The ESM C model is implemented as the `ESMC` class, which inherits from both `nn.Module` and `ESMCInferenceClient`. Its forward pass follows a clean three-stage pipeline: **token embedding → transformer stack → sequence head**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input: Amino Acid Sequence<br/>(e.g. 'MKWVTFISL')"] --> B["EsmSequenceTokenizer<br/>Character-level BPE<br/>+ &lt;cls&gt; ... &lt;eos&gt; wrapping"]
    B --> C["nn.Embedding(64, d_model)<br/>Token ID → Dense Vector"]
    C --> D{"Flash Attention<br/>Available?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["unpad_input()<br/>Remove padding positions"]
    D -- No --> F["Keep padded tensor<br/>[B, L, d_model]"]
    E --> G["TransformerStack<br/>n_layers × UnifiedTransformerBlock<br/>(Standard MHA + SwiGLU FFN)"]
    F --> G
    G --> H{"Flash Attention<br/>Used?"}
    H -- Yes --> I["pad_input()<br/>Restore [B, L, d_model] shape"]
    H -- No --> J["Continue with<br/>[B, L, d_model]"]
    I --> K["LayerNorm"]
    J --> K
    K --> L["RegressionHead<br/>d_model → d_model → GELU → LN → 64"]
    L --> M["ESMCOutput<br/>sequence_logits [B, L, 64]<br/>embeddings [B, L, d_model]<br/>hidden_states [n_layers, B, L, d_model]"]
```

The embedding layer maps 64 possible token IDs (33 standard amino acid tokens plus special tokens including `<cls>`, `<pad>`, `<eos>`, `<unk>`, `<mask>`, and chain break `|`) into a `d_model`-dimensional space. The transformer stack then processes these embeddings through `n_layers` identical `UnifiedTransformerBlock` instances — each comprising LayerNorm → QK-Normed Multi-Head Attention with Rotary Embeddings → residual → LayerNorm → SwiGLU FFN → residual. The final LayerNorm produces the output embeddings, while a `RegressionHead` (a two-layer MLP with GELU activation and intermediate LayerNorm) projects them to sequence logits.

> [!TIP]
> When Flash Attention is available, ESM C uses the **unpad/pad pattern**: before entering the transformer, padding tokens are removed via `unpad_input`, the transformer processes only real tokens, and `pad_input` restores the original batch shape afterward. This eliminates wasted computation on pad positions and can significantly speed up inference on variable-length batches.

Sources: [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L56-L95), [transformer_stack.py](/esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L23-L95), [blocks.py](/esm/layers/blocks.py#L65-L158), [regression_head.py](/esm/layers/regression_head.py#L1-L23), [attention.py](/esm/layers/attention.py#L16-L59)

## Model Variants and Hyperparameters

Two ESM C checkpoints are available for local inference, differing in depth, width, and head count. A larger 6B-parameter variant exists on the Forge API platform but is not distributed for local use.

| Property | ESMC 300M | ESMC 600M |
|---|---|---|
| **Model Name** | `esmc_300m` | `esmc_600m` |
| **Forge Name** | `esmc-300m-2024-12` | `esmc-600m-2024-12` |
| **d_model** | 960 | 1152 |
| **n_heads** | 15 | 18 |
| **n_layers** | 30 | 36 |
| **d_head** | 64 | 64 |
| **FFN Type** | SwiGLU (8/3× expansion) | SwiGLU (8/3× expansion) |
| **Geometric Attention** | None (`n_layers_geom=0`) | None (`n_layers_geom=0`) |
| **Vocab Size** | 64 | 64 |
| **HuggingFace Repo** | `EvolutionaryScale/esmc-300m-2024-12` | `EvolutionaryScale/esmc-600m-2024-12` |

Both models are loaded via `ESMC.from_pretrained(model_name)`, which downloads weights from HuggingFace, applies them to the model, and automatically casts to `bfloat16` on CUDA devices. The `from_pretrained` class method delegates to `load_local_model`, which looks up the model name in the `LOCAL_MODEL_REGISTRY` dictionary and calls the corresponding builder function.

Sources: [pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L69-L105), [models.py](/esm/utils/constants/models.py#L1-L12), [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L108-L118)

## Tokenization Pipeline

ESM C uses a single tokenizer — the `EsmSequenceTokenizer` — which is a character-level BPE tokenizer (with no merge operations, making it effectively a per-character vocabulary lookup). The tokenizer wraps each input sequence with `<cls>` at the start and `<eos>` at the end, and supports `<mask>` tokens for masked positions and `|` for chain breaks. The vocabulary consists of 33 amino acid characters (20 standard + 5 ambiguous + special tokens) plus control tokens, totaling 64 entries.

The `encode` method on the `ESMC` class takes an `ESMProtein` with a `sequence` field, runs it through `_tokenize` (which internally calls `encoding.tokenize_sequence` with `add_special_tokens=True`), and returns an `ESMProteinTensor` containing only the `sequence` tensor — all other tracks (structure, sasa, etc.) are `None`. Conversely, `decode` takes an `ESMProteinTensor`, strips padding and special tokens, and maps token IDs back to amino acid characters.

> [!TIP]
> Because ESM C's `encode` only processes the `sequence` field, any structural coordinates or functional annotations provided in the `ESMProtein` input are silently ignored. If you need structure-aware representations, use [ESM3](8-esm3-multimodal-generative-model) instead.

Sources: [sequence_tokenizer.py](/esm/tokenization/sequence_tokenizer.py#L10-L72), [encoding.py](/esm/utils/encoding.py#L37-L49), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L140-L162), [__init__.py](/esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L57-L58)

## The Inference API: ESMCInferenceClient

ESM C implements the `ESMCInferenceClient` abstract base class, which defines a focused subset of the full `ESM3InferenceClient` interface. This stripped-down contract reflects ESM C's representation-only purpose — there are no `generate`, `forward_and_sample`, or `batch_generate` methods, because ESM C is not a generative model.

| Method | Purpose | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `encode` | Tokenize raw sequence | `ESMProtein` | `ESMProteinTensor` |
| `decode` | Detokenize back to sequence | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProtein` |
| `logits` | Forward pass with configurable output | `ESMProteinTensor` + `LogitsConfig` | `LogitsOutput` |
| `raw_model` | Access underlying `nn.Module` | — | `ESMC` instance |

The `logits` method is the primary entry point for extracting representations. It accepts a `LogitsConfig` that controls what the model returns:

- **`sequence=True`**: Returns per-position logits over the 64-token vocabulary via `ForwardTrackData.sequence` — useful for masked token prediction or pseudo-likelihood scoring.
- **`return_embeddings=True`**: Returns the final-layer embeddings (post-LayerNorm) as a `[B, L, d_model]` tensor — the most commonly used output for downstream tasks.
- **`return_hidden_states=True`**: Returns all intermediate layer outputs as a `[n_layers, B, L, d_model]` tensor — essential for probing layer-wise behavior or selecting task-optimal layers.
- **`ith_hidden_layer`**: When set to a non-negative integer, returns only that specific layer's hidden states instead of all layers — critical for memory-efficient inference with large models (especially the 6B variant on Forge).

The `logits` method automatically wraps the forward pass in `torch.no_grad()` and `torch.autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16)` on CUDA, ensuring efficient inference without manual context management.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L503-L532), [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L378-L411), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L196-L226)

## Output Data Structures

The raw `forward` method returns an `ESMCOutput` dataclass containing three tensors, while the SDK-level `logits` method wraps these into a `LogitsOutput` with configurable availability:

| Field | Shape | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sequence_logits` | `[B, L, 64]` | Per-position logits over the amino acid vocabulary |
| `embeddings` | `[B, L, d_model]` | Final-layer output after LayerNorm (per-residue embeddings) |
| `hidden_states` | `[n_layers, B, L, d_model]` | All intermediate layer outputs (or single layer if `ith_hidden_layer` specified) |

The `hidden_states` tensor is constructed by stacking each `UnifiedTransformerBlock`'s output (the pre-norm residual stream) across all layers. Note that `embeddings` differs from the last entry of `hidden_states`: `embeddings` is the post-LayerNorm output of the full transformer stack, while `hidden_states[-1]` is the pre-norm residual. For most downstream use cases, `embeddings` is the correct choice.

Sources: [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L28-L32), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L108-L138), [transformer_stack.py](/esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L76-L95)

## Usage Patterns

### Local Inference

Loading and running ESM C locally requires only the `esm` package and a GPU (CPU works but is significantly slower):

```python
from esm.models.esmc import ESMC
from esm.sdk.api import ESMProtein, LogitsConfig

model = ESMC.from_pretrained("esmc_300m")  # or "esmc_600m"

protein = ESMProtein(sequence="MKWVTFISLLFLFSSAYSRGVFRR")
protein_tensor = model.encode(protein)

output = model.logits(
    protein_tensor,
    LogitsConfig(
        sequence=True,
        return_embeddings=True,
        return_hidden_states=True,
    ),
)

# Access results
embeddings = output.embeddings          # [1, L, d_model]
logits = output.logits.sequence         # [1, L, 64]
hiddens = output.hidden_states          # [n_layers, 1, L, d_model]
```

### Forge API Inference

For the larger 6B model or cloud-based inference, the Forge API client follows the same `ESMCInferenceClient` interface:

```python
from esm.sdk import client
from esm.sdk.api import ESMProtein, LogitsConfig

model = client(model="esmc-300m-2024-12", url="https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai", token=token)
protein = ESMProtein(sequence="MKWVTFISLLFLFSSAYSRGVFRR")
protein_tensor = model.encode(protein)
output = model.logits(protein_tensor, LogitsConfig(return_embeddings=True))
```

### Raw Forward (Bypassing SDK)

For maximum control, you can call `model.forward` directly with pre-tokenized inputs:

```python
sequences = ["MKWVTFISLLFLFSSAYSRGVFRR", "AQVINTFDGVADYLQTYHKLPDNYIT"]
input_ids = model._tokenize(sequences)  # [B, L] token IDs
output = model(input_ids)               # ESMCOutput directly
```

### Selecting a Specific Hidden Layer

For memory-efficient extraction of intermediate representations (particularly important for the 6B model on Forge), use `ith_hidden_layer`:

```python
# Get only layer 20's hidden states instead of all 30+ layers
output = model.logits(
    protein_tensor,
    LogitsConfig(return_hidden_states=True, ith_hidden_layer=20),
)
# output.hidden_states shape: [1, B, L, d_model] (single layer)
```

Sources: [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L96-L106), [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L196-L226), [esmc.py](/cookbook/snippets/esmc.py#L1-L86)

## ESM C vs ESM3: Architectural Comparison

Understanding when to choose ESM C over ESM3 requires a clear picture of their architectural differences and the resulting trade-offs:

| Dimension | ESM C | ESM3 |
|---|---|---|
| **Input Modalities** | Sequence only | Sequence, Structure, SS, SASA, Function |
| **Attention Type** | Standard MHA (all layers) | Geometric MHA (first `n_layers_geom`) + Standard MHA |
| **Output Heads** | Sequence logits only | Sequence, Structure, SS, SASA, Function logits |
| **Tokenizers Required** | `EsmSequenceTokenizer` only | Full `TokenizerCollection` (6 tokenizers) |
| **Structure Encoder/Decoder** | None | VQ-VAE encoder + decoder |
| **Generative Capability** | None (representation only) | Iterative masked sampling across all tracks |
| **Inference Client** | `ESMCInferenceClient` (3 methods) | `ESM3InferenceClient` (7+ methods) |
| **Embedding Focus** | Primary design goal | Secondary to generation |
| **Deployment Complexity** | Single model file | Model + structure encoder + structure decoder + function decoder |

Choose ESM C when your task requires **high-quality sequence embeddings** for downstream prediction, similarity search, or transfer learning. Choose [ESM3](8-esm3-multimodal-generative-model) when you need to **condition on or generate structural or functional information**, or when iterative masked generation is required.

Sources: [esmc.py](/esm/models/esmc.py#L56-L95), [esm3.py](/esm/models/esm3.py#L50-L80), [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L431-L532)

## Transformer Block Internals

Each of ESM C's `UnifiedTransformerBlock` instances (with `use_geom_attn=False`) executes the following computation per layer:

1. **LayerNorm → QKV Projection**: Input `x` is layer-normalized and linearly projected to query, key, and value via a fused `layernorm_qkv` operation.
2. **QK LayerNorm**: Query and key tensors are independently layer-normalized (controlled by `qk_layernorm=True`), stabilizing attention magnitude.
3. **Rotary Position Embedding**: Applied to queries and keys, encoding relative position information directly into the attention computation.
4. **Multi-Head Attention**: Standard scaled dot-product attention with `n_heads` heads, each with `d_head = d_model // n_heads` dimensions. Sequence identity masks prevent cross-attention between different sequences in a batch.
5. **Residual Connection**: The attention output is divided by a `residue_scaling_factor` (proportional to `sqrt(n_layers / 36)`) before being added to the input — this prevents residual magnitude explosion in deep stacks.
6. **SwiGLU FFN**: The post-attention residual passes through a LayerNorm → Linear(up-project with 8/3× expansion, rounded to 256 multiples) → SwiGLU activation (SiLU gate × value) → Linear(down-project) → residual addition, again with scaling.

The `residue_scaling_factor` is computed as `sqrt(n_layers / 36)`, meaning the 30-layer 300M model uses `sqrt(30/36) ≈ 0.913` and the 36-layer 600M model uses `sqrt(36/36) = 1.0`. This normalization ensures that the variance of the residual stream remains stable regardless of model depth.

Sources: [blocks.py](/esm/layers/blocks.py#L95-L158), [attention.py](/esm/layers/attention.py#L16-L59), [transformer_stack.py](/esm/layers/transformer_stack.py#L43-L60)

## Practical Guidance on Layer Selection

When extracting embeddings for downstream tasks, the choice of which layer to use matters significantly. The `return_embeddings` flag returns the final post-LayerNorm output, which is a strong default for most applications. However, research on transformer representations consistently shows that **different layers encode different levels of abstraction**: early layers capture local biochemical properties (hydrophobicity, charge), middle layers capture structural motifs (secondary structure propensities), and later layers capture global functional and evolutionary signals.

For a blind choice without task-specific probing, the **second-to-last hidden layer** is often a robust pick. An alternative heuristic is to extract the layer approximately **two-thirds through the network** (layer 20 for the 300M model, layer 24 for the 600M model). For the Forge-hosted 6B model with 80 layers, requesting a single layer at a time via `ith_hidden_layer` is not just a recommendation but a practical necessity due to the memory cost of materializing all 80 layers simultaneously.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L378-L398), [2_embed.ipynb](/cookbook/tutorials/2_embed.ipynb)

## Next Steps

- To understand the full multimodal architecture that ESM C simplifies, see [ESM3 Multimodal Generative Model](8-esm3-multimodal-generative-model).
- For details on the sequence tokenizer shared by both models, see [Sequence and Structure Tokenizers](10-sequence-and-structure-tokenizers).
- For the transformer components that ESM C uses, see [Transformer Stack Design](14-transformer-stack-design) and [Rotary Embeddings and SwiGLU](15-rotary-embeddings-and-swiglu).
- To deploy ESM C at scale, see [Forge API Client](19-forge-api-client) or [Local Inference Client](20-local-inference-client).

# Sequence and Structure Tokenizers



ESM3 is a multimodal protein model that operates on discrete tokens across six parallel tracks. Two of those tracks — **sequence** and **structure** — are the foundational modalities: sequence captures the linear amino acid chain, while structure encodes the three-dimensional backbone geometry. This page examines how raw biological inputs are converted into integer token IDs that the transformer can process, and how the two tokenizers embody fundamentally different design philosophies — one a straightforward character-level vocabulary, the other a learned VQ-VAE codebook operating on 3D coordinates.

## The Tokenizer Protocol: A Unified Contract

Before examining the individual tokenizers, it is essential to understand the contract they all satisfy. Every tokenizer in ESM3 implements the `EsmTokenizerBase` protocol, which defines a minimal interface of special tokens and encode/decode methods:

| Protocol Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `mask_token` / `mask_token_id` | Placeholder for unknown or to-be-predicted positions |
| `bos_token` / `bos_token_id` | Beginning-of-sequence marker |
| `eos_token` / `eos_token_id` | End-of-sequence marker |
| `pad_token` / `pad_token_id` | Padding for batch alignment |
| `chain_break_token` / `chain_break_token_id` | Delimiter between protein chains in a complex |
| `encode()` | Convert raw input → token IDs |
| `decode()` | Convert token IDs → raw input |
| `all_token_ids` | Complete set of valid token IDs |
| `special_token_ids` | IDs reserved for control, not data |

Because `EsmTokenizerBase` is a `@runtime_checkable` Protocol (not an abstract base class), tokenizers are free to inherit from whatever parent makes sense — `PreTrainedTokenizerFast` for sequence, or a plain class for structure — while still being substitutable wherever the protocol is required. This duck-typing design allows the `TokenizerCollection` dataclass to aggregate all six tokenizers behind a single `TokenizerCollectionProtocol`, letting downstream code treat them uniformly.

Sources: [tokenizer_base.py](/esm/tokenization/tokenizer_base.py#L1-L26), [__init__.py](/esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L1-L67)

## EsmSequenceTokenizer: Character-Level Amino Acid Encoding

The `EsmSequenceTokenizer` converts a protein sequence string (e.g., `"MVLSEGEW..."`) into a sequence of integer token IDs. Despite inheriting from HuggingFace's `PreTrainedTokenizerFast` and technically using a BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) backend, it performs **no subword merging whatsoever** — the BPE merges list is intentionally empty. This makes it a pure character-level tokenizer where each amino acid symbol maps to exactly one token ID.

### Vocabulary Layout

The vocabulary is defined as a fixed list of 33 tokens in `esm/utils/constants/esm3.py`:

| Index Range | Tokens | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `<cls>` | 1 | BOS /CLS marker |
| 1 | `<pad>` | 1 | Padding |
| 2 | `<eos>` | 1 | End-of-sequence |
| 3 | `<unk>` | 1 | Unknown character |
| 4–25 | `L A G V S E R T I D P K Q N F Y M H W C X B U Z` | 22 | Standard + rare amino acids |
| 26 | `O` | 1 | Pyrrolysine |
| 27 | `.` | 1 | Gap (alignment placeholder) |
| 28 | `-` | 1 | Gap variant |
| 29 | `\|` | 1 | Chain break delimiter |
| 30–32 | (reserved/unused in standard vocab) | — | — |
| 31 | `\|` (chain_break_token) | — | Same as index 29 |
| 32 | `<mask>` | 1 | Mask token for generation |

The 20 canonical amino acids occupy positions 4–23 in frequency-sorted order (Leucine most common at index 4), followed by non-standard residues `X`, `B`, `U`, `Z`, and `O`. The chain break token `|` enables multi-chain proteins to be represented as a single token sequence with explicit chain boundaries.

### Template Processing

When `add_special_tokens=True` (the default), the tokenizer applies `TemplateProcessing` to wrap the encoded sequence:

```
<cls> [amino_acid_tokens] <eos>
```

This means a sequence of length *L* produces a token tensor of length *L + 2*. The BOS token is aliased to `<cls>` — the `bos_token` property explicitly returns `self.cls_token`, and `bos_token_id` returns `self.cls_token_id`, reflecting the convention that ESM3 never uses a separate BOS symbol distinct from CLS.

### Encoding Flow

The `tokenize_sequence` function in `encoding.py` provides the canonical path from raw string to tensor:

1. Replace all underscore mask placeholders (`_`) with the `<mask>` token string
2. Call `sequence_tokenizer.encode()` which applies the character-level BPE mapping plus template processing
3. Wrap the resulting list as a `torch.int64` tensor

> [!TIP]
> When constructing default (fully masked) sequence tokens, the pattern is: fill a tensor of length *L+2* with `mask_token_id`, then set index 0 to `bos_token_id` and index −1 to `eos_token_id`. This is how ESM3 represents "generate this sequence from scratch."

Sources: [sequence_tokenizer.py](/esm/tokenization/sequence_tokenizer.py#L1-L135), [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L1-L131), [encoding.py](/esm/utils/encoding.py#L46-L60)

## StructureTokenizer: Coordinate-Derived Discrete Codes

The `StructureTokenizer` is architecturally distinct from the sequence tokenizer. It does **not** perform string-to-ID mapping — indeed, its `encode()` and `decode()` methods explicitly raise `NotImplementedError`. Instead, it serves as a **registry of special token IDs** for the structure track, while the actual encoding and decoding of 3D coordinates is delegated to the `StructureTokenEncoder` and `StructureTokenDecoder` neural networks (detailed in [VQ-VAE Structure Encoding](11-vq-vae-structure-encoding)).

### Vocabulary Layout

The structure vocabulary consists of a VQ-VAE codebook of size 4096 plus 5 special tokens appended after the codebook entries:

| Token | ID | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Data tokens | 0 – 4095 | VQ-VAE codebook entries (learned 3D structure prototypes) |
| `MASK` | 4096 | Unknown / to-be-predicted structure |
| `EOS` | 4097 | End-of-sequence |
| `BOS` | 4098 | Beginning-of-sequence |
| `PAD` | 4099 | Padding |
| `CHAINBREAK` | 4100 | Chain boundary delimiter |
| `UNDEFINED` | 955 | Special marker within codebook range |

The total vocabulary size is **4101** (4096 + 5). Notice that the special token IDs are computed as offsets from the codebook size, ensuring they never collide with learned codebook entries. The `STRUCTURE_UNDEFINED_TOKEN` (955) is notable — it lives within the codebook range and represents residues where backbone coordinates could not be determined.

### Why No String Representation

The string-access properties (`mask_token`, `bos_token`, etc.) all raise `NotImplementedError` with the message "Structure tokens are defined on 3D coordinates, not strings." This is a deliberate design decision: structure tokens are produced by a neural encoder that maps continuous 3D coordinate tensors to discrete indices, and there is no meaningful human-readable string for a codebook entry. Only the integer ID interface is valid.

Sources: [structure_tokenizer.py](/esm/tokenization/structure_tokenizer.py#L1-L84), [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L14-L38)

## Encoding Pipeline: From Raw Inputs to Token Tensors

The following diagram shows how raw protein data flows through both tokenizers into the unified token representation consumed by the ESM3 transformer:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Inputs
        SEQ["Amino Acid String<br/>'MVLSEGEW...'"]
        COORDS["Atom37 Coordinates<br/>(L, 37, 3)"]
    end

    subgraph Sequence_Path["Sequence Tokenizer Path"]
        SEQ --> MASK_REPLACE["Replace '_' → '&lt;mask&gt;'"]
        MASK_REPLACE --> BPE["Character-Level BPE<br/>(no merges)"]
        BPE --> TEMPLATE["TemplateProcessing<br/>Add &lt;cls&gt; … &lt;eos&gt;"]
        TEMPLATE --> SEQ_TOK["Sequence Tokens<br/>torch.int64 (L+2,)"]
    end

    subgraph Structure_Path["Structure Tokenizer Path"]
        COORDS --> PROTEIN_CHAIN["ProroteinChain.from_atom37()"]
        PROTEIN_CHAIN --> ENCODER_INPUTS["Extract coords, pLDDT,<br/>residue_index"]
        ENCODER_INPUTS --> VQ_ENCODER["StructureTokenEncoder<br/>(Geometric Transformer + EMA Codebook)"]
        VQ_ENCODER --> CODEBOOK_LOOKUP["Nearest Codebook Entry<br/>argmin of L2 distances"]
        CODEBOOK_LOOKUP --> SPECIAL_PAD["Add BOS/EOS tokens<br/>Pad with mask_token_id"]
        SPECIAL_PAD --> STRUCT_TOK["Structure Tokens<br/>torch.int64 (L+2,)"]
    end

    SEQ_TOK --> ESM3["ESM3 Transformer"]
    STRUCT_TOK --> ESM3
```

### Structure Encoding in Detail

The `tokenize_structure` function orchestrates the structure encoding pipeline. Given an atom37 coordinate tensor of shape `(L, 37, 3)` and an optional reference sequence:

1. **ProteinChain construction**: Coordinates are wrapped into a `ProteinChain` object via `from_atom37()`, which extracts the N, CA, C backbone atoms and builds SE(3) frame representations.
2. **Encoder input extraction**: The chain produces `(1, L, 37, 3)` coordinates, `(1, L)` pLDDT scores, and `(1, L)` residue indices — all moved to the encoder's device.
3. **VQ-VAE encoding**: The `StructureTokenEncoder.encode()` method runs a geometric transformer over local KNN neighborhoods (k=16) of backbone frames, projects to a 128-dimensional latent space, then performs nearest-neighbor lookup in the EMA codebook to obtain `(1, L)` integer indices.
4. **Special token insertion**: BOS (4098) is prepended and EOS (4097) is appended, with the interior positions initialized to `mask_token_id` (4096) before being overwritten by the encoder output.

> [!TIP]
> The structure encoder requires the first 3 backbone atoms (N, CA, C) in the atom37 dimension — it explicitly slices `coords[..., :3, :]` before building affine frames. If your input coordinates lack these atoms, the encoder will produce undefined results.

Sources: [encoding.py](/esm/utils/encoding.py#L62-L108), [vqvae.py](/esm/models/vqvae.py#L252-L328)

## Decoding Pipeline: From Token Tensors Back to Biology

Decoding reverses the encoding process, but the two tracks differ significantly in complexity:

### Sequence Decoding

Sequence decoding is a direct table lookup — `sequence_tokenizer.decode()` maps each integer ID back to its character, then post-processing strips `<cls>`/`<eos>` and replaces `<mask>` with the underscore placeholder `_`. This is lossless: encoding then decoding reproduces the original string exactly (modulo mask placeholders).

### Structure Decoding

Structure decoding is **generative**, not lookup-based. The `StructureTokenDecoder` is a 30-layer transformer that takes structure token IDs as input and produces:

| Output | Description |
|---|---|
| `bb_pred` | Predicted backbone atom coordinates (N, CA, C) |
| `plddt` | Per-residue confidence score |
| `ptm` | Predicted TM-score (global quality) |
| `predicted_aligned_error` | Pairwise predicted aligned error matrix |

The decoder validates that BOS and EOS tokens are correctly positioned before processing, and strips them from the output coordinates. After decoding, `ProteinChain.from_backbone_atom_coordinates()` reconstructs the full atom37 representation and infers oxygen atom positions. This means structure decoding is inherently **lossy** — the VQ-VAE compression from continuous 3D to discrete codes introduces quantization error, and the decoder's reconstruction adds further approximation.

Sources: [decoding.py](/esm/utils/decoding.py#L1-L150), [vqvae.py](/esm/models/vqvae.py#L330-L438)

## Comparative Design Analysis

The following table highlights the fundamental architectural differences between the two tokenizers:

| Dimension | Sequence Tokenizer | Structure Tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| **Input modality** | String (characters) | 3D coordinates (tensors) |
| **Vocabulary size** | 33 | 4101 (4096 codebook + 5 special) |
| **Mapping mechanism** | Deterministic character → ID table | Learned VQ-VAE encoder (neural network) |
| **Encode/decode** | Lossless, table lookup | Lossy, neural encode + neural decode |
| **Special token IDs** | Fixed positions 0–32 in vocab | Offset from codebook size (4096–4100) |
| **String representation** | Full (every token is a character) | None (raise `NotImplementedError`) |
| **Parent class** | `PreTrainedTokenizerFast` | Plain class (protocol only) |
| **Reversibility** | Exact round-trip | Approximate round-trip |
| **Vocabulary source** | Hand-defined constant | Learned via EMA codebook updates |

This dichotomy reflects a deeper principle: sequence is inherently discrete (nature already tokenizes proteins as amino acids), while structure is inherently continuous and must be discretized through learned quantization. The VQ-VAE acts as a "perceptual codec" for 3D geometry, analogous to how image codecs compress pixel grids into compact codes.

Sources: [sequence_tokenizer.py](/esm/tokenization/sequence_tokenizer.py#L1-L135), [structure_tokenizer.py](/esm/tokenization/structure_tokenizer.py#L1-L84), [esm3.py](/esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L1-L131)

## Tokenizer Assembly and Model Integration

Tokenizers are not instantiated independently in production use — they are assembled via factory functions in `esm/tokenization/__init__.py`:

- **`get_esm3_model_tokenizers(model)`** returns a `TokenizerCollection` containing all six tokenizers (sequence, structure, secondary_structure, sasa, function, residue_annotations) for the specified ESM3 model variant.
- **`get_esmc_model_tokenizers()`** returns only an `EsmSequenceTokenizer`, reflecting ESM-C's representation-only architecture that lacks the structure track.

The `TokenizerCollection` is passed into the `ESM3` model constructor and stored as `self.tokenizers`. During encoding, `esm/utils/encoding.py` uses the appropriate tokenizer from the collection; during decoding, `esm/utils/decoding.py` uses both the tokenizers (for special token ID lookups) and the neural decoders (`StructureTokenDecoder`, `FunctionTokenDecoder`).

The helper function `get_invalid_tokenizer_ids()` extracts the set of token IDs that should be excluded from sampling — for sequence tokenizers this includes mask, pad, CLS, and EOS; for all others it includes mask, pad, BOS, and EOS. These invalid IDs are used during generation to prevent the model from producing special tokens as predictions.

Sources: [__init__.py](/esm/tokenization/__init__.py#L1-L67), [pretrained.py](/esm/pretrained.py#L1-L135)

## Next Steps

Now that you understand how sequence and structure are tokenized, the natural progression is:

- **[VQ-VAE Structure Encoding](11-vq-vae-structure-encoding)** — Deep dive into the geometric transformer, KNN neighborhood construction, and EMA codebook that make structure tokenization work.
- **[Function and Residue Annotation Tokens](12-function-and-residue-annotation-tokens)** — How the remaining four tokenizer tracks discretize functional annotations.
- **[Encode-Decode Pipeline](22-encode-decode-pipeline)** — The end-to-end pipeline that orchestrates all six tokenizers together for protein encoding and reconstruction.

# VQ-VAE Structure Encoding



The VQ-VAE (Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder) structure encoding pipeline is the mechanism by which ESM3 converts continuous 3D protein backbone coordinates into discrete integer tokens, and vice versa. This discretization is the foundation that allows ESM3's transformer core to treat structure as a native token track—alongside sequence, secondary structure, and function—enabling joint multimodal generation. The encoder compresses local backbone geometry into a **4096-entry codebook** of 128-dimensional vectors, while the decoder reconstructs full backbone atom coordinates from those tokens along with confidence metrics (pLDDT, pAE, pTM).

Sources: [vqvae.py](esm/models/vqvae.py#L1-L438), [esm3.py](esm/utils/constants/esm3.py#L13-L24)

## Architectural Overview

The VQ-VAE is architecturally split into two independent networks—**StructureTokenEncoder** and **StructureTokenDecoder**—that share only the codebook vocabulary size constant. This separation is deliberate: the encoder runs once at input time to tokenize coordinates, while the decoder runs once at output time to convert generated tokens back into 3D structure. Neither network participates in ESM3's main forward pass; instead, ESM3 operates purely on the resulting integer tokens through an embedding table.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Encoding["Encoding Pipeline"]
        COORDS["3D Coordinates\n(B, L, 3, 3)"] --> AFFINE["Affine3D\n(N, CA, C → SE(3))"]
        AFFINE --> KNN["KNN Graph\n(k=16)"]
        KNN --> GEO["Geometric Encoder\n2-layer GeometricAttention"]
        GEO --> PROJ["Pre-VQ Projection\n1024 → 128"]
        PROJ --> CB["EMA Codebook\n4096 × 128"]
        CB --> TOKENS["Structure Tokens\n(B, L)"]
    end

    subgraph ESM3["ESM3 Transformer Core"]
        TOKENS --> EMBED["Token Embedding\n(4096+5) × d_model"]
        EMBED --> XFORM["48-layer Transformer"]
        XFORM --> LOGITS["Structure Logits\n→ 4096-way softmax"]
    end

    subgraph Decoding["Decoding Pipeline"]
        DECODE_IN["Structure Tokens\n(B, L)"] --> DEC_EMBED["Token Embedding\n(4096+5) × 1280"]
        DEC_EMBED --> DEC_XFORM["30-layer Transformer"]
        DEC_XFORM --> DIM6["Dim6Rot Head\n→ Affine3D + Backbone"]
        DEC_XFORM --> PAIR["Pairwise Head\nDistogram + Direction + pAE"]
        DEC_XFORM --> PLDDT["pLDDT Head\n50-bin CategoricalMixture"]
    end

    TOKENS -.-> DECODE_IN
    LOGITS -.-> DECODE_IN
```

Sources: [vqvae.py](esm/models/vqvae.py#L179-L322), [vqvae.py](esm/models/vqvae.py#L325-L438), [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L61-L148)

## Encoder Architecture

The **StructureTokenEncoder** transforms raw backbone coordinates into discrete structure tokens through a multi-stage pipeline that prioritizes **local geometric reasoning** over global sequence context. The encoder's design philosophy is that each structure token should capture the local neighborhood geometry around a residue, not the entire protein's fold topology.

### Pretrained Configuration

| Parameter | Value | Description |
|-----------|-------|-------------|
| `d_model` | 1024 | Internal embedding dimension |
| `n_heads` | 1 | Scalar attention heads (geometric attn dominates) |
| `v_heads` | 128 | Vector attention heads for geometric reasoning |
| `n_layers` | 2 | Geometric encoder layers |
| `d_out` | 128 | Codebook vector dimension |
| `n_codes` | 4096 | Codebook vocabulary size |
| `knn` | 16 | K-nearest neighbor count |

Sources: [pretrained.py](esm/pretrained.py#L24-L34)

### Coordinate-to-Affine Conversion

The encoder begins by converting the three backbone atoms (N, CA, C) at each residue into an **Affine3D** rigid body frame. This frame is constructed via Graham-Schmidt orthogonalization: the CA atom defines the translation, the CA→N vector defines one axis, and the CA→C vector defines the plane. Residues with invalid or missing coordinates receive an identity rotation and a "black hole" translation computed from the average of all valid residues in the protein, preventing numerical collapse in the geometric attention mechanism.

Sources: [affine3d.py](esm/utils/structure/affine3d.py#L512-L561), [affine3d.py](esm/utils/structure/affine3d.py#L417-L429)

### KNN Graph Construction and Local Neighborhood Encoding

Rather than applying global attention across the full sequence, the encoder builds a **k-nearest-neighbor graph** (k=16) in 3D space using Cα coordinates.
