The cost is at most 255 extra features in the expanded dimension—a negligible parameter overhead (< 0.3% for d_model ≥ 960) that pays dividends in sustained hardware utilization across training and inference.

Sources: [blocks.py](esm/layers/blocks.py#L10-L12), [rotary.py](esm/layers/rotary.py#L136-L143)

## Where to Go Next

The rotary embeddings and SwiGLU feed-forward networks operate within the broader transformer stack that orchestrates their interaction with geometric attention and layer-level scaling. For the complete picture of how these components are stacked and configured, see [Transformer Stack Design](14-transformer-stack-design). For the geometric attention mechanism that runs in parallel with the standard attention in ESM3's early layers, see [Geometric Attention and SE(3) Invariance](13-geometric-attention-and-se-3-invariance). For the iterative masked sampling procedure that drives generation through these transformer blocks, see [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling).


# Iterative Masked Sampling



Iterative Masked Sampling is the core generation mechanism that powers ESM3's ability to synthesize novel protein sequences, structures, and functional annotations. Unlike autoregressive models that generate tokens left-to-right in a single pass, ESM3 begins with a fully masked input and progressively unmasks tokens over multiple forward passes, guided by a noise schedule and an unmasking strategy. This process mirrors the masked language modeling objective used during training, making generation a natural extension of the model's pretraining paradigm — a design philosophy inherited from the MaskGIT family of image generators, adapted here for the multi-track, multi-modal reality of protein data.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L355-L534), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L292-L326)

## The Iterative Loop: From All-Mask to Fully Sampled

At the heart of ESM3 generation lies the `iterative_sampling_tokens` function, which orchestrates a fixed number of decoding steps. On each step, the model performs a full forward pass over the current (partially masked) protein tensor, computes logits for every position, samples candidate tokens, and then selectively commits only a subset of those candidates based on a schedule-determined budget. Positions that are not selected remain masked and are reconsidered in subsequent steps. The process terminates when all mask tokens have been replaced or the configured step count is exhausted.

The following diagram illustrates the full lifecycle of a single generation call:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input: ESMProtein or ESMProteinTensor<br/>with masked track"] --> B["Encode to ESMProteinTensor<br/>(if raw protein provided)"]
    B --> C["Create all-mask dummy inputs<br/>for unspecified tracks"]
    C --> D["Stack into batched tensor"]
    D --> E{Step t < num_steps?}
    E -- Yes --> F["Forward pass → logits<br/>for ALL tracks"]
    F --> G["Sample candidate tokens<br/>from logits (all masked positions)"]
    G --> H["Compute unmasking mask:<br/>which positions to commit this step?"]
    H --> I["Merge: commit sampled tokens<br/>at selected positions,<br/>keep old tokens elsewhere"]
    I --> J["Update batched tensor"]
    J --> E
    E -- No --> K["Unpack batched tensor<br/>to list of ESMProteinTensor"]
    K --> L["Restore non-sampled tracks<br/>to original values"]
    L --> M["Decode to ESMProtein<br/>(if raw protein was input)"]
    M --> N["Output: ESMProtein with<br/>sampled track filled in"]
```

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L355-L534), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L130-L166)

## How the Unmasking Mask is Computed

The critical decision in each iteration is *which* masked positions to reveal. This is governed by two interacting controls: the **noise schedule** determines *how many* tokens to unmask at step *t*, and the **unmasking strategy** determines *which* tokens among the currently masked ones get priority.

### Step Budget Calculation

On each step, the noise schedule maps the progress ratio `(step + 1) / num_steps` to a fraction of tokens that should remain masked. The difference between the currently masked count and this target yields the number of tokens to sample this round:

```
still_masked = count of currently masked positions
perc_masked_after_this_step = schedule((step + 1) / num_steps)
num_tokens_masked_after = round(perc_masked_after_this_step × total_to_sample)
num_to_sample = still_masked - num_tokens_masked_after
```

A small epsilon (0.1) is added before rounding to avoid off-by-one errors from floating point imprecision — a practical detail that prevents the model from "stranding" a single mask token across many steps.

### Strategy: Entropy vs. Random

Once the budget is known, the strategy decides *which* positions fill it:

| Strategy | Selection Criterion | Behavior | Best For |
|----------|--------------------|----------|----------|
| **`entropy`** | Unmask positions with **lowest** logit entropy first | Commits the most confident predictions early, letting the model condition on them for later, harder decisions | Precise, high-fidelity generation |
| **`random`** | Uniformly random selection among masked positions | Introduces stochastic diversity in the order of commitment, producing more varied outputs | Exploratory or diverse generation |

The entropy strategy extracts per-position entropy from the forward pass output, masks out non-sampleable positions (already unmasked, BOS/EOS, padding), and selects the top-k lowest-entropy positions. The random strategy simply shuffles the masked indices and takes the first `num_to_sample`.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L241-L330), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L226-L238)

## Temperature Annealing

Temperature controls the sharpness of the categorical distribution from which tokens are sampled. ESM3 supports an optional **temperature annealing** mechanism that progressively reduces temperature over decoding steps, transitioning from exploratory sampling early on to near-greedy selection at the end:

```python
annealed_temperature = max(initial_temperature - step_ratio, 0.001) ** 2
```

where `step_ratio = step / max(1, num_steps - 1)`. The quadratic decay means the temperature drops slowly at first and then steeply, allowing the model to lock in coherent local structure before refining details. When `temperature_annealing=True` (the default when using `use_generative_unmasking_strategy`), the per-step temperature overrides the base `GenerationConfig.temperature`.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L350-L352), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L454-L459)

## The GenerationConfig API

The `GenerationConfig` dataclass is the primary control surface for iterative masked sampling. It specifies *what* to generate, *how* to unmask, and *how* to sample:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `track` | `str` | `""` | Which protein track to sample: `"sequence"`, `"structure"`, `"secondary_structure"`, `"sasa"`, or `"function"` |
| `schedule` | `str` | `"cosine"` | Noise schedule controlling the unmasking pace: `"cosine"` or `"linear"` |
| `strategy` | `str` | `"random"` | Unmasking strategy: `"entropy"` or `"random"` |
| `num_steps` | `int` | `20` | Total number of iterative decoding steps |
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | Sampling temperature for the categorical distribution |
| `temperature_annealing` | `bool` | `True` | Whether to decay temperature quadratically over steps |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold (1.0 = disabled) |
| `invalid_ids` | `Sequence[int]` | `[]` | Token IDs to exclude from sampling |
| `condition_on_coordinates_only` | `bool` | `True` | If True, clear structure tokens and condition only on coordinates |

Two convenience methods provide preset configurations:

- **`use_entropy_based_unmasking_strategy()`** — Sets `schedule="cosine"`, `strategy="entropy"`, `temperature_annealing=False`. Produces deterministic, high-confidence outputs.
- **`use_generative_unmasking_strategy()`** — Sets `schedule="cosine"`, `strategy="random"`, `temperature_annealing=True`. Produces diverse, creative outputs.

> [!TIP]
> When `num_steps` exceeds the number of masked tokens, the system automatically clamps it to the mask count — so you can safely set a high `num_steps` without worrying about over-stepping short sequences.

Sources: [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L390-L393)

## Track-Specific Sampling Behavior

Different protein tracks require distinct sampling treatments due to their token structure:

**Integer token tracks** (`sequence`, `structure`, `secondary_structure`) are sampled via `sample_logits`, which applies temperature scaling, top-p filtering, and invalid-ID masking before drawing from the resulting categorical distribution. When temperature is 0, the distribution collapses to argmax (greedy decoding).

**SASA** is sampled as a soft expectation over discretized bins rather than a hard token selection, producing continuous float values. The entropy is computed separately to handle potential `-inf` logits from invalid-ID masking.

**Function tokens** have a multi-dimensional structure `(L, D)` where `D` is the InterPro quantization depth. A special `<none>` threshold (`p_none_threshold=0.05`) gates whether a position receives any function annotation at all — when the average probability of `<none>` across all depth dimensions exceeds the threshold, the entire position is set to `<none>`, suppressing spurious predictions.

**Residue annotations** use multi-hot binary prediction (Bernoulli, not categorical), so they are sampled by selecting the top-K annotations above a probability threshold rather than from a softmax distribution.

**Coordinates and residue annotations** cannot be iteratively sampled — the system returns an `ESMProteinError` if either is specified as the generation track.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L423-L428), [sampling.py](esm/utils/sampling.py#L153-L196), [sampling.py](esm/utils/sampling.py#L199-L237), [sampling.py](esm/utils/sampling.py#L260-L290)

## The Merging Step: Selective Token Commitment

After sampling candidate tokens for *all* masked positions, the iterative loop must decide which candidates to actually commit. This is the **merge step**, implemented as a `torch.where` operation:

```python
new_track_samples = torch.where(
    where_to_sample,   # Boolean mask: True at positions to commit
    new_track_samples, # Candidate tokens from this forward pass
    old_track_samples  # Existing tokens (already committed or still masked)
)
```

This design ensures that previously committed tokens are never overwritten — once a position is unmasked, its value is frozen for the remainder of generation. Only positions selected by the unmasking mask transition from masked to sampled. This monotonic commitment property is what gives iterative masked sampling its coherence: each step builds upon a growing foundation of resolved tokens.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L499-L509)

## Batched Execution and Per-Prompt Isolation

Although the forward pass is batched for efficiency, sampling is performed **per-prompt** because different prompts may have different `GenerationConfig` settings. The system slices the batched forward output, trims logits to the correct sequence length for each prompt, applies per-prompt temperature annealing, and then computes the unmasking mask individually. Errors are tracked per-prompt — if one prompt fails (e.g., has no mask tokens), it is recorded as an `ESMProteinError` and skipped in subsequent steps without affecting other prompts in the batch.

> [!TIP]
> The current implementation asserts batch size 1 within `_get_iterative_sampling_mask_for_prompt_and_step`. When using the local inference client with batched generation, the system processes each prompt individually inside the per-prompt loop, so this is not a practical limitation — but it means the batch forward pass is the only true parallelism; the sampling and unmasking decisions are sequential over the batch dimension.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L410-L509), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L262-L265)

## Practical Generation Patterns

The iterative masked sampling framework enables several distinct protein design workflows through simple configuration choices:

**Sequence design** — Provide a partially masked sequence (using `_` as the mask character) and generate the missing residues. Lower temperature and entropy-based unmasking produce sequences closer to the training distribution; higher temperature with random unmasking explores more novel territory.

**Structure prediction (folding)** — Provide a full sequence with all other tracks masked, and generate the `structure` track. The cosine schedule with entropy strategy typically yields the most physically plausible folds.

**Inverse folding** — Provide coordinates (and optionally set `condition_on_coordinates_only=True` to bypass structure tokens), mask the sequence track, and generate a sequence compatible with the given backbone.

**Chain-of-thought generation** — Generate tracks in a sequence of separate `generate` calls, feeding the output of one as the input to the next. A common ordering is `secondary_structure → structure → sequence`, which lets the model first establish a coarse structural sketch before committing to atomic-level detail.

Sources: [esm3.py](cookbook/snippets/esm3.py#L49-L137), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L432-L438)

## Relationship to Surrounding Systems

Iterative masked sampling sits at the center of ESM3's generation pipeline, consuming logits from the transformer forward pass and producing updated token tensors. The noise schedules that govern its pacing are documented in detail in [Noise Schedules and Unmasking Strategies](17-noise-schedules-and-unmasking-strategies), and the full parameter reference for `GenerationConfig` and `SamplingConfig` is available in [Generation Configuration Reference](18-generation-configuration-reference). The encode-decode machinery that wraps around iterative sampling (converting `ESMProtein` ↔ `ESMProteinTensor`) is covered in [Encode-Decode Pipeline](22-encode-decode-pipeline).

# Noise Schedules and Unmasking Strategies



ESM3 generates protein tracks through **iterative masked sampling**: at each decoding step, the model predicts logits for all masked positions, samples candidate tokens, then unmasks only a carefully chosen subset before proceeding to the next step. Two interlocking mechanisms govern this process — **noise schedules** control *how many* tokens to unmask per step, while **unmasking strategies** control *which* tokens to unmask. Together, they determine the trajectory from a fully masked input to a complete protein, and their configuration has a profound impact on generation quality, diversity, and coherence.

## From MaskGIT to Protein Generation

ESM3's iterative decoding is architecturally inspired by the MaskGIT (Masked Generative Image Transformer) paradigm, adapted to the multi-track discrete token structure of protein data. In MaskGIT, a cosine schedule controls the fraction of tokens remaining masked at each step, and low-confidence positions are unmasked first. ESM3 generalizes this idea: the `GenerationConfig` exposes both `schedule` and `strategy` as independent, composable parameters, allowing developers to decouple the *rate* of unmasking from the *selection criterion*.

The generation loop lives in `iterative_sampling_tokens`, which orchestrates the full decode across `num_steps` forward passes. At each step `t`, the system computes `perc_masked_after_this_step = schedule((t + 1) / num_steps)`, then derives `num_to_sample = still_masked - floor(perc_masked_after_this_step * total_to_sample)`. This means the schedule function maps normalized step progress `[0, 1]` to a *remaining-mask fraction*, and the number of tokens actually unmasked is the delta between consecutive schedule values — positions that transition from "still masked" to "should be unmasked" by this step's schedule target.

Sources: [noise_schedules.py](esm/utils/noise_schedules.py#L1-L34), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L280-L296), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326)

## The Schedule Registry

Five schedule functions are registered in `NOISE_SCHEDULE_REGISTRY`, each mapping a normalized time step `t ∈ [0, 1]` to the fraction of tokens that should remain masked. All functions return `1.0` at `t = 0` (everything masked) and `0.0` at `t = 1` (nothing masked), but they traverse this range with very different curvature:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Noise Schedule Selection] --> B{Which schedule?}
    B -->|cosine| C["cos(t · π/2)"]
    B -->|linear| D["1 − t"]
    B -->|square_root| E["1 − √t"]
    B -->|square| F["1 − t²"]
    B -->|cubic| G["1 − t³"]
    C --> H[Slow start, fast finish]
    D --> I[Constant unmasking rate]
    E --> J[Fast start, slow finish]
    F --> K[Slow start, very fast finish]
    G --> L[Very slow start, very fast finish]
```

| Schedule | Formula | `t=0.25` | `t=0.50` | `t=0.75` | Behavioral Profile |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **cosine** | `cos(t · π/2)` | 0.924 | 0.707 | 0.383 | Few tokens early, accelerating unmasking. Matches MaskGIT. |
| **linear** | `1 − t` | 0.750 | 0.500 | 0.250 | Uniform unmasking rate across all steps. |
| **square_root** | `1 − √t` | 0.500 | 0.293 | 0.134 | Aggressive early unmasking, then refinement. |
| **square** | `1 − t²` | 0.938 | 0.750 | 0.438 | Very conservative early, rapid late unmasking. |
| **cubic** | `1 − t³` | 0.984 | 0.875 | 0.578 | Extremely conservative early, burst at end. |

The **cosine schedule** is the default and the only schedule officially validated for ESM3 generation through `GenerationConfig`'s field validator (which restricts selection to `"cosine"` or `"linear"`). The remaining three schedules (`square_root`, `square`, `cubic`) exist in the registry for experimental use — they can be accessed when constructing configs programmatically or bypassing the validator, but their behavior in the iterative loop has not been officially characterized for protein generation quality.

> [!TIP]
> The schedule function controls the *remaining mask fraction*, not the *per-step unmask count* directly. Because `num_to_sample = still_masked - round(schedule((step+1)/num_steps) * total_to_sample)`, concave-down schedules (cosine, square, cubic) produce few unmaskings in early steps and many in later steps — the model first commits to "easy" positions and leaves "hard" ones for later when context is richer. Convex-up schedules (square_root) do the opposite, which can prematurely lock in uncertain tokens.

Sources: [noise_schedules.py](esm/utils/noise_schedules.py#L1-L34), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L280-L296), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L297-L299)

## Unmasking Strategies: Entropy vs. Random

While the schedule determines *how many* tokens to unmask at each step, the **strategy** determines *which* of the still-masked positions get selected. ESM3 implements two strategies, both operating within the set of positions that are currently masked (excluding BOS, EOS, and padding):

### Entropy-Based Unmasking (`strategy="entropy"`)

The entropy strategy unmaskes the positions where the model is **most confident** first. After each forward pass, the entropy of the logit distribution is computed per position via `torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=log_probs).entropy`. Positions with the **lowest entropy** are selected for unmasking — these are positions where the model's prediction is sharp and unambiguous. This implements a greedy confidence-based ordering: the model "locks in" easy decisions early, providing increasingly rich context for harder positions in subsequent steps.

For the function track, which has a multi-dimensional token structure `(B, L, D)`, entropies are summed across the depth dimension to produce a scalar per position before ranking. The entropy values are masked with `torch.finfo.max` at non-masked positions so they are excluded from `topk` selection.

### Random Unmasking (`strategy="random"`)

The random strategy selects positions uniformly at random from the set of still-masked positions. The masked indices are shuffled via `torch.randperm`, and the first `num_to_sample` indices are chosen. This introduces stochastic diversity into the unmasking order — different runs with the same prompt can produce different generation trajectories, even at temperature 0.

### Comparative Behavior

| Aspect | Entropy Strategy | Random Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| **Selection criterion** | Lowest logit entropy (highest confidence) | Uniform random among masked positions |
| **Determinism** | Deterministic given same logits | Stochastic per run |
| **Generation diversity** | Lower — converges to high-confidence modes | Higher — explores alternative paths |
| **Quality (pTM)** | Typically higher — model commits to coherent structure | More variable — may lock in uncertain tokens early |
| **Use case** | Precise scaffolding, motif-preserving design | Exploratory design, diverse candidate generation |
| **Temperature annealing** | Disabled by default (not needed) | Enabled by default (compensates for random ordering) |

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L298-L330), [sampling.py](esm/utils/sampling.py#L153-L196), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L303-L326)

## Temperature Annealing

Temperature annealing is a complementary mechanism that linearly decays the sampling temperature across decoding steps. The annealed temperature at step `t` is computed as `max(initial_temperature - t / (num_steps - 1), 0.001)²`, producing a quadratic decay toward near-zero temperature. At early steps, the high temperature encourages diverse sampling; at later steps, the low temperature forces near-greedy argmax selection, refining the protein toward its most probable completion.

The annealing schedule is controlled by the `temperature_annealing` flag in `GenerationConfig`. When using `use_generative_unmasking_strategy()`, annealing is enabled with `schedule="cosine"` and `strategy="random"` — the combination of random unmasking order with decreasing temperature allows the model to explore broadly in early steps then converge in later steps. When using `use_entropy_based_unmasking_strategy()`, annealing is disabled because the entropy-based ordering already provides a natural convergence path: positions are unmasked in confidence order, so temperature can remain constant.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Step Trajectory
        S1[Step 0<br/>High Temperature] --> S2[Step t<br/>Decaying Temperature]
        S2 --> S3[Final Step<br/>Near-zero Temperature]
    end
    subgraph Annealed Temp
        T1["T = max(T₀ − t/(N−1), 0.001)²"]
    end
    S1 -.-> T1
    S2 -.-> T1
    S3 -.-> T1
```

> [!TIP]
> The quadratic decay in `_get_annealed_temperature` means temperature drops slowly at first then plummets. For a 20-step generation with `temperature=1.0`, the temperature at step 10 is `(1.0 - 10/19)² ≈ 0.028` — effectively greedy by the halfway point. If you need more exploration in later steps, consider disabling annealing and using a fixed temperature > 0.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L350-L352), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L454-L459), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L309-L326)

## The Iterative Sampling Loop in Detail

The complete unmasking pipeline is orchestrated by `iterative_sampling_tokens`, which processes a batch of `ESMProteinTensor` inputs through the following loop:

1. **Initialize**: Compute `total_to_sample` (the count of masked, non-special tokens) for each prompt. If `num_steps` exceeds the number of masked tokens, it is clamped down.
2. **Forward pass**: Call `_batch_forward` to get logits for all tracks across the entire batch.
3. **Per-prompt sampling**: For each prompt, apply temperature annealing if enabled, construct a `SamplingConfig` with the current temperature, and call `_sample_per_prompt` to produce candidate tokens at *all* masked positions.
4. **Schedule-gated selection**: Call `_get_iterative_sampling_mask_for_prompt_and_step` to compute `where_to_sample` — a boolean mask indicating which positions should be committed this step. This mask is determined by the schedule (how many) and strategy (which ones).
5. **Selective commit**: Use `torch.where(where_to_sample, new_track_samples, old_track_samples)` to blend: positions marked for unmasking take the newly sampled values; all others retain their previous state (either still-masked or previously unmasked).
6. **Iterate**: Repeat for `max_num_steps`, returning completed proteins as soon as their per-prompt step count is exhausted.

The critical blending step at stage 5 ensures that previously unmasked tokens are never overwritten — the model's commitments are irrevocable within a single generation run. This monotonic unmasking property is what makes the process a *schedule-guided refinement* rather than a diffusion-like denoising.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Prompt (masked tokens)
    participant F as Forward Pass
    participant S as Sampling
    participant G as Schedule + Strategy Gate
    participant U as Updated Tokens

    loop For each step t = 0..num_steps-1
        P->>F: Batch forward (all tracks)
        F->>S: Logits for all positions
        S->>S: Sample candidates at ALL masked positions
        S->>G: Entropy per position + num_to_sample from schedule
        G->>G: Select top-k lowest entropy OR random k positions
        G->>U: where_to_sample mask
        U->>P: torch.where(mask, new, old) — commit selected, keep rest
    end
    P-->>U: Fully unmasked protein
```

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L355-L534), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L226-L330)

## Preset Configurations and API Surface

The `GenerationConfig` dataclass provides two convenience methods that set schedule, strategy, and temperature annealing together as coherent presets:

| Preset Method | Schedule | Strategy | Temp Annealing | Intended Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `use_entropy_based_unmasking_strategy()` | `cosine` | `entropy` | `False` | High-quality, deterministic generation. Best for scaffolding and motif preservation. |
| `use_generative_unmasking_strategy()` | `cosine` | `random` | `True` | Diverse, exploratory generation. Best for candidate enumeration and broad design space exploration. |

The default `GenerationConfig` values (without calling either preset) are `schedule="cosine"`, `strategy="random"`, `temperature_annealing=True`, and `num_steps=20`. This matches the generative unmasking preset, reflecting the design philosophy that the default should encourage diversity.

It is worth noting that the `schedule` field validator in `GenerationConfig` only permits `"cosine"` and `"linear"`, even though the `NOISE_SCHEDULE_REGISTRY` contains five entries. To use the experimental schedules (`square_root`, `square`, `cubic`), you must bypass the validator — for example, by directly modifying the attribute after construction or by using `attr.evolve` on an existing config.

Sources: [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326), [noise_schedules.py](esm/utils/noise_schedules.py#L28-L34)

## Interaction with Track-Specific Entropy Computation

The entropy used for the `"entropy"` strategy is computed per-track in `_compute_track_metadata`, which derives it from `torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=log_probs).entropy`. Different tracks produce entropy tensors of different dimensionalities:

- **Scalar tracks** (sequence, structure, secondary_structure, sasa): entropy is shape `(B, L)` — directly usable for top-k selection.
- **Function track**: entropy is initially shape `(B, L, D)` where `D` is the function token depth; it is summed across `D` to produce `(B, L)` before selection in `_get_iterative_sampling_mask_for_prompt_and_step`. The resulting `where_to_sample` mask is then expanded back to `(B, L, D)` to apply uniformly across all depth dimensions of the function tokens.

This depth-aware handling ensures that a function position is unmasked atomically — all `D` sub-tokens at a position are committed together, maintaining the coherence of the InterPro quantized representation.

Sources: [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L298-L330), [generation.py](esm/utils/generation.py#L786-L823)

## Practical Guidance

**Choosing a schedule**: The cosine schedule is the well-tested default. Its slow-start property means the model builds a coarse scaffold of high-confidence positions before filling in details, which mirrors the hierarchical nature of protein structure (secondary structure elements form first, then loop regions). The linear schedule can be useful for debugging or when you want uniform computational budget across steps. The experimental schedules should be approached with caution — `square_root` unmaskes aggressively early, which can lead to incoherent local structure, while `cubic` defers almost all unmasking to the final steps, creating a computational bottleneck.

**Choosing a strategy**: Use `entropy` when generation quality is paramount and you want reproducible outputs (given the same random seed for the initial forward pass). Use `random` when you need to sample the design space and generate diverse candidates. The `random` strategy with temperature annealing is particularly effective for iterative refinement workflows where you generate many candidates and filter by downstream metrics.

**Setting `num_steps`**: The default of 20 steps provides diminishing returns beyond that point. For short sequences (< 100 residues), fewer steps (8–12) may suffice. For very long sequences, increasing to 30–50 steps can improve coherence. The system automatically clamps `num_steps` to the number of masked tokens if you over-specify, so there is no risk of running empty steps.

For the complete parameter reference, see [Generation Configuration Reference](18-generation-configuration-reference). For the broader context of how iterative sampling fits into the ESM3 generation pipeline, see [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling).


# Generation Configuration Reference



ESM3's generation pipeline is governed by two complementary configuration layers: **GenerationConfig** controls the high-level iterative decoding strategy (which track to sample, how many steps, which unmasking schedule), while **SamplingConfig** governs the low-level per-step token selection (temperature, top-p, valid token filtering). Understanding both layers—and how they compose during the iterative masked sampling loop—is essential for steering protein generation toward desired outcomes. This reference documents every configurable parameter, its default, its valid range, and its precise effect on the generation loop.

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L355-L534)

## GenerationConfig — High-Level Decoding Control

`GenerationConfig` is the primary configuration object passed to `client.generate()` and `client.batch_generate()`. It specifies *what* to generate (the track), *how many* iterative decoding steps to take, and *which strategy* determines the order of token unmasking. Every parameter has a carefully chosen default that works well for general-purpose generation, but each can be tuned for specific design goals.

```python
from esm.sdk.api import GenerationConfig

config = GenerationConfig(
    track="sequence",
    schedule="cosine",
    strategy="random",
    num_steps=20,
    temperature=1.0,
    temperature_annealing=True,
    top_p=1.0,
    condition_on_coordinates_only=True,
    only_compute_backbone_rmsd=False,
    invalid_ids=[],
)
```

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326)

### Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Valid Values | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `track` | `str` | `""` | `"sequence"`, `"structure"`, `"secondary_structure"`, `"sasa"`, `"function"` | Which protein track to iteratively sample. **Not** `"coordinates"` or `"residue_annotations"` — those are derived or handled via separate logic. |
| `invalid_ids` | `Sequence[int]` | `[]` | Any list of integer token IDs | Token IDs to exclude from the sampling vocabulary for the selected track. Useful for suppressing specific residues or structural tokens. |
| `schedule` | `str` | `"cosine"` | `"cosine"`, `"linear"` | Controls the *rate* at which masked tokens are revealed across steps. Cosine unmaskes more tokens early; linear unmaskes at a constant rate. |
| `strategy` | `str` | `"random"` | `"random"`, `"entropy"` | Controls *which* masked positions to unmask each step. `"entropy"` prioritizes lowest-entropy (most confident) positions; `"random"` selects uniformly at random. |
| `num_steps` | `int` | `20` | `1` to sequence length | Number of iterative forward-and-sample rounds. Diminishing returns beyond ~20. Auto-reduced if fewer masked positions exist than `num_steps`. |
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | `0.0` to `∞` | Sampling temperature applied at each step. `0.0` yields greedy (argmax) decoding. Higher values increase stochasticity. |
| `temperature_annealing` | `bool` | `True` | `True`, `False` | When `True`, temperature decays quadratically from `temperature` toward `0.001` over `num_steps`. Produces diverse early samples that converge to confident predictions. |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | `0.0` to `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold. Tokens with cumulative probability ≤ `top_p` are retained; the rest are masked to `-inf` before sampling. `1.0` disables filtering. |
| `condition_on_coordinates_only` | `bool` | `True` | `True`, `False` | When `True` and coordinates are provided, structure tokens are cleared so the model conditions solely on 3D coordinates rather than pre-encoded structure tokens. |
| `only_compute_backbone_rmsd` | `bool` | `False` | `True`, `False` | If `True`, only backbone atoms are considered when computing RMSD during evaluation. Does not affect generation behavior directly. |

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L368-L398)

### Preset Strategies

`GenerationConfig` provides two convenience methods that bundle mutually compatible parameter choices into proven configurations. These presets encode architectural insights about how schedule, strategy, and annealing interact—calling them overwrites the relevant fields.

| Method | Schedule | Strategy | Annealing | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `use_entropy_based_unmasking_strategy()` | `"cosine"` | `"entropy"` | `False` | Deterministic, high-fidelity generation. Lowest-entropy positions are resolved first, creating a cascade of confident predictions. Best for structure prediction and refinement. |
| `use_generative_unmasking_strategy()` | `"cosine"` | `"random"` | `True` | Creative, diverse generation. Random unmasking with annealing encourages exploration in early steps and convergence in later ones. Best for *de novo* protein design. |

```python
config = GenerationConfig(track="sequence")
config.use_entropy_based_unmasking_strategy()  # Deterministic refinement
# Equivalent to: schedule="cosine", strategy="entropy", temperature_annealing=False

config = GenerationConfig(track="structure")
config.use_generative_unmasking_strategy()    # Creative design
# Equivalent to: schedule="cosine", strategy="random", temperature_annealing=True
```

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L315-L326)

## SamplingConfig — Per-Step Token Selection

While `GenerationConfig` orchestrates the iterative loop, `SamplingConfig` governs what happens *inside* each step: how raw logits are converted to token selections. It is organized by track, where each track can receive an independent `SamplingTrackConfig`. This is the configuration passed to `client.forward_and_sample()` for power users who want single-step control.

```python
from esm.sdk.api import SamplingConfig, SamplingTrackConfig

sampling_config = SamplingConfig(
    sequence=SamplingTrackConfig(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, topk_logprobs=5),
    structure=SamplingTrackConfig(temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0),
    secondary_structure=None,   # Skip sampling this track
    sasa=None,
    function=None,
)
```

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L337-L366)

### SamplingTrackConfig Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | Softmax temperature for categorical sampling. `0.0` → greedy argmax; `1.0` → standard sampling; `>1.0` → flatter, more random distribution. |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling cutoff. Only tokens whose cumulative softmax probability ≤ `top_p` are considered. `1.0` disables nucleus filtering. |
| `only_sample_masked_tokens` | `bool` | `True` | When `True`, only positions currently holding a mask token are resampled; unmasked positions are preserved. `False` allows resampling of all non-special positions. |
| `invalid_ids` | `Sequence[int]` | `[]` | Token IDs to exclude from the sampling vocabulary. These are masked to `-inf` in the logit tensor before softmax. |
| `topk_logprobs` | `int` | `0` | Number of top-k log probabilities and token IDs to return per position. `0` disables. Maximum allowed is 32 (per-track `MAX_TOPK` constant). |

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L337-L343), [api.py](/esm/utils/constants/api.py#L1-L5)

### Track-Specific Defaults and Constraints

When `iterative_sampling_tokens` internally constructs a `SamplingConfig` from a `GenerationConfig`, it creates a single `SamplingTrackConfig` for the target track and leaves all others as `None`. The default sampling config factory provides baseline settings per track:

| Track | Default `only_sample_masked_tokens` | Default `temperature` | Default `top_p` | Max `topk_logprobs` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sequence` | `True` | `1.0` | `1.0` | 32 |
| `structure` | `True` | `1.0` | `1.0` | 32 |
| `secondary_structure` | `False` | `1.0` | `1.0` | 32 |
| `sasa` | `False` | `1.0` | `1.0` | 32 |
| `function` | `False` | `1.0` | `1.0` | 32 |

The `only_sample_masked_tokens` flag is `False` for `secondary_structure`, `sasa`, and `function` because these tracks use specialized sampling logic (argmax-based for function with `<none>` filtering, threshold-based for residue annotations, continuous-bin expectation for SASA) where resampling all positions is the expected behavior.

> [!TIP]
> Setting `topk_logprobs > 0` for a track returns both the top-k log probabilities and the corresponding token IDs in the `ForwardAndSampleOutput`. This is invaluable for analyzing model confidence and exploring alternative predictions, but increases output size—use judiciously in batched settings.

Sources: [sampling.py](/esm/utils/sampling.py#L109-L131), [api.py](/esm/utils/constants/api.py#L1-L5)

## Noise Schedules — Unmasking Rate Control

The `schedule` parameter in `GenerationConfig` selects a noise schedule function that maps the current step ratio `t = step / num_steps` (a value in `[0, 1]`) to the *fraction of tokens still masked* after that step. The schedule determines how aggressively tokens are revealed during iterative decoding. Although the registry contains five functions, `GenerationConfig` validates against only `"cosine"` and `"linear"`.

```mermaid
quadrantChart
    title Schedule Comparison: Fraction of Tokens Still Masked vs. Step Progress
    x-axis Early Steps --> Late Steps
    y-axis Few Masked --> Many Masked
    quadrant-1 "Slow start, many masked"
    quadrant-2 "Fast start, many masked"
    quadrant-3 "Slow start, few masked"
    quadrant-4 "Fast start, few masked"
    Cosine: [0.15, 0.75]
    Linear: [0.35, 0.55]
    SquareRoot: [0.25, 0.65]
    Square: [0.45, 0.45]
    Cubic: [0.55, 0.35]
```

| Schedule | Formula | Behavior | Generation Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cosine` | `cos(t · π/2)` | Unmasks many tokens early, fewer late | Rapid coarse structure → fine refinement. Default for both presets. |
| `linear` | `1 - t` | Unmasks a constant fraction per step | Uniform pace throughout decoding. More predictable step-to-step changes. |

The cosine schedule originates from the MaskGIT paper and is the default because its front-loaded unmasking aligns well with how ESM3's multimodal predictions coalesce: early steps establish the global scaffold, and later steps refine local details. The number of tokens unmasked at step `s` is computed as `still_masked - round(schedule((s+1) / num_steps) * total_to_sample + 0.1)`, where a small epsilon prevents rounding errors.

Sources: [noise_schedules.py](/esm/utils/noise_schedules.py#L1-L34), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L282-L296)

## Temperature Annealing — From Exploration to Convergence

When `temperature_annealing=True` (the default for the generative preset), the effective temperature at each step decays quadratically from the initial `temperature` toward `0.001`:

```
annealed_temp(step) = max(initial_temp - step / max(1, num_steps - 1), 0.001)²
```

This creates a generation trajectory that begins with high stochasticity (exploring diverse token candidates) and progressively tightens toward near-greedy selection (locking in confident predictions). The quadratic decay means the transition from exploration to exploitation is smooth rather than abrupt.

| Step Ratio | Effective Temp (initial=1.0) | Sampling Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.0 | 1.000 | Full stochasticity — diverse candidates |
| 0.25 | 0.562 | Moderate exploration |
| 0.50 | 0.250 | Narrowing selection |
| 0.75 | 0.062 | Near-greedy — high confidence |
| 1.0 | 0.000001 | Effectively argmax |

When `temperature_annealing=False` (the entropy-based preset), the temperature remains constant at `config.temperature` throughout all steps. This is appropriate when using entropy-based unmasking, because the strategy itself already handles the confidence ordering—positions are resolved from most-certain to least-certain, making annealing redundant.

> [!TIP]
> Setting `temperature=0.0` with `temperature_annealing=False` produces fully deterministic greedy decoding. However, partial temperature 0 (where some positions are 0 and others are not) is not supported and will raise an assertion error.

Sources: [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L350-L352), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L454-L459), [sampling.py](/esm/utils/sampling.py#L185-L189)

## Unmasking Strategies — Position Selection Logic

The `strategy` parameter controls *which* masked positions are selected for unmasking at each step. After the schedule determines *how many* positions to unmask, the strategy determines *which ones*.

### Entropy-Based Strategy (`"entropy"`)

At each step, the model computes per-position entropy from the logit distributions. The `num_to_sample` positions with the **lowest entropy** (highest confidence) are selected for unmasking. This creates a cascade effect: resolving confident positions first provides stronger conditioning for adjacent uncertain positions in subsequent steps.

```python
# Internal logic (simplified):
track_entropy = entropy_forward_output[track]       # (B, L) or (B, L, D)
if track == "function":
    track_entropy = track_entropy.sum(-1)            # (B, L, D) → (B, L)
track_entropy.masked_fill_(~sampling_mask, max_val)  # Exclude non-masked
_, indices = track_entropy.topk(num_to_sample, largest=False)
where_to_sample = sampling_mask & is_top_k
```

### Random Strategy (`"random"`)

At each step, the masked positions are randomly shuffled, and the first `num_to_sample` are selected. This provides no positional bias, which increases output diversity across runs—ideal for generative design where you want to explore the solution space rather than converge to a single prediction.

```python
# Internal logic (simplified):
masked_indices = sampling_mask.nonzero()
shuffled = masked_indices[torch.randperm(len(masked_indices))]
selected = shuffled[:num_to_sample]
```

Sources: [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L298-L330)

## Configuration Composition in the Iterative Loop

The following diagram shows how `GenerationConfig` and `SamplingConfig` compose during `iterative_sampling_tokens`—the core generation routine. `GenerationConfig` parameters are used to derive a per-step `SamplingTrackConfig` that governs each forward-and-sample call.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[GenerationConfig] --> B{temperature_annealing?}
    B -- Yes --> C["Compute annealed temp<br/>for current step"]
    B -- No --> D[Use constant temperature]
    C --> E["Build SamplingTrackConfig<br/>temp=annealed, top_p=config.top_p<br/>invalid_ids=config.invalid_ids"]
    D --> E
    A --> F["schedule → compute<br/>num_to_sample this step"]
    A --> G["strategy → select<br/>which positions to unmask"]
    E --> H["SamplingConfig with<br/>single track config"]
    H --> I["forward_and_sample<br/>single model step"]
    I --> J["Raw sampled tokens<br/>for ALL positions"]
    F --> K["Compute where_to_sample mask"]
    G --> K
    J --> L["torch.where(where_to_sample,<br/>new_samples, old_tokens)"]
    K --> L
    L --> M["Update batched tokens<br/>for next iteration"]
```

The key insight is that `GenerationConfig` parameters are **not** passed directly to the sampling functions. Instead, at each step `t`, the iterative loop: (1) computes the annealed temperature if enabled, (2) constructs a `SamplingTrackConfig` from the `GenerationConfig` fields, (3) wraps it in a `SamplingConfig` for the target track, (4) runs a full forward-and-sample to get predictions for *all* positions, then (5) uses the schedule and strategy to select *which* of those predictions to commit. This means `top_p` and `temperature` from `GenerationConfig` affect the per-step sampling, while `schedule` and `strategy` control the inter-step commitment logic.

Sources: [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L410-L534)

## Unsupported Tracks and Edge Cases

The iterative sampling loop explicitly rejects certain track combinations and handles edge conditions that are important to be aware of:

| Scenario | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `track="coordinates"` | Raises `ESMProteinError(500)` — coordinates are not iteratively sampled; they are decoded from structure tokens via the VQ-VAE decoder. |
| `track="residue_annotations"` | Raises `ESMProteinError(500)` — residue annotations are multi-hot Bernoulli predictions, not categorical, and are derived from the function track logits using threshold-based selection. |
| `num_steps > number of masked tokens` | `num_steps` is automatically reduced to the count of masked positions. No warning is emitted. |
| Input has no masked positions in the target track | Raises `ValueError("Cannot sample {track} when input has no masks.")` — at least one mask token must be present to begin generation. |
| `topk_logprobs > MAX_TOPK (32)` | `validate_sampling_config` emits a warning (or raises if `on_invalid="raise"`). Output is truncated to the maximum. |
| Function track with `invalid_ids` | A warning is issued: `"For function sampling, invalid_ids sampling config is not supported."` The parameter is ignored for function tokens. |

Sources: [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L423-L428), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L390-L393), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L277-L278), [sampling.py](/esm/utils/sampling.py#L133-L150), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L642-L643)

## Practical Configuration Recipes

The following table maps common generation goals to recommended `GenerationConfig` settings. These are starting points—fine-tune `temperature` and `top_p` based on your specific sequence length and desired diversity.

| Goal | Track | Schedule | Strategy | Annealing | Temperature | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sequence from structure | `"sequence"` | `"cosine"` | `"entropy"` | `False` | `1.0` | Inverse folding: use `entropy` for high-fidelity sequence recovery. |
| Structure from sequence | `"structure"` | `"cosine"` | `"entropy"` | `False` | `1.0` | Structure prediction: entropy resolves confident positions first. |
| De novo sequence design | `"sequence"` | `"cosine"` | `"random"` | `True` | `1.0` | Creative: random unmasking + annealing explores diverse sequences. |
| De novo structure design | `"structure"` | `"cosine"` | `"random"` | `True` | `1.0` | Creative structure generation with convergence. |
| High-temperature exploration | `"sequence"` | `"cosine"` | `"random"` | `True` | `1.5` | Broader diversity at cost of local coherence. |
| Low-temperature refinement | `"sequence"` | `"cosine"` | `"entropy"` | `False` | `0.5` | Sharper predictions, less variety. |
| Partial track inpainting | `"sequence"` | `"cosine"` | `"entropy"` | `False` | `1.0` | Mask only specific residues; entropy preserves context fidelity. |

Sources: [api.py](/esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L326), [generation.py](/esm/utils/generation.py#L350-L352)

---

**Next steps**: For the mathematical foundations of the iterative masked sampling loop, see [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling). For a deep dive into how noise schedules control unmasking dynamics, see [Noise Schedules and Unmasking Strategies](17-noise-schedules-and-unmasking-strategies). To put these configurations into practice with the Forge API, see [Forge API Client](19-forge-api-client) or [Local Inference Client](20-local-inference-client).

# Forge API Client



The **Forge API Client** is the remote inference gateway to EvolutionaryScale's cloud-hosted ESM models. It provides a fully-featured Python SDK that mirrors the abstract inference interfaces defined in `ESM3InferenceClient` and `ESMCInferenceClient`, translating every local method call into an authenticated HTTP request against the Forge REST API at `https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai`. The SDK ships three specialized client classes—**ESM3ForgeInferenceClient** for multimodal generative inference, **ESMCForgeInferenceClient** for representation-level inference, and **SequenceStructureForgeInferenceClient** for folding and inverse folding—all built on a shared HTTP transport layer with automatic retry, connection pooling, and both synchronous and asynchronous execution paths.

Sources: [__init__.py](esm/sdk/__init__.py#L1-L37), [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L1-L33)

## Architecture Overview

The Forge client follows a layered architecture where abstract interfaces define the contract, a shared base class handles HTTP transport, and concrete clients implement request/response serialization for each model family. Every public method exists in both synchronous and `async_` variants, and all are decorated with an automatic retry mechanism that handles transient server errors.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Public API Layer"
        A["esm.client()<br/>Factory Function"]
        B["esm.batch_executor()<br/>Batch Context Manager"]
    end

    subgraph "Abstract Interface Layer"
        C["ESM3InferenceClient<br/>generate / encode / decode /<br/>logits / forward_and_sample"]
        D["ESMCInferenceClient<br/>encode / decode / logits"]
    end

    subgraph "Forge Implementation Layer"
        E["ESM3ForgeInferenceClient"]
        F["ESMCForgeInferenceClient"]
        G["SequenceStructureForgeInferenceClient"]
    end

    subgraph "Transport Layer"
        H["_BaseForgeInferenceClient<br/>HTTP POST / Auth / Retry"]
    end

    subgraph "Remote Forge API"
        I["forge.evolutionaryscale.ai<br/>/api/v1/*"]
    end

    A --> E
    B --> E
    E --> C
    E --> H
    F --> D
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H -->|httpx| I
```

The factory function `esm.client()` returns an `ESM3ForgeInferenceClient` by default, reading the API token from the `ESM_API_KEY` environment variable. The `esm.batch_executor()` returns a `ForgeBatchExecutor` context manager for parallel batch workloads. Both the ESM3 and ESM-C clients use **multiple inheritance**—combining their respective abstract interface with `_BaseForgeInferenceClient`—to enforce the full API contract while reusing the HTTP transport.

Sources: [__init__.py](esm/sdk/__init__.py#L9-L23), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L431-L532), [base_forge_client.py](esm/sdk/base_forge_client.py#L10-L33)

## Client Initialization and Authentication

All three Forge clients share a common initialization pattern through `_BaseForgeInferenceClient`. The **token** parameter is mandatory—an empty string triggers an immediate `RuntimeError`. The token is stored as a Bearer credential in the `Authorization` header and attached to every outgoing request.

```python
from esm.sdk import client

# Recommended: token from environment variable ESM_API_KEY
forge_client = client(model="esm3-sm-open-v1")

# Explicit token and custom endpoint
forge_client = client(
    model="esm3-sm-open-v1",
    url="https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai",
    token="your_api_token_here",
    request_timeout=300,
)
```

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `model` | `str` | `"esm3-sm-open-v1"` | Model identifier for the Forge API |
| `url` | `str` | `"https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai"` | Forge server URL |
| `token` | `str` | `""` (reads `ESM_API_KEY` env var) | API authentication token |
| `request_timeout` | `int \| None` | `None` | Per-request timeout in seconds (None = wait indefinitely) |
| `min_retry_wait` | `int` | `1` | Minimum seconds before first retry |
| `max_retry_wait` | `int` | `10` | Maximum seconds between retries |
| `max_retry_attempts` | `int` | `5` | Maximum number of retry attempts |

> [!TIP]
> Always use the `esm.client()` factory for ESM3 models and construct `ESMCForgeInferenceClient` directly only when working with ESM-C models. The factory reads `ESM_API_KEY` from your environment automatically, avoiding the common mistake of passing an empty token.

The base client lazily instantiates `httpx.Client` and `httpx.AsyncClient` on first access, supporting both sync and async usage from the same instance. It also implements the context manager protocol (`__enter__`/`__exit__` and `__aenter__`/`__aexit__`) for proper connection cleanup.

Sources: [__init__.py](esm/sdk/__init__.py#L9-L23), [base_forge_client.py](esm/sdk/base_forge_client.py#L10-L68), [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L66-L93)

## ESM3ForgeInferenceClient — High-Level Endpoints

`ESM3ForgeInferenceClient` is the primary client for ESM3 multimodal generative models. It implements the full `ESM3InferenceClient` interface with six core operations, each available in synchronous and asynchronous variants.

### Generate

The **generate** endpoint is the highest-level API—it accepts either an `ESMProtein` (raw track space) or `ESMProteinTensor` (tokenized space) and iteratively fills the specified track according to a `GenerationConfig`. When called with `ESMProtein`, the client internally calls the `/api/v1/generate` endpoint; when called with `ESMProteinTensor`, it calls `/api/v1/generate_tensor` instead.

```python
from esm.sdk.api import ESMProtein, GenerationConfig

protein = ESMProtein(sequence="_______________")  # 15 mask tokens
config = GenerationConfig(track="sequence", num_steps=20, temperature=1.0)

# Synchronous
result = forge_client.generate(protein, config)

# Asynchronous
result = await forge_client.async_generate(protein, config)
```

The generate method includes a safety guard: if `num_steps` exceeds the sequence length, it is automatically capped and a warning is printed. Additionally, when generating tracks other than `"function"` or `"residue_annotations"`, the input's `function_annotations` are preserved in the output since function token encoding/decoding is lossy.

### Encode and Decode

**Encode** converts an `ESMProtein` in raw representation (sequence strings, coordinate tensors) into an `ESMProteinTensor` in tokenized representation. **Decode** performs the inverse, converting tokenized data back to raw tracks including predicted `plddt` and `ptm` metrics. These are the two halves of the [Encode-Decode Pipeline](22-encode-decode-pipeline).

```python
# Encode: raw → tokenized
protein_tensor = forge_client.encode(ESMProtein(sequence="MKWVTFISL"))

# Decode: tokenized → raw
protein = forge_client.decode(protein_tensor)
```

### Forward and Sample

**forward_and_sample** is the power-user endpoint. It runs a single forward pass through the model and samples tokens according to a per-track `SamplingConfig`. Unlike `generate`, it does not iterate—it performs exactly one forward pass, returning `ForwardAndSampleOutput` with sampled tokens, log-probabilities, entropy, top-k predictions, and optional embeddings. The request uses the `Accept: application/x-es-pickle` header to negotiate efficient binary serialization of tensor data.

```python
from esm.sdk.api import ESMProteinTensor, SamplingConfig, SamplingTrackConfig

sampling_config = SamplingConfig(
    sequence=SamplingTrackConfig(temperature=0.5, top_p=0.9),
    return_mean_embedding=True,
    return_per_residue_embeddings=True,
)
output = forge_client.forward_and_sample(protein_tensor, sampling_config)
# output.protein_tensor  — sampled ESMProteinTensor
# output.mean_embedding  — sequence-level embedding
# output.entropy         — per-track entropy ForwardTrackData
```

### Logits

The **logits** endpoint returns raw model logits and is primarily intended for advanced use cases. The API discourages frequent use because logit tensors are very large. The `return_bytes=True` default enables efficient binary transfer via base64-encoded pickle serialization, which is then decoded client-side using `deserialize_tensors`.

### Batch Generate

`batch_generate` and `async_batch_generate` parallelize multiple `generate` calls. The synchronous variant uses a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, while the asynchronous variant uses `asyncio.gather`. Individual failures are captured as `ESMProteinError` results rather than raising exceptions for the entire batch.

Sources: [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L285-L928), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L291-L428)

## ESM3ForgeInferenceClient — Endpoint Summary

| Endpoint | Sync Method | Async Method | Input Type | Output Type | API Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Generate (raw) | `generate()` | `async_generate()` | `ESMProtein` | `ESMProtein` | `/api/v1/generate` |
| Generate (token) | `generate()` | `async_generate()` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `/api/v1/generate_tensor` |
| Encode | `encode()` | `async_encode()` | `ESMProtein` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `/api/v1/encode` |
| Decode | `decode()` | `async_decode()` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProtein` | `/api/v1/decode` |
| Forward & Sample | `forward_and_sample()` | `async_forward_and_sample()` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ForwardAndSampleOutput` | `/api/v1/forward_and_sample` |
| Logits | `logits()` | `async_logits()` | `ESMProteinTensor` | `LogitsOutput` | `/api/v1/logits` |
| Batch Generate | `batch_generate()` | `async_batch_generate()` | `Sequence[ProteinType]` | `Sequence[ProteinType]` | (parallelized `generate`) |

Sources: [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L621-L928)

## ESMCForgeInferenceClient — Representation Model Client

`ESMCForgeInferenceClient` implements the `ESMCInferenceClient` interface for ESM-C representation models. Unlike ESM3, ESM-C operates exclusively on the **sequence track**—it does not process structure, secondary structure, SASA, or function tokens. This constraint is reflected in its simplified encode/decode/logits implementations.

```python
from esm.sdk.forge import ESMCForgeInferenceClient

esmc_client = ESMCForgeInferenceClient(
    model="esmc-300m-2024-12",
    token=os.environ.get("ESM_API_KEY", ""),
)

# Encode: only sequence is processed
protein_tensor = esmc_client.encode(ESMProtein(sequence="MKWVTFISL"))
# protein_tensor.sequence is populated; all other tracks are None

# Logits: only sequence logits are available
logits_output = esmc_client.logits(protein_tensor, LogitsConfig(sequence=True))
```

| Endpoint | Input Type | Output Type | Tracks Processed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encode | `ESMProtein` | `ESMProteinTensor` | sequence only |
| Decode | `ESMProteinTensor` | `ESMProtein` | sequence only |
| Logits | `ESMProteinTensor` | `LogitsOutput` | sequence only |

Sources: [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L931-L1117)

## SequenceStructureForgeInferenceClient — Folding Endpoints

`SequenceStructureForgeInferenceClient` provides three specialized endpoints for structure prediction and MSA retrieval, independent of the ESM3/ESM-C generation APIs.

### Fold

**fold** predicts 3D coordinates from a protein sequence. It sends the sequence to `/api/v1/fold` and returns an `ESMProtein` with `coordinates`, `ptm`, and `plddt` populated.

### Inverse Fold

**inverse_fold** generates a protein sequence from 3D coordinates—the structure-to-sequence direction. It accepts coordinates as a `torch.Tensor`, an `InverseFoldingConfig` for sampling parameters, and returns an `ESMProtein` with the predicted sequence.

### MSA Retrieval

**_fetch_msa** retrieves a multiple sequence alignment for a given sequence via `/api/v1/msa`. This is a long-running operation (the client prints "Fetching MSA ... this may take a few minutes"). The `|` and `:` characters are both accepted as chainbreak tokens and are normalized internally.

| Endpoint | Sync Method | Async Method | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fold | `fold()` | `async_fold()` | sequence `str` | `ESMProtein` with coordinates |
| Inverse Fold | `inverse_fold()` | `async_inverse_fold()` | coordinates `Tensor` + `InverseFoldingConfig` | `ESMProtein` with sequence |
| MSA | `_fetch_msa()` | `_async_fetch_msa()` | sequence `str` | `MSA` object |

Sources: [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L65-L283)

## HTTP Transport and Request Pipeline

All Forge clients route requests through `_BaseForgeInferenceClient._post()` (synchronous) and `_BaseForgeInferenceClient._async_post()` (asynchronous). The pipeline follows a consistent sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["prepare_request()<br/>Inject auth header<br/>Set return-bytes flag"] --> B["httpx POST<br/>/api/v1/{endpoint}"]
    B --> C["prepare_data()<br/>Check response status<br/>Assemble message<br/>Lift 'data' key"]
    C --> D{"Success?"}
    D -->|Yes| E["Return dict"]
    D -->|No| F["Raise ESMProteinError"]
```

The `prepare_request` method merges the Bearer token into headers and optionally sets the `return-bytes: true` header for endpoints that support binary serialization. The `prepare_data` method checks `response.is_success`, and on failure raises `ESMProteinError` with the HTTP status code and response body. On success, it calls `assemble_message` to parse the response, and lifts the `"data"` key if the response uses Next.js-style nesting. Any `warning_messages` in the response are printed to stderr in red.

> [!TIP]
> The Forge API uses a Next.js-style response envelope where outputs may be nested under `data.outputs`. The client's `prepare_data` method auto-lifts this nesting. If you inspect raw HTTP responses, expect this indirection; the SDK handles it transparently.

Sources: [base_forge_client.py](esm/sdk/base_forge_client.py#L70-L162)

## Automatic Retry Mechanism

Every public client method is decorated with `@retry_decorator`, which wraps the call in a `tenacity`-based retry loop. The decorator inspects the function at decoration time to determine whether it is a coroutine, and applies the appropriate sync or async wrapper.

**Retry triggers** — The decorator retries on `ESMProteinError` exceptions (or return values) with HTTP status codes `{429, 500, 502, 504}`. These correspond to rate-limiting and transient server failures. Client errors (4xx other than 429) are **not** retried.

**Retry timing** — Uses `wait_incrementing` with a configurable start (`min_retry_wait`, default 1s) and maximum (`max_retry_wait`, default 10s), incrementing by 1 second per attempt. The maximum number of attempts is controlled by `max_retry_attempts` (default 5).

**Skip mechanism** — A `ContextVar` named `skip_retries_var` allows callers to disable retries for specific operations, useful in batch contexts where you want to handle failures explicitly.

**Error callback** — On final failure after all retry attempts, `return_last_value` returns the last `ESMProteinError` as a value rather than raising it, matching the client's pattern of returning `ESMProtein | ESMProteinError` unions.

```python
from esm.sdk.retry import skip_retries_var

# Disable retries for a specific call
token = skip_retries_var.set(True)
try:
    result = forge_client.generate(protein, config)
finally:
    skip_retries_var.reset(token)
```

Sources: [retry.py](esm/sdk/retry.py#L1-L86)

## Configuration Data Types

The Forge client relies on several `attrs`-defined configuration classes from `esm.sdk.api`. These are serialized directly into the JSON request body for each endpoint.

### GenerationConfig

Controls the iterative generation process for the `generate` endpoint.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `track` | `str` | `""` | Target track to generate (sequence, structure, etc.) |
| `invalid_ids` | `Sequence[int]` | `[]` | Token IDs to exclude from sampling |
| `schedule` | `str` | `"cosine"` | Unmasking schedule: `"cosine"` or `"linear"` |
| `strategy` | `str` | `"random"` | Token selection strategy: `"random"` or `"entropy"` |
| `num_steps` | `int` | `20` | Number of iterative decoding steps |
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | Sampling temperature |
| `temperature_annealing` | `bool` | `True` | Whether to anneal temperature across steps |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold |
| `condition_on_coordinates_only` | `bool` | `True` | Condition generation on coordinates only |

Two convenience methods configure common strategies: `use_entropy_based_unmasking_strategy()` sets cosine schedule + entropy strategy + no annealing, and `use_generative_unmasking_strategy()` sets cosine schedule + random strategy + annealing enabled. See [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling) and [Noise Schedules and Unmasking Strategies](17-noise-schedules-and-unmasking-strategies) for the underlying theory.

### SamplingConfig and SamplingTrackConfig

Control the single-pass `forward_and_sample` endpoint, with per-track granularity.

| SamplingTrackConfig Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | Sampling temperature for this track |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold |
| `only_sample_masked_tokens` | `bool` | `True` | Only sample at masked positions |
| `invalid_ids` | `Sequence[int]` | `[]` | Token IDs to exclude |
| `topk_logprobs` | `int` | `0` | Number of top-k log probabilities to return |

`SamplingConfig` aggregates five optional `SamplingTrackConfig` instances (sequence, structure, secondary_structure, sasa, function) plus flags for `return_per_residue_embeddings` and `return_mean_embedding`.

### InverseFoldingConfig

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `invalid_ids` | `Sequence[int]` | `[]` | Token IDs to exclude |
| `temperature` | `float` | `0.1` | Sampling temperature (low for deterministic output) |
| `seed` | `int \| None` | `None` | Random seed for reproducibility |
| `decode_in_residue_index_order` | `bool` | `False` | Decode in residue index order |

### LogitsConfig

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sequence` | `bool` | `False` | Return sequence logits |
| `structure` | `bool` | `False` | Return structure logits (not supported on Forge) |
| `secondary_structure` | `bool` | `False` | Return SS logits (not supported on Forge) |
| `sasa` | `bool` | `False` | Return SASA logits (not supported on Forge) |
| `function` | `bool` | `False` | Return function logits (not supported on Forge) |
| `return_embeddings` | `bool` | `False` | Return per-residue embeddings |
| `return_mean_embedding` | `bool` | `False` | Return mean-pooled embedding |
| `return_hidden_states` | `bool` | `False` | Return hidden states |
| `ith_hidden_layer` | `int` | `-1` | Which transformer layer to extract (-1 = last) |

Sources: [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L291-L428)

## Error Handling

The Forge client uses `ESMProteinError` as its unified error type. It subclasses both `Exception` and `ProteinType`, carrying an `error_code` (HTTP status) and `error_msg`. Two error handling patterns coexist:

**Returned as value** — Most high-level methods (`generate`, `encode`, `decode`, `fold`, `inverse_fold`) catch `ESMProteinError` internally and return it as a value from their `ProteinType | ESMProteinError` union. This lets callers inspect failures without try/except:

```python
result = forge_client.generate(protein, config)
if isinstance(result, ESMProteinError):
    print(f"Error {result.error_code}: {result.error_msg}")
else:
    print(f"Generated sequence: {result.sequence}")
```

**Raised as exception** — The transport layer (`_post`, `_async_post`) raises `ESMProteinError` on HTTP failures or unexpected exceptions. The retry decorator catches these and may re-raise after exhausting attempts. Lower-level methods like `forward_and_sample` and `logits` propagate exceptions rather than returning them as values.

The `ESMProteinError` is also used as a validation guard: `_validate_protein_tensor_input` raises `ValueError` if an `ESMProteinError` is accidentally passed where an `ESMProteinTensor` is expected, preventing silent misuse of error results as model inputs.

Sources: [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L286-L289), [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L53-L63), [base_forge_client.py](esm/sdk/base_forge_client.py#L85-L132)

## Data Serialization

The Forge client handles bidirectional conversion between Python objects and JSON payloads. This involves several serialization patterns:

**Tensors → Lists**: `maybe_list()` converts `torch.Tensor` instances to nested Python lists for JSON serialization, with `convert_nan_to_none=True` replacing NaN values with `None` (since JSON has no NaN representation).

**Lists → Tensors**: `maybe_tensor()` performs the reverse conversion, with `convert_none_to_nan=True` restoring `None` values to NaN in the resulting tensor.

**Function annotations**: `FunctionAnnotation` objects are serialized as tuples via `to_tuple()` and deserialized back via the constructor.

**Binary logits**: For the `logits` and `forward_and_sample` endpoints, the client can request binary serialization via the `Accept: application/x-es-pickle` header and the `return-bytes: true` custom header. Binary responses are base64-encoded pickle payloads decoded by `deserialize_tensors`, which is significantly more efficient than JSON for large tensors.

Sources: [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L35-L50), [forge.py](esm/sdk/forge.py#L597-L619)

## Batch Execution

Beyond the per-client `batch_generate` method, the SDK provides a dedicated `ForgeBatchExecutor` context manager via `esm.batch_executor()`. This is designed for high-throughput workloads that need progress tracking and resilience beyond what `batch_generate` offers.

```python
from esm.sdk import batch_executor

with batch_executor(max_attempts=10, show_progress=True) as executor:
    executor.execute_batch(fn, **kwargs)
```

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_attempts` | `int` | `10` | Maximum retry attempts before giving up |
| `show_progress` | `bool` | `True` | Display a tqdm progress bar |

Sources: [__init__.py](esm/sdk/__init__.py#L26-L37)

## What's Next

- **Local Inference**: To run ESM models without network dependencies, see [Local Inference Client](20-local-inference-client) for the offline inference path using `esm.pretrained`.
- **Encode-Decode Internals**: For details on the tokenization pipeline that Forge's encode/decode endpoints invoke server-side, see [Encode-Decode Pipeline](22-encode-decode-pipeline).
- **Generation Theory**: To understand the iterative masked sampling algorithms behind `generate`, see [Iterative Masked Sampling](16-iterative-masked-sampling) and [Generation Configuration Reference](18-generation-configuration-reference).
- **Scale Deployment**: For SageMaker-based batch execution, see [SageMaker and Batch Execution](21-sagemaker-and-batch-execution).


# Local Inference Client



The Local Inference Client enables you to run ESM models entirely on your own hardware—no API keys, no network calls, no rate limits. Both the **ESM3** multimodal generative model and the **ESM C** representation model ship as `nn.Module` subclasses that directly implement their respective inference client interfaces (`ESM3InferenceClient` and `ESMCInferenceClient`), meaning the same `encode` → `generate` → `decode` workflow you use with the [Forge API Client](19-forge-api-client) works identically locally. This architectural decision—models *are* clients—eliminates the need for a separate local wrapper and ensures your code is portable across local and remote execution with zero refactoring.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L181-L184), [esmc.py](esm/models/esmc.py#L44-L53), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L431-L501)

## Architecture: Models as Inference Clients

The central design principle is that every model class inherits from both `nn.Module` and an abstract inference client. This dual inheritance means the model object itself satisfies the client protocol—there is no adapter layer, no proxy, and no indirection. When you call `model.encode(protein)`, the model directly invokes its tokenizers and structure encoder; when you call `model.generate(protein, config)`, it runs iterative sampling on the same object that holds the transformer weights.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Abstract Client Protocols"
        ESM3IC["ESM3InferenceClient<br/>(ABC)"]
        ESMCIC["ESMCInferenceClient<br/>(ABC)"]
    end

    subgraph "Concrete Model Classes"
        ESM3["ESM3<br/>(nn.Module + ESM3InferenceClient)"]
        ESMC["ESMC<br/>(nn.Module + ESMCInferenceClient)"]
    end

    subgraph "Pretrained Builders & Registry"
        REG["LOCAL_MODEL_REGISTRY"]
        LLM["load_local_model()"]
        FP3["ESM3.from_pretrained()"]
        FPC["ESMC.from_pretrained()"]
    end

    subgraph "Sub-Models (Lazy-Loaded)"
        SE["StructureTokenEncoder"]
        SD["StructureTokenDecoder"]
        FD["FunctionTokenDecoder"]
    end

    ESM3IC --> ESM3
    ESMCIC --> ESMC
    REG --> LLM
    LLM --> FP3
    LLM --> FPC
    FP3 --> ESM3
    FPC --> ESMC
    ESM3 -.->|"lazy init"| SE
    ESM3 -.->|"lazy init"| SD
    ESM3 -.->|"lazy init"| FD
```

The `ESM3` class holds lazy references to its sub-models (`_structure_encoder`, `_structure_decoder`, `_function_decoder`). These heavy sub-models are only instantiated when first accessed via `get_structure_encoder()`, `get_structure_decoder()`, or `get_function_decoder()`, which is critical for VRAM management—you can load only what you need and explicitly free memory with `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` between stages.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L181-L258), [esmc.py](esm/models/esmc.py#L44-L98), [pretrained.py](esm/pretrained.py#L114-L134)

## Loading a Local Model

There are two equivalent entry points for loading a pretrained model, both backed by the same `LOCAL_MODEL_REGISTRY`:

| Entry Point | Syntax | Auto-casts to bfloat16 | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Class method** | `ESM3.from_pretrained("esm3_sm_open_v1")` | ✅ (on CUDA) | Recommended — type-safe, concise |
| **Registry function** | `load_local_model("esm3_sm_open_v1", device)` | ❌ (raw model) | When you need float32 or custom device control |
| **ESMC class method** | `ESMC.from_pretrained("esmc_300m")` | ✅ (on CUDA) | Same convenience for ESM C models |

The `from_pretrained` class methods are the idiomatic choice. They auto-detect CUDA availability, load weights from the local data root, and upcast to `bfloat16` when running on GPU—matching the precision the models were trained with. The `load_local_model` function gives you the raw model without dtype conversion, which is useful when you need full float32 precision or want to apply custom quantization.

### Available Local Models

| Model Key | Architecture | Parameters | Tracks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `esm3_sm_open_v1` | ESM3 (small, open) | 1.4B | Sequence, Structure, SS, SASA, Function |
| `esmc_300m` | ESM C | 300M | Sequence (representation-focused) |
| `esmc_600m` | ESM C | 600M | Sequence (representation-focused) |
| `esm3_structure_encoder_v0` | VQ-VAE Encoder | — | Structure → Tokens |
| `esm3_structure_decoder_v0` | VQ-VAE Decoder | — | Tokens → Coordinates |
| `esm3_function_decoder_v0` | Function Decoder | — | Function Tokens → InterPro |

The model name normalization layer handles alias resolution transparently—`"esm3-open"`, `"esm3-open-2024-03"`, and `"esm3-sm-open-v1"` all resolve to the same `ESM3_OPEN_SMALL` key in the registry.

Sources: [pretrained.py](esm/pretrained.py#L95-L134), [models.py](esm/utils/constants/models.py#L1-L29)

## The High-Level API: encode → generate → decode

The high-level API mirrors the [Forge API Client](19-forge-api-client) exactly. You work with two data types—`ESMProtein` (human-readable) and `ESMProteinTensor` (tokenized)—and three core operations that form a complete inference pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    EP["ESMProtein<br/>(raw tracks)"] -->|"encode()"| PT["ESMProteinTensor<br/>(tokenized)"]
    PT -->|"generate()<br/>or forward_and_sample()"| PT2["ESMProteinTensor<br/>(filled tracks)"]
    PT2 -->|"decode()"| EP2["ESMProtein<br/>(predicted tracks)"]
    PT -->|"logits()"| LO["LogitsOutput<br/>(logits + embeddings)"]
```

**`encode(ESMProtein) → ESMProteinTensor`** tokenizes every provided track using the model's attached tokenizers. For ESM3, this includes running the structure encoder (VQ-VAE) to convert 3D coordinates into discrete structure tokens. Any track left as `None` in the input is passed through as `None` in the output—you only pay the computational cost for the tracks you provide.

**`generate(ProteinType, GenerationConfig) → ProteinType`** runs iterative masked sampling to fill in the target track. When given an `ESMProtein`, it internally calls `encode` → `batch_generate` → `decode`; when given an `ESMProteinTensor`, it skips the encoding/decoding steps and operates directly in token space. The `GenerationConfig` controls which track to generate (`track`), the unmasking schedule (`cosine` or `linear`), the unmasking strategy (`random` or `entropy`), and sampling parameters (`temperature`, `top_p`).

**`decode(ESMProteinTensor) → ESMProtein`** is the inverse of encode—it runs the structure decoder and function decoder to convert tokenized representations back to human-readable coordinates and function annotations.

> [!TIP]
> For ESM3, always call `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` between encode/generate and decode stages. The structure and function decoders are large sub-models loaded lazily; freeing the main model's KV-cache before decoding prevents avoidable out-of-memory errors on consumer GPUs.

Sources: [esm3.py](esm/models/esm3.py#L376-L501), [api.py](esm/sdk/api.py#L293-L334), [raw_forwards.py](cookbook/local/raw_forwards.py#L88-L151)

## The Low-Level API: forward, logits, and forward_and_sample

When the high-level `generate` abstraction doesn't give you enough control, the low-level API exposes the raw forward pass and per-step sampling. This is the escape hatch for power users building custom chain-of-thought pipelines, guided generation, or research experiments.

### Raw Forward Pass

The `forward()` method accepts individual token tensors and returns an `ESMOutput` containing logits for **all six tracks simultaneously**—sequence, structure, secondary structure, SASA, function, and residue annotations—plus the embedding tensor.
